g.description: Using an argument aimed at deceiving one's audience.
g.example: Everything rare is expensive. A cheap horse is rare. So a cheap horse is expensive.

g.description: Through a rhetorical or other device, you make sure that the discussion does not proceed as planned.
Targeting the opponent themself rather than challenging their arguments.
g.example: How can you claim that your health policy will work when you have not even managed to quit smoking?

g.description: Directly attacking the individual presenting arguments instead of countering them.
g.example: Don't tell me how to chop garlic. A drug addict is not going to teach me how to feed myself.

g.description: Without even examining an opponent's proposal, addressing them with coarse words aimed at personally injuring them.
g.example: Don't you have anything better to say? Only a fool could be concerned with such trifles.

g.description: A profound lack of respect is demonstrated by an offensive action, here, shoe throwing.
g.example: In the midst of our debate on foreign policy, he suddenly took off his shoe and threw it on the table, claiming my ideas 'stink' as much as an old sole.

g.description: Without even examining an opponent's proposal, addressing them with gestures or words intended to offend them.
g.example: Only someone as ignorant as you could think that's a good idea.

g.description: Seeking to discredit an opponent by wrongfully and publicly attributing to them an act that may harm their reputation.
g.example: It is well known that this company bribes to get contracts. How can you consider their file?

g.description: Mocking one's interlocutor with ridicule instead of discussing their idea.
g.example: At least we'll know who to blame when there's no more coffee due to global warming.

g.description: Mocking the person presenting an argument instead of addressing the argument itself.
g.example: Oh, so now you're the expert, huh? Tell me more about how this works!

g.description: Refusing an argument by criticizing the way it is presented rather than its content.
g.example: As long as you continue with that condescending attitude, I refuse to discuss with you.

g.description: Rejecting an idea by criticizing its origin rather than its content.
g.example: I won't take advice on selecting wine from an American.

g.description: Rejecting an argument simply because it comes from someone with whom one disagrees.
g.example: Your opinion is worthless to me; it's clear you would be against my propositions regardless.

g.description: Not accepting others' perspectives on faith unless they match one's own belief.
g.example: You aren't even part of our church, how can you understand the meaning of our traditions?

g.description: Automatically dismissing arguments coming from outside one's own discourse community.
g.example: Arguments from a philosopher? Thanks, but I'd rather listen to a real scientist.

g.description: Blindly supporting popular causes within one's group.
g.example: Everyone on this forum thinks it's a good idea, so I don't see why you're against it.

g.description: Believing that everyone one dislikes is exactly the same.
g.example: I'm not surprised you agree with him; you're all from that same incompetent party.

g.description: Assuming opposing opinion is incorrect and attempting to explain why the other person is wrong.
g.example: Of course, you're criticizing my budget management because you're just jealous of not being in my position.

g.description: Discarding someone's argument on grounds of his or her lack of achievement in the field being debated.
g.example: How dare you claim that breakfast is the most important meal of the day? Are you a doctor? A dietitian?

g.description: Excessive reliance on credentials, especially academic degrees, of an author in determining the value of their claims.
g.example: No matter what you say about climate change, unless you have a PhD in the field, it's just your opinion.

g.description: Dismissing someone's opinion by accusing them of lacking the minimum social skills, implying they must live with their parents.
g.example: Instead of spouting such nonsense, you'd better get out of your parents' basement and find yourself a job.

g.description: Ignoring a critique by claiming the person is not qualified to make it.
g.example: I will not discuss my economic policy with a career historian.

g.description: Attacking the arguer's self-confidence about their argument in place of the argument or evidence themselves.
g.example: You seem nervous when presenting your project—do you not believe in it yourself?

g.description: Discrediting someone with a compliment that insinuates the opposite of what it appears to express.
g.example: In my view, it is exaggerated to suggest, as some sometimes do, that his line of thought is worthless.

g.description: Arguing against an opponent by highlighting aspects of their background or beliefs to discredit their argument.
g.example: Fred is wrong to claim that prisoners can reintegrate into society, because he is a reformed ex-convict.

g.description: Implying that an opponent is motivated by undisclosed favoritism or affiliation with an external group.
g.example: If you dislike our tax system so much, why don't you go somewhere you think is better?

g.description: Discrediting an opponent's argument by presenting it as biased.
g.example: The journalists from that media outlet are all left-wing, so obviously they won't produce objective reports on right-wing politicians.

g.description: Questioning an argument by suggesting that its proponent may have hidden motives.
g.example: The referee comes from the same village as the opposing team, so it is only natural that he favored them.

g.description: Rejecting an opponent's arguments by declaring them to be in the pay of an agency or organization.
g.example: This scientist cannot be objective in his climate research, as he is funded by the petroleum lobby.

g.description: You attribute the negative qualities of one person or idea to another simply because they have something in common.
g.example: This boy is friends with the most talkative students in the class; he therefore needs to be kept under watch.

g.description: Denying the human qualities of certain people or groups, treating them as inferior.
g.example: This group of people are nothing more than a savage horde, they do not deserve our compassion or respect.

g.description: Attempting to discredit someone by associating them with malevolent images or ideas.
g.example: How can someone who supports an extremist group have a valid opinion on social justice?

g.description: Judging the validity of a proposal based on the identity of its author's community, without considering its merits.
g.example: These ideas about income equality? They can only come from people who have never had to work hard in their lives.

g.description: Belittling environmental protection efforts and rejecting any arguments in favor of it.
g.example: Next thing we know, the environmentalists will have us living in huts and eating grass!

g.description: Discrediting an opponent by falsely associating them with a terrorist organization.
g.example: By refusing to support this war, you're siding with those who don't hesitate to terrorize innocents.

g.description: Attempting to discredit an opponent or excuse oneself by accusing homosexuals of being responsible for various societal issues.
g.example: The influence of certain minorities in our city is leading to the erosion of our family traditions.

g.description: Discrediting someone by groundlessly accusing them of being a communist.
g.example: Only a brainwashed communist could question the merits of our market economy.

g.description: Discarding an argument by unjustly associating it with Hitler or Nazism.
g.example: Your argument about regulation is exactly what Hitler would have said!

g.description: Pointing out inconsistencies or contradictions in an interlocutor, or opposing them with erroneous arguments that may nevertheless seem valid to them.
g.example: To hear you tell it, every purchase is immoral. Yet I saw you shopping the sales the other day, and my morality allows it.

g.description: Attributing fictitious fallacious arguments to an opponent.
g.example: You are trying to manipulate me through emotion and asking me to prove more than necessary. I will not fall for your scheme.

g.description: Portraying an opponent as irrational and overly emotional.
g.example: Your criticism of the lack of diversity in our company seems more like a result of your personal frustration than an objective analysis.

g.description: Rejecting the foundational principle of an opponent's argument.
g.example: You claim that our activity increases CO2, warming up the atmosphere. But you're assuming the very link between human activity and climate that you purport to prove.

g.description: Drawing a grotesque picture of an opponent's thesis in order to criticize it easily.
g.example: Oh, so you suggest we should spend all our days sifting through garbage to sort waste? That's no way to live!

g.description: Drawing a false conclusion from an opponent's thesis by distorting its spirit.
g.example: You criticize train delays; so you want them to depart without respecting the timetable?

g.description: Pushing someone's argument to an illogical extreme to render it absurd.
g.example: You argue that censorship is sometimes necessary, so I suppose you're fine with censoring me right now, aren't you?

g.description: Discrediting the opponent's position by asserting the opponent's failure to act consistently in accordance with that position
g.example: How can we take Jean-Jacques Rousseau's writings on child education seriously when he abandoned his own children?

g.description: Arguing that an opponent has opinions that change with time.
g.example: You were saying that there are too many humans on the planet and now you have two children.

g.description: Redirecting critique by highlighting the opponent's hypocrisy or failure to condemn a similar issue.
g.example: If you care so much about my health, why do you allow him to smoke?

g.description: Disrupting the debate to steer it to one's advantage or to limit its scope.
g.example: Let's move to my office so we can discuss why your request for a raise is absurd.

g.description: Discrediting the other party through prejudicial information in order to weaken their position.
g.example: Should we be reminded that vascular surgery was developed by a Nazi sympathizer?

g.description: Inventing arguments that seem to fit an opponent's logic but are actually fallacious.
g.example: Some say my policy would increase taxes, but what about the healthcare spending it aims to prevent?

g.description: Replying to a weak argument with an equally disputable counter-argument, prioritizing victory over truth.
g.example: You disqualify my proposal for my so-called lack of experience, but shall we talk about your advanced age?

g.description: Offering an opponent an absurd idea, putting them in an uncomfortable position regardless of their response.
g.example: So, if you disagree with the death penalty, would you be willing to release all murderers?

g.description: Attributing one's own flaws to an opponent to divert attention from one's errors.
g.example: It's not surprising that you accuse me of avoiding the subject: after all, that is exactly what someone who lacks arguments would do, like you.

g.description: Denying the abuse committed, then accusing the victim of being responsible for it or of being the aggressor themselves.
g.example: I've never done such a thing. It's actually you who's creating a toxic atmosphere here. By falsely accusing me, you're the one harassing me.

g.description: Advancing objections which, without convincing one's interlocutor, aim to influence the audience.
g.example: You see, this kind of argument is exactly what we would expect from someone who has no real interest in the wellbeing of our community.

g.description: Asking questions that insinuate an accusation to suggest wrongdoing without directly naming it.
g.example: Isn't it strange that all the faulty products come from your workshop?

g.description: Deliberately complicating the discussion to prevent reaching a clear resolution.
g.example: I do not see how we could discuss this topic; in any case, there are far too many variables to take into account.

g.description: Raising minor objections to undermine significant arguments.
g.example: You say walking to the supermarket is healthy, but I don't care because I never go to the supermarket.

g.description: Rejecting realistic solutions by demanding an unattainable ideal.
g.example: I am opposed to the mandatory wearing of seatbelts because this measure does not prevent road accidents altogether.

g.description: Criticizing disproportionately in order to embarrass one's interlocutor and avoid the substance of the issue.
g.example: How can you be absolutely certain that it happened exactly as you describe it?

g.description: Constantly demanding further explanations while avoiding reaching a clear conclusion.
g.example: But why? And where does that information come from? And why should I trust that source?

g.description: Demanding specific expertise to discredit any non-specialist's opinion.
g.example: Unless you are a climatologist, your opinion does not count on these complex issues.

g.description: Considering an interlocutor incompetent if unable to recite specific data or technical details on a topic.
g.example: If you can't quote the latest economic growth statistics, then your views on economic policy are invalid.

g.description: Using a procedure that makes it possible to avoid addressing the substance of the debate.
g.example: That's an interesting question, but let's first look at this broader context...

g.description: Offering a minor pretext to avoid exposing more serious reasons.
g.example: You're a great person, I'm sure you'll find someone better than me to accompany you.

g.description: Explicitly refusing to answer the question posed.
g.example: I am not in a position to answer this question at the moment.

g.description: Attributing to another person or group a responsibility that is actually one's own.
g.example: If we failed, it's because the team was complacent and didn't follow my directions.

g.description: Pretending not to understand the argument in order to avoid responding to it.
g.example: I really don't see where you're going with this 'theory'. It seems so convoluted that I'm not even going to try to understand.

g.description: Questioning the legitimacy of the posed question to avoid answering it.
g.example: This question is based on incorrect assumptions and does not warrant an answer.

g.description: Rejecting or diverting an argument on the basis that it may offend part of the audience's sensitivities.
g.example: Don't look into those people's beliefs. Religion is a matter of conscience and should never be criticized.

g.description: Disqualifying the question being asked on the grounds that it does not accurately represent one's words or stance.
g.example: You are putting words in my mouth that I didn't say.

g.description: Refusing criticism by attributing an error to translation, without addressing the issue itself.
g.example: Your argument might hold up in your language, but in English, it loses all its meaning.

g.description: Challenging the question being asked instead of answering it.
g.example: Why this question? I ask you the same, I'd be curious to know the answer.

g.description: Pretending not to grasp the argument in order to avoid answering it.
g.example: Why are you asking me that? What do you think of the situation?
g.text: Turning the question back on the interlocutor

g.description: Requesting that the question being asked be reformulated and clarified to stall for time or in hopes of dissuading an opponent from insisting.
g.example: Could you clarify what you mean by 'success' in this context?

g.description: Avoiding an opponent's question by means of diversion or distraction.
g.example: Sorry, I have to take this urgent call now, I can't give you more time.

g.description: Refusing to respond to a question by completely ignoring it.
g.example: When I was asked for details about the budget, I simply talked about the project's benefits without giving any figures.

g.description: Acknowledging the posed question without providing a direct answer.
g.example: Your question about the risks of delay is excellent. Now, let me tell you about the benefits of this method.
g.text: Acknowledging the question without answering it

g.description: Overwhelming an interlocutor with a rapid and continuous flow of arguments and claims, making a thorough and thoughtful refutation difficult.
g.example: How can you be competent if you don't even respond to my points on taxation, education, health care, and the environment? And I haven't even started on foreign policy yet!

g.description: Hiding a flaw in one's argument behind large amounts of mostly irrelevant information.
g.example: I got a bad grade, but my marbles were stolen: Jean won the first one, he went to the bathroom, and Sandrine asked me for my snack.

g.description: Providing an answer that is irrelevant to the question posed, pretending to address it.
g.example: This medication has not been approved for sale. Yet, it's been proven it does no harm.

g.description: Failing to say what one really thinks.
g.example: That's definitely an option I hadn't considered, yet you're free to suggest it...

g.description: Introducing an item that distracts from the original subject of discussion.
g.example: Before criticizing me for being late, can you explain why you're walking around dressed like that?

g.description: Wrongly assuming that two different actions have the same moral value.
g.example: Some argue that vehicle speeds should be limited for safety, but opposing space travel because it is risky would be ridiculous.

g.description: Justifying a position because it is held by the majority.
g.example: Most kids ask for fries every day in the cafeteria; that's what we should serve them daily.

g.description: Erroneously believing that combining two wrongs can produce a right outcome.
g.example: The boss doesn't pay his taxes, so I won't feel guilty about taking some cash from the till.

g.description: Arguing by comparing with either the best or worst scenarios to deflect from the actual issue.
g.example: You should already be happy to have received something. Many children don't get that chance.

g.description: Feeling guilty or frustrated because of thinking one should be more grateful in one's current situation, or using this feeling in others to assert control.
g.example: I should be happy to have a job, even though I hate it.

g.description: Opposing a proposition with a false alternative to justify one's point of view.
g.example: Look at how this country struggles with its healthcare system. We should be thankful for what we have in our country.

g.description: Diverting attention by introducing an unrelated topic to avoid addressing criticism.
g.example: Let's instead discuss the importance of developing the economy. We should focus on job creation and economic improvement; that's the most pressing issue.

g.description: Asking a question that lacks relevance to create confusion and divert attention from the real issues of the debate.
g.example: How can we expect the economy to follow the laws of gravity?

g.description: Constantly modifying the bases of one's argument so as not to admit defeat on any one of them and to disorient the interlocutor.
g.example: You're questioning my project management? What about your delay on the report last week? And let's not forget your failure in last month's presentation...

g.description: Avoiding an opponent's victory by preventing them from concluding and altering the course of the debate to one's advantage.
g.example: Allow me to bounce back on what you just said. Isn't it more urgent to debate about the disappearing bees threatening our ecosystems?

g.description: Intentionally diverting attention from significant issues by creating a shocking scandal or controversy.
g.example: My dear compatriots, we will have to postpone the examination of this law, because I have some shocking news to share. Do you know that one of our politicians is involved in a corruption scandal?

g.description: Diverting from the main topic to address a secondary issue, thus shifting the focus.
g.example: Before diving into the effects of this reform on small businesses, let me emphasize the critical importance of supporting education in our country.

g.description: Evading debate by means of preventing a rational argumentative discussion.
g.example: My positions are clear, known to all, and I don't have to debate them.

g.description: Repeating one's point of view insistently instead of providing real evidence or arguments.
g.example: It's obvious our new product will be a global success, there's no need for market research.

g.description: Relies on telling a lie so huge that people doubt it can be false, thinking no one would dare to lie that much.
g.example: We only lost this election due to massive fraud, the scandal of the century that involved complicity at every level.

g.description: Claiming to have won a debate despite the arguments being unconvincing, often ignoring the substantive issues discussed.
g.example: Our army brilliantly executed a strategic retreat after inflicting heavy losses on the enemy.

g.description: Rejecting contrary evidence completely without justification, instead of responding to it.
g.example: What you're opposing me with is a study conducted by people. But my knowledge comes from God.

g.description: You consider the forced absence of a response to an argument to be acceptance, disregarding the ethics of debate.
g.example: Our president wasn't spared during the question and answer session he organized for the new year. However, nobody challenged his decision to continue the war. Thus, it is assumed to be unanimously supported.

g.description: Insisting on the rejection of a well-founded argument, showing an irrational stubbornness.
g.example: You can show me all the studies you want on climate change. I've never been colder in my house than these past few weeks, and that's all that matters to me.

g.description: Denying reality or established consensus to remain aligned with one's personal beliefs.
g.example: COVID is just an invention of our rulers to control our lives and inject poison into our bloodstream.

g.description: Refusing to acknowledge proven historical facts, often for ideological reasons.
g.example: These so-called 'historical facts' are just rumors amplified over time; I only believe what I've learned from our leaders.

g.description: Assigning a particular, often unexpected meaning to terms to support one's viewpoint.
g.example: When I talk about 'freedom', I'm not talking about the absence of constraints; it's the ability to choose among constraints.

g.description: Repeating one's point of view excessively in an attempt to impose it, without responding to objections.
g.example: Dairy products are our friends for life. They are great for your health. Furthermore, they are really good for us. They keep us in shape.

g.description: So fixated on a notion that it's constantly repeated, disregarding ongoing discussions.
g.example: Let's not let this distract us from our main goal: Carthage must be destroyed.

g.description: Employing a combination of intense repetition and psychological manipulation to influence or drastically change an individual's views and beliefs.
g.example: I know you're skeptical, but just think about it every night before you sleep, and you'll see that my theory is the only one that makes sense.

g.description: You speak so quickly that your audience does not have time to understand your arguments or identify their flaws.
g.example: So, I divide by 5, move x to the other side, square the whole thing, take the hyperbolic tangent, and end up at the same result. You got all that?

g.description: Speaking extremely fast to present as many arguments as possible in the least amount of time, making it hard for the opponent to respond to all points.
g.example: My opponent should now answer my arguments about various economic, social, and environmental policies, covering implications in the short and long term, impacts on vulnerable populations, geopolitical considerations, and legal and ethical aspects.

g.description: Using overly complex definitions that obscure rather than clarify what is being said.
g.example: You say that ether is responsible for this phenomenon. But what is ether? It is a subtle and invisible body.

g.description: Distorting the debate by pretending to explain facts or concepts.
g.example: No matter what your arguments are: the real explanation is that we do not need this product. Everyone knows it.

g.description: Attempting to explain a phenomenon that, in reality, does not occur.
g.example: The reason billions of children die of hunger every year is because we live in a world that doesn't care.

g.description: Basing an argument on incorrect or undemonstrated assumptions.
g.example: The reason why most singles are shy is that their mothers were overbearing.

g.description: Explaining only an isolated situation without considering its connections with other elements.
g.example: People suffer from schizophrenia because their brains start to malfunction.

g.description: Failing to engage with the underlying causes of a phenomenon, thus resorting to superficial assertions.
g.example: My dog goes through our garbage because, well, that's just what dogs do.

g.description: Dismissively rejecting a proposition without offering any explanation or evidence.
g.example: What you're saying can't be true because it sounds utterly absurd.

g.description: Disregarding parts of the opposing argument as unimportant.
g.example: Let's not dwell on the details of the deal. What matters is that we move forward.

g.description: You make a claim that is impossible to confirm or refute, preventing any rational exchange.
g.example: An inner voice ordered me to do that…

g.description: Presenting a claim that cannot be empirically tested, thus making it beyond dispute.
g.example: Because my horoscope warned me, I was able to avoid the disaster it predicted.

g.description: Proposing an argument that remains unchallenged regardless of objections, as it evades all justification.
g.example: Whatever happens was meant to be; there's no arguing with fate.

g.description: Claiming that truth is subjective and specific to each individual.
g.example: That may be true for you, but it isn't true for me.

g.description: Equating errors of different severity as being identical in nature.
g.example: He may have sped through a red light, but you jaywalked. You're both in the wrong.

g.description: Claiming that a particular idea is true for others but not for oneself, thereby avoiding applying it to oneself.
g.example: Yes, smoking is bad for health, but not for me.

g.description: Claiming that one's opinion holds as much weight as a proven fact, without the need for justification.
g.example: I believe these medicines are more harmful than beneficial. Everyone's entitled to their opinion, after all.

g.description: Asserting something is true because it feels true personally, regardless of the absence of concrete evidence.
g.example: I don't need statistics to know climate change is a myth: I can see it for myself.

g.description: Violating the norms of rational debate
Arguing under the influence of a cognitive bias, which hinders the ability to reason in a balanced manner.
g.example: To me, all the members of this group look alike; how do they recognize one another?

g.description: Reasoning on the basis of the strict, exclusive application of theoretical concepts.
g.example: In cooking, only olive oil is really worth using. So I make my pastries without butter.

g.description: Adopting unproven beliefs or principles that serve one's interests or argumentative purposes.
g.example: If I didn't delve deeper into my analysis, it's because I operate under the assumption that truth always emerges in a straightforward manner.

g.description: You assume that a person's perceptual anomalies similarly influence their interactions with the world.
g.example: The painter, being shortsighted, depicted his subjects with blurred edges to represent how he sees the world.

g.description: Assuming that because things are typically bundled together, they must always be bundled together.
g.example: Without their costumes and traditional stage settings, opera singers couldn't convey the emotions of their art as well.

g.description: The belief that the world is inherently fair and that people ultimately get what they deserve.
g.example: If that man is living on the streets, it must be because he mishandled his life; you reap what you sow.

g.description: Arguing that events happening in a virtual setting have no real-world consequences.
g.example: He just posted those insults online, it doesn't count in real life.

g.description: Claiming that something, if not making sense in a literal or rational way, is in fact, spiritual.
g.example: But all the Holy Scriptures contain horrors. They should be read in a spiritual way to see the truth of the spirit.

g.description: Adhering to ideas or theories that seem profound or significant but lack scientific or logical foundation.
g.example: The vibrations from these crystals will cleanse your aura.

g.description: Using logic or rationality in a way that appears correct on the surface, but is fundamentally wrong or misleading.
g.example: Based on rational analysis, I concluded that our company should invest heavily in this new technology. This is the market trend, and all the data indicates that it will only grow.

g.description: Displaying an attitude of skepticism while actually rejecting new information or evidence without objective examination.
g.example: These new scientific theories can't be true; I remain skeptical regardless of the evidence.

g.description: Presenting or adhering to beliefs or practices that are presented as scientific, but which lack empirical evidence or rigorous scientific methodology.
g.example: This healing method is said to have miraculous effects, demonstrated by very modern methods.

g.description: Arguing from a reference to quantum physics to justify a lack of reasoning.
g.example: Since quantum physics allows for strange phenomena on the micro scale, my dreams of intersidereal space travel could finally become reality.

g.description: Using jargon or concepts that seem deep or philosophical, but are actually vague, insubstantial, or devoid of practical meaning.
g.example: When a problem arises, I see it as a spiritual growth opportunity rather than looking for practical solutions.

g.description: Adhering strictly and literally to a set of core principles, often with an hostile view of other perspectives.
g.example: All our traditions must be respected to the letter, because they have always guided our community.

g.description: Showing rigid loyalty and adherence to a specific group or ideology, often accompanied by hostility toward other groups.
g.example: Our group holds the absolute truth, and those who are not with us are against us.

g.description: You join or defend an organization or movement characterized by extreme or unconventional beliefs or practices.
g.example: This community has shown me the true meaning of life.

g.description: Adopting or defending ideas, attitudes or actions that are extreme or radical, often in defiance of the accepted social norm.
g.example: To achieve our vision, we must go beyond the limits accepted by society.

g.description: Justifying or participating in the use of violence and intimidation, especially against civilians, for political or ideological purposes.
g.example: Our radical actions are necessary to draw attention to our cause and provoke change.

g.description: Showing excessive zeal or passion for a cause or ideology, often without consideration for differing opinions.
g.example: My cause is the only just one, and I am ready to do anything to defend it, even against those who don't understand it.

g.description: Advocating fundamental or extreme changes in the political or social structure, often without consideration of the consequences.
g.example: We must overturn the established order to build a completely new and fair society.

g.description: Favoring strict control and unquestioning obedience to authority, often at the expense of individual freedom.
g.example: Following our leaders' orders without question is crucial to maintaining order.

g.description: Supporting an authoritarian and centralized political system that tolerates no opposition or criticism.
g.example: A strong government controlling every aspect of society is necessary to maintain order and security.

g.description: Reasoning from an unquestionable and irrefutable belief, without considering contrary evidence.
g.example: The company has always favored this technology, so there's no point in considering other options on the market.

g.description: Believing that reality is entirely mental or spiritual, and that the material world is an illusion.
g.example: The external world is just a projection of my mind; nothing truly exists outside my own consciousness.

g.description: Thinking that only one's own mind is certain to exist, doubting the existence of the outside world or other minds.
g.example: I can only be sure of my own existence; everything else could be just an illusion.

g.description: Adhering to the belief that there is a vital force beyond physical and chemical processes, necessary for life.
g.example: There is a special life force that differentiates living beings from inanimate matter.

g.description: Believing that the only reality is matter and that all phenomena, including consciousness, can be explained by material processes.
g.example: The mind and consciousness are merely products of physical brain activity.

g.description: Believing that science is the ultimate source of knowledge and is superior to other forms of understanding or knowledge.
g.example: Only scientific explanations can be considered true. Other forms of knowledge are inferior.

g.description: Relying solely on experience and observation to understand the world, rejecting any theory or speculation.
g.example: If I can't see it or measure it, then it doesn't exist.

g.description: Supporting an approach that combines empiricism and formal logic, asserting that the meaning of a proposition is its method of verification.
g.example: A statement is meaningful if and only if it can be logically or empirically verified.

g.description: Adhering to an approach that attributes all human behavior to the environment and external stimuli, neglecting internal factors such as thoughts and emotions.
g.example: When my colleague got angry in the meeting, it was clearly because of the noise and surrounding stress.

g.description: Believing that the only realities are phenomena as they are perceived, rejecting the existence of an objective reality independent of perception.
g.example: The world only exists in my perception; nothing is real outside of what I can perceive.

g.description: Adhering to an approach that systematically reduces phenomena to simpler components, neglecting emergent aspects.
g.example: All human behavior can be explained solely by biology and genetics.

g.description: Adhering to the philosophy that the only true knowledge is that obtained through positive sciences, rejecting metaphysics.
g.example: Only empirically verifiable statements have meaning; metaphysical questions are meaningless.

g.description: Encapsulating oneself within the logic of one's own language, viewing it as a reference model while neglecting the complexity and nuances that exist beyond language.
g.example: We always analyze our experiences in terms of linguistic categories, therefore anything that cannot be clearly expressed in words is not truly meaningful.

g.description: Assessing and interpreting the world mainly from a human-centered perspective, often overlooking the needs and perspectives of other species and the environment.
g.example: It's just a forest, we can clear it for development. After all, human needs come first.

g.description: Emphasizing the freedom and autonomy of the individual, often downplaying the role of society or community.
g.example: Everyone is the master of their own destiny and should only rely on their own efforts to succeed.

g.description: Adhering to a philosophy that emphasizes the importance of objectivity and reason, sometimes at the expense of compassion or empathy.
g.example: Personal emotions and feelings should not interfere in rational decision-making.

g.description: Having one's positions influenced by one's cultural context.
g.example: Those people are to be pitied: they have neither a television nor a car...

g.description: You argue from a subjective point of view without clearly distinguishing it from an objective judgment.
g.example: This work of art does not deserve to be exhibited here: I do not find it beautiful.

g.description: Categorizing and treating money differently depending on its source or intended use.
g.example: I easily spend my bonus because I consider it 'extra' money.

g.description: Overestimating or underestimating the real value of money based on non-economic factors or without accounting for inflation..
g.example: Since this product costs €11, I am more cautious about how I use it.

g.description: Underestimating the total sum by assessing its parts individually.
g.example: I spend more buying items separately than if I had estimated their total cost.

g.description: Evaluating an option as better when considered in isolation as opposed to when compared directly with other options.
g.example: I prefer a small, elegantly wrapped gift to a larger, less well presented gift.

g.description: Spending smaller denominations more easily than larger sums.
g.example: I mindlessly spend coins but think twice before breaking a bill.

g.description: Being influenced by others' suggestions or expectations, altering one's memories or perceptions.
g.example: When someone suggests that I may have forgotten something, I begin to doubt my memory.

g.description: Perceiving a statement as more accurate if it rhymes or has a rhythmic flow.
g.example: Rhyming phrases resonate with us, such as 'What is clearly conceived is clearly stated.'

g.description: Tending to adopt more extreme or riskier positions in a group than individually.
g.example: In the meeting, the group leaned towards a bolder strategy than what individual members might have chosen on their own.

g.description: Adopting beliefs or behaviors simply because they are popular or widely accepted.
g.example: Everyone uses this app, so I downloaded it too.

g.description: Perceiving people as more attractive when they are in a group than when they are alone.
g.example: People seem more attractive in a group than when they are alone.

g.description: Letting a person's positive quality influence one's overall judgment of that person.
g.example: Because he's attractive, I guess he's also smart and kind.

g.description: Giving more credibility or trust to the opinions or statements of authorities or experts.
g.example: If this renowned scientist says it, then it must be true.

g.description: Evaluating oneself by comparing oneself to others, with envy or by viewing oneself favorably.
g.example: I'm smarter than most of my colleagues.

g.description: Responding or acting in a way to be favorably viewed by others.
g.example: I say that I attach great importance to recycling in order to appear eco-responsible.

g.description: Altering or creating false memories in response to misleading information.
g.example: After hearing a misleading version of an event, I begin to doubt my own memory.

g.description: Presenting certain traits or characteristics as natural and inherent to groups or categories.
g.example: Women are naturally more empathetic than men.

g.description: Struggling to conceive uses for an object beyond its usual function.
g.example: I would never have thought of using this object as a paperweight.

g.description: Interpreting and judging the world primarily through the lens of one's own culture, influencing the perception of and interaction with other cultures.
g.example: I do not understand their ways of doing things in that country; our methods are simply more civilized and more effective.

g.description: The preference for cultural practices of other cultures over those of one's own society.
g.example: I only buy imported products. Local products just don't measure up.

g.description: Adopting or using elements from a foreign culture, often without a deep understanding or ignoring their original cultural context.
g.example: I decided to wear this traditional Asian attire to the party because I find it aesthetically beautiful, even though I don't really know its cultural significance.

g.description: Idealizing cultures perceived as "less developed" or "closer to nature", often in a simplistic and romantic way.
g.example: I dream of living in a distant tribe, far from the complexity of modern life. Life there is so much more authentic and pure.

g.description: Avoiding or denying the realities of one's own culture or environment by immersing oneself in a different culture or context.
g.example: I spend all my time watching shows from faraway countries to forget how boring my life is here.

g.description: Fascination or obsession with certain racial characteristics, often perceived as exotic or superior.
g.example: I only date people of a certain race because I find them so much more attractive than others.

g.description: Adopting an excessively favorable view towards the interests or culture of an external group
g.example: We must understand the cultural and historical context that led this country to this decision. It's important to maintain stable diplomatic relations.

g.description: Exhibiting an excessive admiration for certain foreign cultures, often while disparaging one's own culture.
g.example: I'm so enamored with European culture and lifestyle that I find our local way of life dull and less sophisticated by comparison.

g.description: Feeling admiration or affection for groups different from one's own, to the point of biasing one's judgment.
g.example: I am fascinated by their culture; I would very much like to be like them.

g.description: Experiencing a sense of inferiority about one's own culture compared with those of other countries.
g.example: The music of our country is not as refined as the music we import.

g.description: Experiencing repulsion or aversion towards one's own culture or environment.
g.example: I don't really like our local traditions, I prefer those of other countries.

g.description: Treating people differently or unfairly because of certain personal or social characteristics.
g.example: I don't think this person is suitable for the position due to their age.

g.description: Discriminating against people based on their age.
g.example: I doubt he will be able to understand new technologies, given his age.

g.description: Judging people primarily based on their physical appearance.
g.example: She doesn't really look like a leader, don't you think?

g.description: Holding biases against people based on their size or weight.
g.example: I don't think she's cut out for this role, she doesn't have the required figure.

g.description: Building and perpetuating prejudices concerning social class membership.
g.example: People from your class prefer buying yachts over saving the planet.

g.description: Using rhetoric that mobilizes the population against an elite perceived as corrupt or out of touch, often by simplifying complex issues.
g.example: The elites don't understand the real problems of the people. Only a true change can put them in their place.

g.description: Arguing and maintaining prejudices of a religious nature.
g.example: If they want to practice their religion of hate, they should do it back in their country.

g.description: Arguing and perpetuating biases based on national identity.
g.example: Our empire was the greatest and most just; it's because we are an exceptional nation.

g.description: Your argument relies on and perpetuates prejudices related to sex or gender.
g.example: The team has been failing because of the female director; it's well known that women can't manage.

g.description: Viewing romantic relationships as the societal norm to follow.
g.example: It's strange that at his age he's still single. Something must be missing.

g.description: Viewing heterosexuality as the norm, excluding other sexual orientations.
g.example: It's normal for a girl to want a boyfriend, not a girlfriend.

g.description: Assuming the existence of races within the human species, some of which are superior to others.
g.example: The main problems in our country come from this ethnic group; they will never truly be able to integrate.

g.description: Relying on generalized, often simplistic beliefs about the characteristics of a group of people.
g.example: I assume that all engineers communicate poorly with others.

g.description: Forming automatic judgments and attitudes towards people or groups without being aware of it.
g.example: Without realizing it, I have different expectations of people depending on their social or ethnic group.

g.description: Attributing the actions or behaviors of an individual to the perceived characteristics of the group they belong to.
g.example: He did something wrong, that's typical of people in his company.

g.description: Incorrectly attributing the causes of behaviors or events, often underestimating the impact of external circumstances.
g.example: When my coworker missed his deadline, I immediately thought he was lazy, never mind the family emergencies he had to deal with.

g.description: Assuming that big effects must have big causes, which is not always the case.
g.example: I can't believe such a massive disaster was caused by something as minor as an oversight.

g.description: Believing that criticism or persecution of one's ideas proves their validity.
g.example: They say my methods are unconventional, but they're conformists, and I'm a maverick. This proves I'm right.

g.description: Attributing an outcome to specific causes when it might just be a return to statistical average.
g.example: After 11 days of being sick, I drank this peach tea, and it cured my flu.

g.description: Adhering to simplistic conspiracy theories to explain complex events.
g.example: This political group is in the pay of the Freemasons; that is the only possible explanation for their controversial decisions.

g.description: Suggesting a series of events is secretly orchestrated by a hidden group.
g.example: The recent foreign policy decision is said to have been influenced by a group of hidden investors seeking to profit from the situation.

g.description: Attributing failures to external causes outside of one's group and successes to the group's inherent qualities.
g.example: It's not your team's fault the project failed; the competition played dirty.

g.description: Perceiving members of an external group as more similar to each other than members of one's own group.
g.example: People in this town all seem to think the same way. They are not as diverse as us.

g.description: Having difficulty recognizing and differentiating faces of people from a race different from one's own.
g.example: I find it more difficult to distinguish the faces of people of a different race than myself.

g.description: Expressing an inflated sense of pride and superiority for a group to which one belongs, often coupled with depreciating other groups.
g.example: Our nation is undoubtedly the greatest of all, and those who don't recognize this are either ignorant or jealous.

g.description: Preferring members of one's own group over those from an external one.
g.example: Our local team is the best. The other teams win only because of biased referees.

g.description: Suggesting that one's community alone holds the truth, discounting external perspectives.
g.example: Our traditions and teachings are the only true source of wisdom on this matter.

g.description: Assuming that the opposition must agree with one's conclusion from the outset, falsely setting the stage for the argument.
g.example: If you don't accept my explanation, then you're simply part of the problem.

g.description: Rejecting ideas, research, or products not developed within one's own group or organization.
g.example: If this idea didn't come from our team, it definitely isn't good.

g.description: Assigning less value to an offer or proposal simply because it comes from an adversary or rival.
g.example: Any proposal from this competing company is automatically suspect.

g.description: Attributing one's own actions to situational factors, but others' actions to their personality.
g.example: I'm late because of traffic, but if he's late, it's because he's lazy.

g.description: Attributing unpredictable variable characteristics to oneself and others based on observed behaviors.
g.example: She smiled; she must be a happy person.

g.description: Attributing lucky outcomes to one's own merits or skills.
g.example: I achieved success through my hard work

g.description: Falsely attributing one's own actions or decisions to external forces or agents.
g.example: I didn't really choose this career; It's as if circumstances pushed me to it.

g.description: Attributing behavior to internal characteristics rather than external circumstances.
g.example: He's late because he's lazy. He knew how important this meeting was.

g.description: Interpreting ambiguous actions of others as hostile, even in the absence of concrete evidence.
g.example: When someone bumped into me on the subway, I immediately thought they were doing it on purpose to annoy me.

g.description: You assign responsibility to the person concerned in order to convince yourself that you would not experience a similar situation.
g.example: He probably didn’t steal it if he finds himself in this situation.

g.description: Overemphasizing personal characteristics in explaining someone's behavior while underestimating situational factors.
g.example: When people work well, they earn enough money.

g.description: Having arguments reflect the limits and reflexes tied to the human perspective.
g.example: Nature is so wise that it made a river run through every city.

g.description: Allowing one's judgment and reasoning to be swayed by current emotions.
g.example: If they want war, they'll get it. I won't let myself be intimidated by these grand theories.

g.description: Centering oneself in one's thoughts and perceptions.
g.example: Everyone must be interested in my new project.

g.description: Having an excessively positive view of oneself.
g.example: I am clearly the most intelligent and competent member of my team.

g.description: Assuming one's perspective of the world to be the exact reflection of reality.
g.example: In these times of great uncertainty for our company, it seems inconceivable to me that you could refuse this pay cut.

g.description: Having difficulty adopting an appropriate perspective towards others.
g.example: I think I didn't behave as they expected.

g.description: Assigning personal responsibility, including praise or blame, for events over which one has little or no control.
g.example: It's my fault the meeting went poorly.

g.description: Feeling the need to constantly prove that one's opinions and actions are correct.
g.example: I must win this argument to show I'm right.

g.description: Expecting others to change to meet one's needs and desires, often involving social control.
g.example: If my partner really loved me, they would change for me.

g.description: Attributing one's own flaws to one's opponent to divert attention from one's errors.
g.example: It's not surprising that you think I'm dodging the issue; after all, that's exactly what someone who lacks arguments, like you, would do.

g.description: Blaming oneself for a misfortune for which one is not responsible.
g.example: I knew I shouldn't have been in that neighborhood so late at night. It's my fault I got mugged.

g.description: Holding the victim responsible for the harm they have suffered.
g.example: You were wearing a mini-skirt that night? And you admit you had too much to drink?

g.description: Attributing to another person or group a responsibility that is actually one's own.
g.example: If we failed, it's because the team was careless and failed to follow my directions.

g.description: Giving more weight to information that confirms one's existing beliefs.
g.example: I mostly read articles that support my political point of view.

g.description: Allowing oneself to act against one's principles or values after performing a positive or moral act.
g.example: After donating to charity, I feel less guilty about making selfish purchases.

g.description: Assessing the strength of an argument based on the belief in its conclusion.
g.example: I completely agree with what you say and I find it hard to believe that things could be presented any other way.

g.description: Judging a decision based on its outcome rather than the information available at the time of the decision.
g.example: After all, it wasn't such a bad decision, was it?

g.description: Believing a piece of information to be true because it has personal meaning to one.
g.example: This horoscope must be true, it describes exactly what I feel.

g.description: Underestimating the likelihood of negative events if they haven't occurred recently.
g.example: An earthquake here? It never happens, I don't worry.

g.description: Avoiding negative or threatening information.
g.example: I don't like reading the news because it's too depressing.

g.description: Modifying one's memories to be consistent with current beliefs.
g.example: I remember always supporting this cause, although in reality my opinions have changed over time.

g.description: Justifying one's past choices to make them appear better.
g.example: I chose this car because it has always been reliable.

g.description: Valuing something more highly simply because one already owns it.
g.example: I don't want to sell this old piece of furniture; it has great sentimental value to me.

g.description: After an event, you believe that you had predicted or expected that outcome.
g.example: I told you it was a bad idea.

g.description: Current emotional state influencing the retrieval of memories with a similar emotional state.
g.example: When I'm sad, I more easily remember times when I was also sad.

g.description: Valuing a result more when one has worked hard for it.
g.example: I appreciate my degree more because I had to work hard to get it.

g.description: Tendency to sell winning assets too soon and hold onto losing assets too long.
g.example: I'm keeping these stocks in losses, hoping they'll come back one day.

g.description: Continuing a futile action because one has already invested time, money, or effort.
g.example: I'm finishing this boring book because I've already read half of it.

g.description: Valuing things more highly because one has invested time and effort into them.
g.example: I love this shelf that I put together myself, even though it's not perfect.

g.description: Finding more value in information that is difficult to process.
g.example: This complex book must be important because it is difficult to understand.

g.description: Believing something to be true because it is felt strongly, even in the absence of evidence.
g.example: I feel worthless, therefore I must be worthless.

g.description: Tendency to preserve one's existing beliefs even when faced with contrary evidence.
g.example: Despite the new evidence, I cannot believe that my favorite candidate is involved in a scandal.

g.description: Seeking or emphasizing irrelevant information in decision-making.
g.example: Can you detail all the options for me before we decide?

g.description: Disproportionate focus on trivial matters over more important ones.
g.example: More time is spent discussing paint color than planning the project budget.

g.description: Judging negative actions as being worse than equivalent inactions.
g.example: I find it less acceptable to cause harm through action than through inaction, even if the result is the same.

g.description: Resisting doing what one is told to do to preserve one's freedom of choice.
g.example: The more they tell me not to do it, the more I want to do it.

g.description: Preferring to maintain the current state of affairs, even when better alternatives exist.
g.example: I prefer to stay in my current job, even if the other offers a better salary. Better to avoid changes.

g.description: Discredited information continues to influence one's beliefs and perceptions.
g.example: I know this rumor has been debunked, but I think there is some truth to it.

g.description: Defending the status quo, even if doing so goes against one's own interests.
g.example: This system might not be perfect, but it's the best we can do.

g.description: Predicting one's future emotional state, often overestimating the intensity or duration of one's affective reactions.
g.example: I know I'm going to regret this decision. I'll feel terrible about it tomorrow.

g.description: Fearing losses more than valuing gains.
g.example: I prefer to avoid losing 100 euros rather than gaining 100 euros.

g.description: Faster fading of negative emotions associated with past memories.
g.example: Over time, I recall the good moments and forget the bad ones.

g.description: Believing that society or the world is constantly deteriorating.
g.example: In my time we knew how to live better.

g.description: Remembering the past more positively than it actually was.
g.example: Our vacations were always perfect when I was a child.

g.description: Neglecting one's psychological ability to adapt to negative events.
g.example: I was worried that the move would make me miserable, but I adapted faster than I expected.

g.description: Constructing an imperfect representation of a future event, leading to inaccurate predictions.
g.example: I thought working from home would be relaxing, not realizing how much home distractions would affect my productivity.

g.description: Overestimating the emotional impact of future events, both in intensity and duration.
g.example: After being promoted, I quickly realized that the expected happiness was not as great as expected.

g.description: Wrongly attributing one's current emotions and preferences to future events.
g.example: If I win the lottery, I will be happy forever.

g.description: Focusing too much on certain aspects of a future event, ignoring other important factors.
g.example: I thought living in a big city would be exciting, but I underestimated the stress of the noise and crowds.

g.description: Having one's prior expectations alter one's actual experience of the event.
g.example: I was expecting to hate this jazz concert; despite the quality of the performance, I didn't enjoy it.

g.description: Drawing logical consequences from facts which are insufficient to support such an entailment.
g.example: There is catfood in that bowl, therefore there is a cat in the house.

g.description: Reasoning in all-or-nothing terms, without nuance: if one is not perfect, considering oneself a complete failure.
g.example: Either I get a passing grade, or I’m completely hopeless. — Dichotomy: there is no other grade between “passing” and “completely hopeless,” even though a 20-point grading scale offers much finer granularity.

g.description: Ignoring or minimizing the probability of events in one's evaluations and decision-making.
g.example: I don't want to go to the hospital for treatment because you catch illnesses there.

g.description: Avoiding options with uncertain or unknown outcomes.
g.example: I prefer clear and defined choices, even if they are not the best.

g.description: Using a generalisation rule which is invalid in the considered situation.
g.example: My cats have always been sweet; therefore, cats must be harmless animals.

g.description: Perceiving an outcome as certain when it is actually uncertain in multi-step decision-making.
g.example: After getting through the first step of the game, I'm certain I can finish it without any problem.

g.description: Preferring to completely eliminate a small risk rather than reducing a larger risk.
g.example: I'd prefer you take care of this small bothersome task. I'll manage the bigger one.

g.description: Being overly optimistic or pessimistic because of the valence, positive or negative, of the emotions one feels.
g.example: I drive carefully: I don't need insurance as comprehensive as the kind most people choose.

g.description: Attributing successes to one's own merits and failures to external factors.
g.example: I succeeded because of my intelligence, but I failed because of unfair questions.

g.description: Having excessive confidence in the correctness of one's beliefs or predictions.
g.example: I am 100% sure that my team will win the match.

g.description: Overestimating the degree to which others share one's opinions and behaviors.
g.example: Everyone surely hates getting up early just as I do.

g.description: Underestimating the impact of external rewards on one's own motivation and behavior.
g.example: I work hard because I love my job, not because of the bonus I might receive.

g.description: Overestimating one's ability to control impulses or behaviors.
g.example: I can quit smoking whenever I want, I'm not addicted.

g.description: Believing one can control or influence events over which one actually has little to no influence.
g.example: I'm sure that if I wear my lucky jersey, my team will win.

g.description: Overestimating one's own qualities and abilities compared to those of others.
g.example: I'm a better driver than most people.

g.description: Believing that media messages affect others more than they affect oneself.
g.example: The ads have no effect on me, but they sure influence others.

g.description: Believing one is above average in various areas, even in the absence of evidence.
g.example: I'm sure I'm smarter than the average person.

g.description: Assuming others are more selfish and manipulative than oneself.
g.example: People pretend to be nice, but they all have a hidden agenda.

g.description: Being less aware of one's own biases than those of others.
g.example: I am objective in my opinions, but others are often biased.

g.description: Believing oneself less likely than others to have negative experiences.
g.example: I don't think I'll ever be fired; I'm too competent.

g.description: Better recall of the positive aspects of a person or experience over time by learning from the negative aspects.
g.example: Looking back on the past, I mostly remember the good times.

g.description: Overestimating the value or usefulness of innovations.
g.example: This new technology will solve all our problems.

g.description: Systematically underestimating the time needed to complete a task.
g.example: This project is simple. Expect me to finish it within a week.

g.description: Focusing one's thinking on unfavorable and pessimistic considerations to the detriment of possible positive elements.
g.example: The report indicates that the new policy improved nine out of ten indicators: fewer accidents, fewer delays, lower costs, and greater user satisfaction. But I reject it because one indicator declined slightly. — Negativity bias: one limited negative element outweighs several significant positive elements.

g.description: Interpreting events irrationally, often seeing them as overly positive or negative without concrete evidence.
g.example: I'm convinced everyone hates me because nobody talked to me at the party.

g.description: Feeling guilty or frustrated because of thinking one should be more grateful in one's current situation, or using this feeling in others to assert one's control.
g.example: I should be happy to have a job, even though I hate it.

g.description: Using imperative statements like "must" or "should", imposing unrealistic expectations on oneself or others.
g.example: I should always be able to control my emotions.

g.description: Focusing only on the negative aspects of a situation, filtering out all positive aspects.
g.example: I only see the mistakes I made in the report, not the successful parts.

g.description: Exaggerating the importance of problems or minimizing the importance of one's successes.
g.example: My success in this project is not that important, and then what you call a minor failure is a total disaster for me.

g.description: Rejecting positive experiences by insisting they don't count.
g.example: That compliment doesn't count, they were just being polite.

g.description: Underestimating the likelihood of positive events and overestimating those of negative events.
g.example: Everything will go wrong.

g.description: Viewing resources as limited in such a way that one's gain is necessarily another's loss.
g.example: If my colleague is promoted, that means I won't be.

g.description: Erroneously assuming that the amount of available work in an economy is fixed, overlooking the potential for job creation.
g.example: I believe that immigration reduces the jobs available to citizens.

g.description: Believing that if something can go wrong, it probably will.
g.example: Whenever I'm in a hurry, there are always traffic jams.

g.description: Doing the opposite of what one is told, thinking it's what the other person really wants.
g.example: He says I shouldn't buy this car, so he must really think it's a good buy.

g.description: Paying more attention to certain types of information based on one's interests or emotional state.
g.example: When I'm worried about my health, I notice all the information about illnesses.

g.description: Noticing and retaining more easily information that confirms one's beliefs.
g.example: I tend to only notice news that confirms my perspectives.

g.description: Identifying connections or patterns in random or unrelated data or events, creating meanings where none exist.
g.example: Every time I wear this hat, my team wins. It must be a good luck charm!

g.description: Attributing intentions or actions to elements of nature or inanimate objects that are typical of living beings.
g.example: The earthquakes are Earth's way of warning us that we're treating it poorly. It's its way of telling us to change our destructive behaviors.

g.description: Attributing human characteristics to objects, animals, or phenomena.
g.example: I think my car is happy when I clean it.

g.description: Basing an argument solely on a singular incident, which is insufficient to establish a general rule.
g.example: I got good grades in math after drinking blackcurrant juice; therefore, blackcurrant juice must be good for math.

g.description: Overestimating one's interpretive and predictive abilities in the presence of correlations.
g.example: I'm sure my intuition about which stocks to buy is correct.

g.description: Perceiving a relationship between two unrelated variables.
g.example: Every time I wear this sweater, my team wins. It must bring them luck.

g.description: Not considering the sample size when evaluating data reliability.
g.example: I believe in this poll, even though it only asked 10 people.

g.description: Simplifying memories by omitting details and exaggerating salient elements.
g.example: I remember the broad strokes of the story, but not the details.

g.description: Taking more risks when feeling secure.
g.example: I drive faster with my seat belt on.

g.description: Being too confident in one's answers to difficult questions and not confident enough in one's answers to easy questions.
g.example: I doubt my answer to this simple question as much as I doubt my answer to this difficult question.

g.description: Underestimating the time it takes to travel a familiar route compared to an unfamiliar one.
g.example: I always think the drive to my parents takes less time than it actually does.

g.description: Perceiving recent events as more remote in time and older events as more recent than they actually are.
g.example: It seems to me that this concert was last year, but in reality it was three years ago.

g.description: Judging an experience mostly on its peak intensity and its end.
g.example: I mostly remember the best part and how it ended.

g.description: Overestimating the time saved when increasing speed.
g.example: If I drive faster, I will save a lot of time on my commute.

g.description: Underestimating the importance of the length of an experience in its overall evaluation.
g.example: It doesn't matter how long it lasted, it's the end result that matters.

g.description: Being more likely to accept something simply because it has become familiar.
g.example: I prefer to vote for this political party because its name and ideas are familiar to me.

g.description: Looking for answers where it is easy to look, while ignoring more important but less accessible leads.
g.example: We analyzed sales data from the last three months because they were readily available, even though they do not reflect the long-term trends that might be more relevant for our market strategy.

g.description: Assessing the frequency or likelihood of an event based on how easily examples can be brought to mind.
g.example: I think plane crashes are more common because they are highly publicized.

g.description: Perceiving an item as occurring more frequently once it has come to one's attention.
g.example: Since I bought my car, I see the same model everywhere.

g.description: Discounting by gradually reducing one's discount factor.
g.example: I'd rather have €50 right now than €100 in a year, or €300 in three years. Immediate benefits feel more important to me.

g.description: Better memory retention for the most recent information.
g.example: I remember the last chapter of the book I read better than the earlier ones.

g.description: Arguing that an idea or proposition is good, valid or true solely because it is newer.
g.example: This technology has just been released: it must therefore be the best option. Why bother with old models?

g.description: Being more moved by the fate of one identifiable person than by a large number of people.
g.example: The story of this refugee child affected me more than the statistics of millions of displaced people.

g.description: Experiencing or exploiting the fact that false information, when repeated enough, eventually comes to be accepted.
g.example: I've heard so many times that this diet works that it must surely be effective.

g.description: Having one's memory influenced by the environment in which information is learned or retrieved.
g.example: I remember my childhood better when I return to that alley where I ran so much.

g.description: How information is processed affects its memorization.
g.example: I remember words better that I associated with images or stories.

g.description: Remembering information better after generating it oneself.
g.example: I always remember quiz answers better when I guess them myself.

g.description: Relying excessively on automated systems, sometimes at the expense of one's own judgment or abilities.
g.example: I trust my GPS so much that I don't even check the route myself anymore.

g.description: Forgetting about easily accessible information online, relying on the ability to search for it directly.
g.example: I don't remember the address of my favorite restaurant; I know I can always Google it.

g.description: Better retention of information spread over multiple sessions than concentrated in a single one.
g.example: I learn better by studying a little each day rather than doing one intensive study session.

g.description: Better retention of information after revising or being tested on it.
g.example: After taking quizzes, I remember the subjects studied better.

g.description: Forgetting or failing to pay attention to a task due to a lack of focus.
g.example: I never remember where I put my keys when I'm distracted.

g.description: Struggling to recall information just before having to perform.
g.example: Remind me what you told me just before it was my turn; I was distracted, I didn't catch it.

g.description: Perceiving changes relative to an initial reference point rather than absolutely.
g.example: A salary increase of €100 seems less significant when you already earn €3,000 per month.

g.description: Remembering information directly related to oneself better.
g.example: I remember birthdays that are close to my own.

g.description: One's expectations unconsciously influence the behavior of others.
g.example: My students do better when I expect them to succeed.

g.description: Believing that one's view of the world is objective reality.
g.example: My way of seeing things is the only correct way to understand this situation.

g.description: Confusing subjective experience of reality with the essence of that which is being observed.
g.example: I'm so scared of kids. You are so brave to be raising your own.

g.description: Believing one understands others better than they understand one.
g.example: I can easily read others, but no one really seems to understand me.

g.description: Believing one knows what others are thinking, often overestimating one's ability to understand their thoughts and emotions.
g.example: I know my colleague is angry with me, I can see it in his eyes.

g.description: Overestimating how much one's actions or appearances are noticed by others.
g.example: I'm sure everyone noticed the little stain on my shirt.

g.description: Having difficulty imagining what it is like not to know something already known.
g.example: I don't understand why they don't understand this concept; it seems so obvious to me.

g.description: Overestimating how much one's thoughts, emotions, or mental states are apparent to others.
g.example: I'm sure everyone can see how nervous I am during this presentation.

g.description: Reacting differently based on how information or a situation is presented.
g.example: I prefer an operation with a 90% chance of survival than an operation with a 10% chance of death.

g.description: Being influenced by an additional option that makes one of the existing options more attractive.
g.example: I'll choose this product because it looks better compared to this third option which is clearly worse.

g.description: Relying too heavily on the first piece of information received when making decisions.
g.example: I was initially told the car cost €20,000, so even after negotiating I think paying €18,000 is a good deal.

g.description: Better memory retention for items that distinctly stand out from others.
g.example: In the shopping list, I only remember the most unusual item.

g.description: Better memory retention for strange, funny, or unusual information.
g.example: I always remember that weird commercial with talking cats.

g.description: Better memory retention for information presented in a humorous way.
g.example: I always remember the jokes the professor tells in class, but not the boring parts.

g.description: Having one's judgment influenced by the comparison of contrasting alternatives, thereby altering the perception of their actual value or quality.
g.example: After seeing tiny apartments, this one seems huge to me, even though it is simply average-sized.

g.description: Preferring a lesser or smaller alternative when evaluated on its own, but not when it is directly compared to other options.
g.example: I was so happy with my bronze medal last year. This year's silver leaves me feeling bitter.

g.description: Arguing in a way that presents similar alternatives to emphasize their differences, which can distort the perception of those alternatives.
g.example: In the same category, I can offer you the latest model from this brand you're undoubtedly familiar with. It's a bit pricier but comes with these additional features.

g.description: Better memory for information presented in a certain modality (serial, visual, auditory, etc.).
g.example: I remember things better when I see them written than when I hear them.

g.description: Forgetting information in the absence of contextual cues associated with its memory.
g.example: Since we no longer see each other, I have forgotten most of our passionate discussions.

g.description: Tending to retain about seven pieces of information (plus or minus two) in short-term memory.
g.example: I easily remember a shopping list of about 5-9 items, but beyond that I forget.

g.description: Involuntarily inhibiting access to certain information in memory when retrieving other information.
g.example: When I try to remember the names of all the students in my class, some names block me from accessing the others.

g.description: Forgetting information related to what is being actively retrieved due to the memory selection process.
g.example: After studying intensively for my European history exam, I found it more difficult to remember details of American history.

g.description: Access to part of the information can inhibit recall of the rest.
g.example: When I'm given a few clues, I have trouble remembering the rest.

g.description: Better memory retention for images than for words or texts.
g.example: I remember company logos better than their names.

g.description: Better memory of the first and last items in a list.
g.example: In a shopping list, I often remember the beginning and end, but forget the middle.

g.description: Tendency to forget the final items in a series if they are followed by non-relevant items.
g.example: I can't remember the last words of a list if I'm told something else right after.

g.description: Remembering items in the order they were presented.
g.example: I can recite a list in the exact order I learned it.

g.description: Better memory for the first items in a series.
g.example: I always remember the first points discussed in a meeting.

g.description: Lowering one's standards to defend an indefensible position, distorting the debate.
g.example: Sure, it might not have been our most shining moment, but it allowed our team to showcase its true potential.

g.description: Rejecting responsibility for one's past statements by claiming they are too old.
g.example: It was a mistake of youth, the world has changed, I have learned a lot since then and my opinions have evolved over time.

g.description: Arguing that one must continue simply because a lot has already been invested.
g.example: We can't stop the project now, think of all the hours we've already spent on it!

g.description: Accepting a conclusion without justification to end a distressing situation.
g.example: Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, once this man is behind bars, the families here can finally begin their long journey of mourning.

g.description: Claiming one's approach is worth at least for the effort devoted to it.
g.example: Maybe my invention doesn't work yet, but you can't deny I've been working on it day and night for months.
