g.description: Defending against an accusation of prejudice by relying on the support of just one person concerned.
g.example: To put an end to this controversy over our candidate's alleged Islamophobia, let's listen to the testimony of a Muslim who supports him.

g.description: Evaluating the validity of a proposition based on the community of individuals to which its author belongs, regardless of its merits.
g.example: Those ideas about income equality? They can only come from people who have never had to work hard in their lives.

g.description: You attribute a product's effectiveness to an active ingredient present in a minute quantity.
g.example: This lavender essence gives this cream all its unique properties and incredible beauty results.

g.description: Considering a symbolic gesture as an adequate substitute where real action is needed.
g.example: To prove that we are not sexist, we have decided to include a woman on the board of directors.

g.description: Asserting everything is true, thus nullifying the value of any truth statements.
g.example: All statements are true: this medicine always cures, never cures, and both at the same time.

g.description: Defending a position that is not one's own, sometimes that of one's opponent, to test its strength.
g.example: I am not saying that this is what should be done, but I will defend the privatization of common goods for a moment to show you the flaws in your argument.

g.description: Basing reasoning on the absence of evidence, even though that absence is not evidence in itself.
g.example: Giraffes did not exist in the time of Julius Caesar. The proof is that he never mentions them.

g.description: Avoiding taking any clear stand so as never to be proven wrong.
g.example: If I accidentally offended someone here, I apologize; however, my actions were in good faith.
g.text: Having Your Cake and Eating It

g.description: Preparing a quick way to deflect or drop an argument as soon as pressure mounts.
g.example: Of course, if contrary evidence is presented, I would be open to reconsidering my position.

g.description: Setting forth an argument while allowing for the possibility of its abandonment when it happens to be convenient.
g.example: I'm not saying this method will work for everyone, but it definitely has something unique that might suit some.

g.description: Exploring a proposition simply because it seems harmless, without assessing its actual drawbacks or considering alternatives.
g.example: Let's try this new product. After all, if it doesn't help, it surely won't harm you, will it?

g.description: Refining a claim to dodge counter evidence and then acting as if the revised claim is the original one.
g.example: I just said I would change my way of working on this contract. Not that I was giving it up.

g.description: Claiming to be unbiased while one's statements quickly reveal the opposite.
g.example: I'm not sexist, but it's clear that men are better suited for certain jobs than women.

g.description: Denying any responsibility to avoid being held accountable for one's actions or words.
g.example: I always mentioned there was a significant risk associated with our new marketing strategy.

g.description: Refining an argument after it has been rebutted or debunked to avoid losing face.
g.example: I didn't say the investment was safe, I just highlighted its interesting potential in the current circumstances.

g.description: Presenting apologies that indirectly may blame the receiver.
g.example: I'm sorry you were offended; I thought you could take a joke.

g.description: Offering apologies that seem conditional and subtly shift the blame onto the other party.
g.example: If my words have offended someone, I deeply regret it, as it was never my intention to do so.

g.description: Admitting mistakes without explicitly taking personal responsibility for them.
g.example: I deeply regret any potential negligence in my services in handling our clients' files. In today's competitive world, defining the limits of information use is challenging.

g.description: Articulating a denial in such an ambiguous way that it could seem like a covert affirmation.
g.example: I have never taken bribes; they were merely 'business dinners'.

g.description: Blending several elements in an argument that can be interpreted in multiple ways.
g.example: In our approach to this international conflict, we support a policy that respects the sovereignty of nations and the right of peoples to self-determination.

g.description: Skillfully playing with the pros and cons, confusing the audience until one's real point of view is no longer clear.
g.example: It's crucial to preserve our traditions and what can enrich our culture.

g.description: Employing different arguments depending on the audience, all leading to the conclusion that serves one's interests.
g.example: If our competitors raise their prices, we'll say they're taking advantage of their customers. But if they keep their prices the same, we'll say they're sacrificing quality and innovation for short-term gains.

g.description: Adjusting the definition of the terms of the debate according to the interlocutor's perception in order to always position oneself favorably.
g.example: When I say “social networks,” am I talking about tools that isolate people and spread false information, or tools that connect them and encourage the exchange of ideas?

g.description: You present a point of view without ever stating it explicitly, making your position impossible to pin down.
g.example: Of course, I support freedom of expression. However, I am not sure it is wise to disseminate every opinion.

g.description: Stating one's ideas vaguely enough to make one's real position difficult to understand.
g.example: We are vigilantly monitoring the conflict between employees and employers. In this context, we are fully committing ourselves to the industrial sector.

g.description: Drowning one's point in a flood of generalities, thus avoiding committing to anything specific.
g.example: I recognize your legitimate anger. In these troubled times, we all must exhibit a high sense of responsibility.

g.description: You express yourself in hollow, pompous terms so that your speech is completely empty while giving the illusion of being profound.
g.example: Considering the current circumstances, it is necessary to consider all the issues already at our disposal, in order to take the essential measures effectively.

g.description: Increasing one's demands as one's interlocutor complies with them.
g.example: — You don't know how to drive. — But I have my driver's license! — Yes, but you've never been able to parallel park properly...

g.description: Criticizing the use of specialized terms to minimize the strength of the opposing argument, suggesting they mask a lack of substance.
g.example: Oh, stop using your fancy terms like 'climatology' and 'complex systems'! It's just puffery to disguise that you have no strong argument!

g.description: Assuming a proposition to be true until proved false or vice-versa.
g.example: I need to prove my product is safe? Isn't it rather for you to show how it's harmful?

g.description: Assuming that it is up to an opponent to disprove the existence of a phenomenon one believes in, rather than providing evidence for it.
g.example: If you cannot prove that the Loch Ness monster does not exist, then it must exist.

g.description: Forcing one's interlocutor to prove their thesis with only one kind of evidence.
g.example: If the accused was truly at the restaurant at the time of the crime, show us a receipt proving it.

g.description: Considering an interlocutor incompetent if they cannot recite specific data or technical details on a topic.
g.example: If you can't quote the latest economic growth statistics, then your views on economic policy are invalid.

g.description: Conflating the cause of an act with its justification to evade criticism.
g.example: You suggest that poverty and oppression lead to radicalization and terrorism? How can you excuse such acts?
g.text: Confusing an explanation with an excuse

g.description: Considering every defense as proof of guilt.
g.example: If you have so many excuses, it's because you indeed have something to feel guilty about.

g.description: Refusing to engage in a discussion on the grounds that it would validate one's opponent's argument.
g.example: I won't debate with that far-right party, as it would give them an undue platform.

g.description: Indefinitely accumulating objections without making a decision, thus ignoring the practical consequences of inaction.
g.example: I always had a good reason for postponing my marriage proposal. Eventually, she married someone else.

g.description: Constantly modifying the bases of an argument to avoid admitting defeat on a specific point and to disorient one's interlocutor.
g.example: You're questioning my project management? What about your delay on the report last week? And let's not forget your failure in last month's presentation...

g.description: Challenging the entire credibility of a person due to a single mistake.
g.example: How can you still take this scientist's theories seriously? Don't forget he once supported an absurd conspiracy theory.

g.description: Systematically doubting all information from a media source because it has made errors in the past.
g.example: Surveys from this institute are valueless, as they got the last presidential election completely wrong.

g.description: Incorrectly claiming that because science has been wrong in the past, it is inevitably wrong now.
g.example: Why should we trust scientists about cellphone radiation levels? Remember, once they said asbestos and smoking were safe.

g.description: Demanding an unrealistic level of certainty before agreeing to take a position.
g.example: Scientists can't even predict the weather next week. How can they predict the climate in 100 years?

g.description: Demanding justification for each justification, in a never ending process.
g.example: But why? And where does that information come from? And why should I believe that source?

g.description: Discarding any solution less than perfect.
g.example: I oppose mandatory seatbelt use because this measure does nothing to prevent road accidents.

g.description: Arguing that a part of the universe can only be understood if one knows the entire universe.
g.example: We can't comprehend the laws of the solar system unless we know the physics of elementary particles.

g.description: Presenting events or facts in a misleading light.
g.example: I am not responsible for your decision: I told you the product had passed certain tests, but I omitted to mention that it had failed others.

g.description: Focusing on specific aspects of the argument while ignoring other relevant dimensions.
g.example: Wine is excellent for your health: it contains antioxidants. No need to talk about the risks linked to alcohol.

g.description: Not noticing a significant element because of being too focused on a specific task or detail.
g.example: During our last quality control, I was so focused on checking the finishes that I completely missed a major flaw in the materials used for our products.

g.description: You unknowingly influence the results or their interpretation through your expectations or your behavior toward the subject being studied.
g.example: During the experiment, I smile at and encourage the participants who give the answers I expect more than the others, without realizing it.

g.description: Building an argument merely to confirm preexisting beliefs instead of seeking objective truth.
g.example: I am convinced that my candidate is honest; the corruption allegations against him are therefore just political attacks.

g.description: Having one's opinions or conclusions swayed by funding sources instead of being based on objective facts.
g.example: Our latest study indicates there is no significant link between soda consumption and obesity among adolescents. These results should reassure our sponsors about the quality of their products.

g.description: Preferentially disseminating studies yielding positive results while omitting those that fail or are inconclusive.
g.example: The studies we've published all show a positive effect of our treatment.

g.description: Citing only research with significant results in an argument, excluding research without notable findings.
g.example: Why haven't these findings showing that we're not progressing been published? Oh, no one cares about such bad news.

g.description: Highlighting outcomes that support one's good intentions while ignoring negative impacts or failures.
g.example: All the studies I've come across recently lead me to believe we can be very optimistic about curing all cancers soon.

g.description: Cherry-picking only the facts necessary to reach one's conclusion, ignoring any contradictory information.
g.example: The statistics indicate that cities like ours, which prioritised police budgeting, have the lowest crime rates. Clearly, our social welfare cuts were justified.

g.description: Denying events one has experienced because they are unbearable.
g.example: I couldn't have made such a mistake. It must be some sort of error.

g.description: Focusing solely on the elements that fortify one's argumentation, excluding anything that might contest it.
g.example: I read dozens of articles supporting my view, which surely proves I'm right.

g.description: Deliberately ignoring key evidence that challenges one's standpoint.
g.example: We have the same tastes, we belong to the same community, we could save a lot by being together: let's get married!

g.description: Selectively highlighting the weakest arguments of the opposing side to discredit their overall position.
g.example: I see that your argument is rife with errors and lists endless testimonies that fail to provide any substantive information on the matter.

g.description: Applying a rule unevenly, based on preference or convenience, rather than applying it equally to all relevant parties.
g.example: I always critique people who eat poorly, but having an ice cream occasionally doesn't count for me—it's different.

g.description: Arguing in bad faith.
g.example: Of course your opinion matters, I encourage all voices to be heard in our association, but it's only natural that the more experienced among us have a greater influence, right?

g.description: Presenting only the facts necessary to a conclusion while ignoring conflicting facts.
g.example: Increasing working hours means increasing employees' purchasing power, their family well-being, and therefore their job satisfaction.

g.description: Assigning blame to an individual or group for a problem.
g.example: The current economic crisis is entirely due to immigrants taking our jobs and straining the system. If we had stronger border control, our economy would be much stronger.

g.description: Disregarding evidence of an argument's invalidity.
g.example: All swans are white.

g.description: Citing something as an exception to the rule without justifying the exception.
g.example: I am against violence to children, but in this case, he really needs a good smack on the backside.

g.description: Appealing to pathos in an argument and pleading for special consideration.
g.example: This grade will probably decide whether I get into college, professor.

g.description: Calling upon irrelevant, unqualified, unidentified, biased, or fabricated sources in support of an argument.
g.example: A “scientific committee” whose members no one knows claims that this hand cream is the true recipe for happiness.

g.description: Confusing the source of information, attributing an idea or memory to the wrong origin.
g.example: I was sure it was Professor Martin who said that in class, but it was actually in an article I read.

g.description: Thinking one had an original idea when in reality it came from a forgotten outside source.
g.example: I thought I had this great idea for a book, but I just realized it was the plot of a movie I saw a long time ago.

g.description: Relying on sources that do nothing but reference each other, without any verifiable foundation.
g.example: All these articles discuss free energy discovered through the work of an obscure scientist; with so many sources agreeing, there must be some truth to it.

g.description: Believing in the existence or truth of a thesis because of its repetition in the media or literature, based on a source to which the thesis is wrongly attributed.
g.example: Everyone is talking about this revolutionary new health theory, it must be true.

g.description: Spreading quotes that seem valid only because they are repeated, thus creating a pseudo-credibility.
g.example: An article on an independent researcher's blog claims copper water pipes have healing properties, now echoed by a TV report!

g.description: You twist quotations away from their original meaning by isolating them from their context, in order to make them appear to support your argument.
g.example: - You said you found this movie dazzling. - Dazzling in its stupidity!

g.description: Presenting biased versions of historical events to align with one's beliefs, regardless of established facts.
g.example: Gold on top of pyramids is the best conductor for electricity, used in their constructions; this proves we haven't invented anything new.

g.description: Interpreting words too literally, disregarding implications or the larger context.
g.example: You wrote in your email "Freeze all ongoing projects." So, I instructed the staff to stop working immediately.'

g.description: Choosing quotes out of context to make them seem to support one's viewpoint.
g.example: You clearly said: "Sometimes compromises have to be made." So, how can you now oppose this new corporate strategy?'

g.description: Summarizing an argument with a catchy, attention-grabbing quote that may be misleading or simplistic.
g.example: You are surprised by these budget cuts, yet our fellow citizens demanded that the government initiate a supply-side shift.

g.description: Stating something known to be false.
g.example: Santa Claus is watching you, so behave.

g.description: Passing oneself off as something one is not (expertise, identity, experience) in order to strengthen an argument.
g.example: I am a certified locksmith… So you can trust me with your keys with complete confidence.

g.description: Relying on a compulsion to lie.
g.example: But officer, I swear my dog ate it.

g.description: Violating an oath made to an authority.
g.example: My testimony represents my understanding of the facts at the time of the events.

g.description: You progressively conceal facts or reasons to prevent them from being examined.
g.example: There's no need to discuss this mistake, let's focus on the success.

g.description: You modify the reasons or facts during the discussion in order to preserve your conclusion.
g.example: Following a reevaluation, our results now show a performance superior to that initially announced.

g.description: You invent reasons as the discussion unfolds to support your conclusion.
g.example: We know there are weapons of mass destruction in this country: several confidential reports confirm it.

g.description: Making people believe in a promise or value with no foundation.
g.example: This software will revolutionize the way you work: double your productivity in less than a week.

g.description: Using an argument to impress in a more subjective than objective manner.
g.example: Our service is the most extraordinary one you can find!

g.description: Making blatantly false statements aimed solely at gaining an audience's approval.
g.example: If you entrust me with the reins of our country, I will put an end to all this endemic corruption within the first month of my term.

g.description: Using an argument to justify a minor, easily forgivable mistake.
g.example: It was the dog that knocked over the vase.

g.description: Using an argument to deceive an opponent in order to mock them or provoke a reaction.
g.example: I just heard that our company is going to be acquired by a famous multinational in the videogame industry. They're planning to turn our offices into an interactive theme park. Incredible, isn't it?

g.description: Stating a falsehood to convey or suggest the opposite.
g.example: Of course, if we interpret the data this way, it seems to indicate the opposite of what everyone believes to be true.

g.description: Relying on widely accepted but inaccurate facts to support one's claims.
g.example: We all know that the pyramids were built by slaves. — Widely believed, but historically false: the workers at Giza were paid laborers who were housed and fed on site.

g.description: Basing an argument on popular cultural elements without regard for their truthfulness.
g.example: That viral meme on global warming is hilarious, so climate change can't be that serious, right?

g.description: You base your argument on a false or dubious narrative presented as a foundational story or as one that conveys meaning.
g.example: It's commonly believed that eating carrots enhances your night vision.

g.description: Basing an argument on a hostile stereotyped narrative about a religion or culture.
g.example: You cannot call yourself Muslim and feminist. The true representation of Islam consists in killing infidels and oppressing women. Just look at the Middle East.

g.description: Basing an argument on a scare-inducing narrative of questionable origin.
g.example: It was at that turn that I saw the White Lady.

g.description: Basing an argument on a story of dubious origin.
g.example: A friend told me there are crocodiles in the sewers of New York.

g.description: Supporting an argument with unverified information that circulates from person to person.
g.example: Everybody says this restaurant is the best in town.

g.description: Sharing informal stories or rumors about other people's private lives, often unverified and private.
g.example: I heard our boss is going on vacation with his assistant, how intriguing!

g.description: Spreading rumors or information without naming the involved parties, often to avoid legal repercussions.
g.example: A certain famous actor, who I will not name, is rumored to have had a secret affair.

g.description: Spreading frightening and exaggerated rumors about imminent danger to deliberately and unnecessarily instill public fear about an issue.
g.example: Did you know that tap water is very rarely checked and often contaminated, unlike this mineral water?

g.description: Inciting indignation by portraying certain actions as immoral to provoke a strong emotional reaction.
g.example: This new dance which is spreading among young people is a sign of moral decadence, which leads straight to depravity.

g.description: Disseminating negative information, often vague, to sow fear and mistrust and rally the public to one's cause.
g.example: I heard that our competitor was in serious trouble. Given their financial situation, it would be a miracle if they lasted until spring.

g.description: Creating a climate of tension to justify extreme measures.
g.example: Have you heard about the recent explosions? I'm sure this is just a taste. They're going to have to step up security, otherwise who knows what could happen...

g.description: Spreading false or exaggerated accusations, malicious gossip, or slanderous claims about a person or group, intending to damage their reputation or credibility.
g.example: During the political race, one candidate launches a smear campaign, using social media to spread rumors about the opponent's alleged financial misconduct and ethical violations, despite lack of concrete evidence.

g.description: Spreading damaging rumors or innuendo about a target, while avoiding being detected.
g.example: In the office, a whispering campaign starts against Martin. His colleagues anonymously spread rumors about his alleged incompetence and lack of ethics, causing distrust among his peers without any direct confrontation.

g.description: Knowingly spreading incorrect information to mislead an interlocutor.
g.example: I've read somewhere that this technology has been completely discredited.

g.description: Mass disseminating repeated messages across multiple channels (media, social networks), without regard for truth or consistency.
g.example: Government channels, supported by a fleet of online bots and anonymous accounts, publish a flood of contradictory reports on the economic situation, each contradicting the other, flooding the informational space and making it impossible to understand the true economic conditions.

g.description: Intentionally diverting attention from significant issues by creating a shocking scandal or controversy.
g.example: My dear compatriots, we will have to postpone the examination of this law, because I have some shocking news to share. Do you know that one of our politicians is involved in a corruption scandal?

g.description: Relying on an unverified story to justify an unfounded claim.
g.example: There's an article suggesting our competitor plans to release a similar product very soon.

g.description: Creating the illusion of a popular movement or widespread opinion to strengthen one's position.
g.example: Thousands of people have expressed their support for our cause on social media.

g.description: Presenting an argument by relying on opinions that circulate without being questioned.
g.example: To lose weight, you must eliminate these 5 foods from your diet.

g.description: Relying on false information knowingly presented as news.
g.example: I just read an article claiming that taxes will increase by 50% next year for all citizens. It's outrageous, and we need to act immediately to prevent it.

g.description: Mixing true and false information to distort reality.
g.example: It's true that our product had some minor issues, but it's important to remember that it's the most innovative on the market and the competition is far behind.

g.description: Basing an argument on alleged memories that are actually incorrect.
g.example: I clearly remember you saying that we could change our minds later on.

g.description: Inventing stories as an argument progresses, often to fill gaps in evidence or reasoning.
g.example: I clearly recall reading a study that supports your point; I'll find the reference for you. My argument builds from there.

g.description: Acknowledging certain truths while denying others to minimize damage to an argument.
g.example: I admit there were a few minor issues with our latest product, but let's forget these details and focus on our past successes.

g.description: To falsely claim that certain consequences directly follow from one's premises.
g.example: The fact that the flu spared our family this year proves the effectiveness of my homemade remedy, even though science doesn't acknowledge it.

g.description: Starting with a flawed foundation to build an argument.
g.example: If we assume that the resources we will have are nearly limitless, then our current consumption model is perfectly sustainable.

g.description: Intentionally resorting to deception by claiming that the end justifies the means.
g.example: The negotiations were complex, but we finally agreed on a mutual beneficial arrangement, even if it involved making some commitments we won't keep.

g.description: Failing to say what one really thinks.
g.example: That's definitely an option I hadn't considered, yet you're free to suggest it...

g.description: Omitting facts necessary for an argument to be valid.
g.example: I would like to highlight the exceptional savings that will be made through this restructuring plan of our department, which will benefit everyone.

g.description: Using an argument designed to reveal as little of the truth as possible without being a lie.
g.example: I've heard your accusation, and I can inform you that the company has complied with all the relevant environmental regulations this year.

g.description: Defending incorrect ideas believing they will unite the group around a common cause.
g.example: If you're good, Santa Claus will bring you lots of presents.

g.description: Deliberately telling an untruth to avoid upsetting or offending someone.
g.example: You fought well and did not disgrace yourselves. Now take a well-earned rest and let our team of professionals finish the job.

g.description: Relying on outdated data that is no longer current to support one's arguments.
g.example: According to a 1998 study, this method is the best.

g.description: Misrepresenting a situation or an opponent's position in such a way as to distort understanding.
g.example: They replaced the expression “global warming” with “climate change” because, according to them, global warming has stopped.

g.description: Exaggerating the importance of problems or minimizing the importance of one's successes.
g.example: My success in this project isn't very significant, and what you might call a minor failure, I view as a complete disaster.

g.description: Amplifying certain aspects excessively to strengthen one's argument.
g.example: This situation is an absolute disaster! If we don't act immediately, everything will be lost!

g.description: Caricaturing the other person's argument so it can be refuted more easily.
g.example: So, you're suggesting we should dedicate all our days to digging through trash to sort out recycling? That's no way to live!

g.description: Intentionally diminishing elements of the truth, the importance of another's issues or feelings, to minimize their impact or to deflect responsibility.
g.example: It's not that bad, everyone makes mistakes and it's not going to change anything. No need to make a mountain out of a molehill.

g.description: Using language in a way that misleads or misrepresents the truth.
Phrasing statements that have several possible meanings.
g.example: He painted the lady's portrait in black.

g.description: You present your argument in the form of a narrative that can be interpreted in several ways.
g.example: Last Monday you handed your work in on time. Today we need to talk.

g.description: Raising an issue that serves multiple objectives, making the solution ambiguous.
g.example: We need to reform our educational system to improve the economy and strengthen the moral values of our society.

g.description: Misleading by making it appear that arguments come from allies when they actually come from opponents.
g.example: My fellow citizens, as a member of the parliamentary majority, it is my duty to inform you that your government has chosen to sell your interests to this country that claims to be our ally.

g.description: Making false statements or asking misleading questions in order to observe reactions and uncover the truth.
g.example: I heard that your teammate discussed our strategy with our competitors. What's your take on their behavior?

g.description: Conducting an interrogation without disclosing one's intentions or identity, engaging the person in relaxed conversation to extract information.
g.example: So, how's work going these days? I heard your company is working on an exciting project. Can you tell me more about it?

g.description: Hiding the true origin of information to make it seem more credible, without revealing one's intentions or affiliations.
g.example: This documentary presents impressive statistics about our product.

g.description: Spreading damaging rumors or innuendo about a target, while avoiding being detected.
g.example: In the office, a whispering campaign starts against Martin. His colleagues anonymously spread rumors about his alleged incompetence and lack of ethics, causing distrust among his peers without any direct confrontation.

g.description: Crafting an argument that subtly introduces implicit propositions.
g.example: That day, you indeed arrived on time.

g.description: Arguing by insinuating things without stating them clearly, leaving the audience to interpret the implied meanings.
g.example: You were alone in the room, and now my wallet is missing.

g.description: Spreading rumors or information without naming the involved parties, often to avoid legal repercussions.
g.example: A certain famous actor, whom I won't name, is rumored to have had a secret affair.

g.description: Discrediting someone through a compliment that actually suggests the opposite.
g.example: It would be an exaggeration to suggest, as some do, that his line of thought is worthless.

g.description: Exploiting the different senses of a single word to make one's statement ambiguous.
g.example: That bear ate an avocado—or a lawyer.

g.description: A word is used whose meaning is unclear because its usual meaning is not the same as its original.
g.example: The old inn's sign says 'He who sleeps dines', so we're skipping dinner tonight assuming it means not needing to eat.

g.description: Arguing based on the assumption that language perfectly maps onto reality.
g.example: I thought we were both talking about love, that unique feeling that binds us forever.

g.description: Of two positions that have similarities, defending the modest consensual position and claiming to prove the complex controversial position.
g.example: Sure, celestial bodies influence nature. Look at the tidal effects.

g.description: Basing an argument on an idealized and misleading representative version of reality.
g.example: Advertisements show family happiness as just acquiring the latest tech gadget.

g.description: Confusing a representation or model with the reality it is meant to represent.
g.example: By analyzing statistical data on social well-being, we concluded that society is healthy.
g.text: Mistaking the map for the territory

g.description: Confusing the use of a word with the object it describes, treating the word as if it were the object itself.
g.example: You asked me for love. Well, this letter is full of it.

g.description: Treating something abstract as a concrete thing.
g.example: When I'm wealthy, I'll buy his love.

g.description: Thinking that because a word exists, what it represents must also certainly exist.
g.example: Everyone knows what 'happiness' is; therefore, it is impossible that it does not exist.

g.description: Believing that a word and the object it refers to are inseparably bound, leading to ambiguity.
g.example: What I felt for her was love at first sight.

g.description: Using one concept as a substitute for another, conceptually related, without clear justification.
g.example: Given how many pens this company gives out, they're clearly writing their own success.

g.description: Confusing a general concept (type) with a specific instance (token), making the argument ambiguous.
g.example: You tell me that this restaurant serves around twenty different dishes. How can they stay afloat with so few customers?

g.description: Using a polysemous word or one whose meaning has evolved, which may cause confusion.
g.example: During the meeting, he used the term “network” to talk about his contacts; I thought he was talking about the Internet.

g.description: Using different terms to represent the same ideas or the same term to reflect different ideas.
g.example: We both say we want equality, but when I talk about 'justice', I don't think we're speaking about the same concept.

g.description: Constructing an argument using a term with multiple meanings, causing confusion.
g.example: The poet was drunk and counting the feet of his glass.

g.description: Basing an argument on a word that can mean multiple things depending on the context.
g.example: When he said he 'supported' his team, I thought he meant cheering them on, not financing their travels.

g.description: You misunderstand or inaccurately report a phrase because it sounds like another one.
g.example: He hears “older wedding, happier marriage” instead of “rainy wedding, happy marriage.”

g.description: Using terms so vague that they do not allow the audience to clearly understand what is meant.
g.example: When I told you it was 'accessible', I meant accessible on foot, not by wheelchair or with a stroller.

g.description: Considering that the application of one concept necessarily leads to that of another because the boundary between the two is gradual without clear distinction.
g.example: Allowing abortion will inevitably lead to legalizing infanticide because there's no clear line where the embryo becomes a baby.

g.description: Refusing to distinguish between two states by arguing that there is no clear boundary between them.
g.example: There's a risk in everything. If we start wearing helmets for biking, might as well wear one all the time!

g.description: Presenting numerical data in a manner that implies better precision than is justified, often to pretend exaggerated accuracy.
g.example: This dinosaur skeleton is 100,000,005 years old because 5 years ago, an expert determined it was 100 million years old.

g.description: Using ambiguous sentence structures, that have several possible understandings.
g.example: I prefer chicken with olives—or chicken over olives.

g.description: Using an invented word or one borrowed from another language, making the statement uncertain.
g.example: The bravitude of this people is impressive.

g.description: Making a grammatical error in a sentence that creates ambiguity, even though the words used are correct.
g.example: I couldn't go to the movie, with the hairdresser.

g.description: Using intonation or emphasis to suggest a message different from the words used.
g.example: I did not say that she STOLE the money.

g.description: Attributing to the speaker a specific prosody that alters the perceived meaning of their words.
g.example: You 'imagine' he's the guilty one? You sure have a vivid imagination.

g.description: Modifying the logical meaning by confusing the scope of a modal term (necessary, possible, certain).
g.example: If I know something, I cannot be mistaken. But if I cannot be mistaken, then I am certain of it. Certainty is therefore a necessary condition of knowledge.

g.description: Changing the meaning of a statement by shifting the quantifiers.
g.example: In every town, there is a restaurant considered the best in that town. Therefore, there exists a restaurant considered the best in all towns.

g.description: Using a sentence which may be interpreted in more than one way due to ambiguous punctuation.
g.example: The committee members who approved this file will be summoned. — Restrictive: only the members who approved this file will be summoned. The committee members, who approved this file, will be summoned. — Non-restrictive: all the members will be summoned, and it is specified that they approved this file.

g.description: Reasoning on the basis of illegitimate associations of elements brought together incorrectly.
g.example: School is like prison: you don't enter it or leave it whenever you want.

g.description: Using a shared property between A and B to ascribe any property of B to A.
g.example: Jane is good at mathematics. Jane is dyslexic. Therefore, all dyslexic people are good at mathematics.

g.description: You wrongly associate a person or thing with a negative category based on a single point in common.
g.example: You're a vegetarian? We don't need an environmental activist here.

g.description: You draw a parallel between two things based solely on one feature they share, while overlooking their important differences.
g.example: No one stops a surgeon from consulting their notes during a complex surgery. So why would you want to prevent me from using notes during this exam?

g.description: Drawing an improper parallel between two distinct arguments or situations, assuming them to be equivalent based on a superficial similarity.
g.example: You're asking me to do my homework after school; but then, I don't ask you to do overtime when you return from work.

g.description: Considering two things that resemble each other to be related or similar.
g.example: Self-driving cars are like automatic elevators. In both cases, there is no need for a human operator to control the movement. So, if automatic elevators are safe and reliable, self-driving cars are too.

g.description: Suggesting that because two things are alike in some way and one of those things is like something else, then both things must be like that "something else".
g.example: If someone thinks it's okay to harvest animals for their meals, then they should not theoretically have a problem with an advanced alien species culling us for their food.

g.description: You use an analogy that already assumes the conclusion you are trying to prove by questionably equating two situations.
g.example: Access to the internet is a human right, just like access to clean water. Everyone needs water to live, so everyone must need the internet to live.

g.description: Reasoning on the basis of an incorrect comparison.
g.example: Managing a class is like operating a machine: if one part slows down the system, you simply replace it. — Faulty comparison: a class is not a machine, and students are not interchangeable parts. The comparison erases essential differences.

g.description: Distinguishing between two elements that are, in fact, similar or have no significant difference.
g.example: I told you to do it, not to try to do it.

g.description: Comparing things while retaining only certain aspects, thereby distorting the overall comparison.
g.example: Meat is cheaper than coffee; it is also better adapted than bananas for local production.

g.description: Using overlapping categories, thereby distorting the comparison.
g.example: I see you painting, but didn't you tell me you were a scientist?

g.description: Using a comparison without providing all the necessary data, which makes it unverifyable.
g.example: You should buy this product, because it is better.

g.description: Defining terms in a way that favors one's argument while setting aside their established meaning.
g.example: I quit smoking five times a day, after each cigarette.

g.description: Defining terms in inconsistent, logically faulty ways.
g.example: A good education must awaken critical thinking; yet a person endowed with critical thinking never lets themselves be influenced by anyone.

g.description: Arguing in a way that raises problems concerning the application of logic to knowledge.
g.example: I assert that any question of philosophy cannot be resolved through rational thought.

g.description: You define a term by means of the very notion it represents and that you claim to be defining.
g.example: We define God as the thing that created the universe. The universe exists. Therefore, God exists and created the universe.

g.description: Defining a term by using other terms that are just as undefined.
g.example: If you think it's good because it makes you feel good, then you should do it.

g.description: Claiming that the reality described by a term depends strictly on its dictionary definition.
g.example: This country cannot be communist, because what happens there does not match Marx's definition of communism.

g.description: Using an argument that contradicts itself and therefore cannot be valid.
g.example: The only certainty is uncertainty.

g.description: Denying a concept while continuing to use it in an argument.
g.example: Reason and logic are not always reliable; therefore, we should not rely on them to establish the truth.

g.description: Inventing a tailor-made definition for one's terms without respecting their common meaning.
g.example: Love is knowing how to forgive. So how can you reproach me for my infidelity?

g.description: Defining terms in ways that are biased towards one conclusion.
g.example: This man is an atheist, someone who has not been touched by the grace of God.

g.description: Attributing particular and unexpected meanings to terms in order to support one's point of view.
g.example: When I talk about 'freedom', I don't mean the absence of constraints; for me, it's about choosing among the constraints.

g.description: Using buzzwords to make an argument appealing, without considering their relevance.
g.example: Alternative medicine costs the taxpayer so much less.

g.description: Making a simple yet typically dishonest assertion that is difficult and time consuming for an opponent to rebut.
g.example: The real question is, why should we pay for those who do not work while we are making an effort?

g.description: Deliberately using terms with distorted and deceptive meanings to hide reality.
g.example: Let's not talk about 'staff reductions', but rather about maximizing the operational efficiency of the team.

g.description: Relying on ready-made, ideologically loaded formulas to influence the audience.
g.example: This country needs stable, strong leadership.

g.description: Using words that create an impression that a specific or meaningful statement has been made, when instead it was only a vague or ambiguous claim.
g.example: This revolutionary product, designed with state-of-the-art next-generation materials, guarantees top-flight performance.

g.description: Manipulating mutually exclusive terms in a misleading way.
g.example: I adore you, so I do not love you.

g.description: Rejecting realistic solutions by demanding an unattainable ideal.
g.example: I am opposed to mandatory seat belt use, because this measure does not prevent all road accidents.

g.description: Presenting two options as the only, mutually exclusive, possibilities, when there are other possibilities.
g.example: If new technologies do not interest you, nothing is stopping you from going back to living in a cave.

g.description: Seeing things in black and white, without nuance. If not perfect, considering oneself a total failure.
g.example: Either we are in good health, or we are sick. — Dichotomy: the definition admits no state between “good health” and “sick,” even though health is a continuum offering every intermediate degree.

g.description: You demand that the people you are talking to take a position either for or against you.
g.example: If you don't support our proposition, you have chosen the side of the republic's enemies.

g.description: Taking advantage of the pressure of urgency to ignore long-term issues.
g.example: We must deal with the crime problem on our streets before we can tackle improving our schools.

g.description: Saving a generalization from a counterexample by changing its definition in order to exclude the latter.
g.example: — All Scots are red-haired. — Angus is Scottish, but he is not red-haired. — Then he is not a true Scot.

g.description: Introducing alternatives when, in fact, there are none.
g.example: Whether he's the right man for the job? Let's just say I know him well.

g.description: Using different verbs to describe the same behavior depending on whether the person involved is approved of or not.
g.example: I am persistent, but my opponent is stubborn.

g.description: Claiming there is a significant difference between two concepts, situations, or objects, when in fact the difference is nonexistent or insignificant.
g.example: I'm not against free speech, I just think some opinions shouldn't be publicly expressed.

g.description: Defining the terms of the debate in a manner that blurs their differences.
g.example: Atoms are part of nature; this chemical powder is made up of atoms, so it is a natural product.

g.description: Arguing on the basis of concepts whose definitions are either too broad or too narrow.
g.example: I consider my apartment a three-room apartment. After all, if I can hang a curtain to separate my bed from the rest, it's like having a living room and a bedroom, isn't it?

g.description: Arguing on the basis of too narrow a definition.
g.example: A cow is a quadruped that is black and white.

g.description: Arguing on the basis of too broad a definition.
g.example: A cow is the animal that gives us milk.

g.description: Using definitions that are vague enough to open argumentative leeway.
g.example: When I said I would be there in five minutes, that could also have meant in an hour. It's an expression; it wasn't meant to be taken literally.

g.description: Using a term or concept that has different interpretations and whose meaning is inherently disputed, leading to misunderstandings or endless debate.
g.example: The term 'freedom' is used by various political groups, but each interprets it differently depending on their own values and ideologies.

g.description: Basing one's argument on a crucial concept that is not clearly defined.
g.example: The concept of 'quality' is so broad that it's difficult to define precisely; therefore, my argument is based on my personal interpretation.

g.description: Using overly complex definitions that obscure rather than clarify the argument.
g.example: You say ether is responsible for this phenomenon. But what is ether? It is a subtle and invisible body.

g.description: Reaching a conclusion through flawed reasoning.
Drawing conclusions that do not logically follow from the starting assumptions.
g.example: If no solution is found, it must be because there is no problem.

g.description: Using a syllogism, or 3-step (major premise - minor premise - conclusion) argument in a faulty way.
g.example: Fish live in the sea. Whales live in the sea. Therefore, whales are fish.

g.description: Your argument relies on additional, unjustified premises.
g.example: If cars require gasoline to operate and this motorcycle operates, then this motorcycle is a car.

g.description: Leveraging a false implicit premise.
g.example: The kitchen light is on, so someone must be at home.

g.description: Using a syllogism that involves at least four terms instead of three.
g.example: All lawyers defend clients in court. This fruit is an avocado. Therefore, this fruit defends clients in court. — “Lawyer” and “avocado” are the same word in French, but its meaning changes: it refers to the legal profession in the first premise and to the fruit in the second. The reasoning therefore actually contains four terms instead of three.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism that wrongly uses at least one negative statement.
g.example: No feathered animal is a mammal. No mammal is a bird. Therefore, no bird has feathers.

g.description: Drawing a syllogical conclusion from two negative premises.
g.example: No feline is a dog. Some dogs are not cats. Therefore, some cats are not felines.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism that draws a negative conclusion from two positive premises.
g.example: All people are human. All humans are citizens. So, some citizens are not people.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism that has a positive conclusion and at least one negative premise.
g.example: No reptiles have fur, and no mammals are reptiles, therefore all mammals have fur.

g.description: Using a syllogism in which one term is wrongly distributed or undistributed.
g.example: If everyone who knows Julie likes her, and Paul likes her too, then surely, Paul must know her.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism in which a term that is undistributed in a premise is distributed in the conclusion.
g.example: All cats are felines. All felines are mammals. Therefore, all mammals are felines.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism in which the minor term is undistributed in its premiss but is distributed in the conclusion.
g.example: All whales are animals. All mammals are animals. Therefore, all animals are mammals.

g.description: Making a categorical syllogism in which the major term is undistributed in its premiss but is distributed in the conclusion.
g.example: All dogs are animals. No cat is a dog. Therefore, no cat is an animal.

g.description: Neither of the premises accounts for all members of the middle term, which consequently fails to link the major and minor term.
g.example: All students carry a backpack. My grandfather carries a backpack. Therefore, my grandfather must be a student.

g.description: Your argument claims that an action is desirable simply because it constitutes a change.
g.example: For the situation to improve, it must change. We are changing the situation, so we are improving the situation.

g.description: Using mutually exclusive assertions or premises.
g.example: I didn't damage this notebook; not only did I take the greatest care of it, but I never even touched it.

g.description: Drawing a conclusion that is incompatible with at least one of the premises.
g.example: Since everything has a cause and we can't infinitely trace back in time, God must necessarily exist.

g.description: Including elements within an argument that contradict one another.
g.example: We must always defend free speech, yet some opinions should never be expressed publicly.

g.description: Using three assertions from which only two can be simultaneously true.
g.example: Alice is always honest and always tells the truth. Alice claimed that if she were elected president, she wouldn't raise her salary. However, Alice gave herself a raise after being elected.

g.description: Cumulating several valid arguments that unfortunately contradict each other.
g.example: First, I did not borrow the pot; second, it already had a hole in it when I got it; third, I returned the pot in perfect condition.

g.description: Drawing a conclusion from incompatible premises.
g.example: I asked you to trust no one. Do you trust me? Then why didn't you listen to me?

g.description: Denying a concept while continuing to use it in the reasoning.
g.example: Reason and logic are not always reliable, so we shouldn't rely on them to establish the truth.

g.description: Drawing logical consequences from facts which are insufficient to support such an entailment.
g.example: This bowl is filled with cat food; therefore, there is a cat in the house.

g.description: Assigning a negative label to oneself or others based on a mistake or isolated event.
g.example: I'm a loser because I failed at this one task.

g.description: Predicting negative outcomes without any solid evidence.
g.example: I am definitely going to fail this interview, I have a feeling.

g.description: Assuming one knows what others think based on their behavior and nonverbal communication, without concrete evidence.
g.example: I'm sure my boss thinks I'm incompetent the way he looks at me.

g.description: Stacking several weak arguments in the hope of forming a strong argument.
g.example: This politician can't be honest; he doesn't smile in photos, my neighbor doesn't like him, and he often misspeaks.

g.description: Claiming to provide proof or evidence when in reality, no proof or evidence is actually presented.
g.example: Everyone knows that this policy is ineffective. Experts talk about it all the time on television.

g.description: Overwhelming an opponent with a rapid, continuous flow of arguments and claims, making a thorough and thoughtful refutation difficult.
g.example: How can you be competent if you don't even respond to my points on taxation, education, health care, and the environment? And I haven't even started on foreign policy yet!

g.description: Asking for a claim to be accepted without any reason or logical explanation.
g.example: You can believe me when I say that our product is superior to all others on the market.

g.description: Making two arguments or pieces of evidence appear to be logically equivalent when in fact they are not.
g.example: You ask me to do my homework after school, but I don't ask you to work overtime when you come home from the office.

g.description: Wrongly assuming that two different actions have the same moral value.
g.example: Some argue that vehicle speeds should be limited for safety, but opposing space travel because it is risky would be ridiculous.

g.description: Relying on premises that don't logically support the conclusion being made.
g.example: He was the best salesperson of the month; clearly, he would make an excellent team leader.

g.description: Defending a thesis using arguments that actually prove a different point.
g.example: Tobacco is expensive and addictive, so it makes sense to ban its use in public places.

g.description: Concluding that a phenomenon does not exist merely because the theoretical explanation offered is incorrect or inadequate.
g.example: They claim climate change is caused by human activities, but their predictive model has flaws. Therefore, climate change must not be real.

g.description: Misinterpreting the premises in order to arrive at an erroneous conclusion.
g.example: Since I believe in the sanctity of marriage, I think it should be between a man and a woman.

g.description: Offering insincere justifications to make a claim acceptable, without addressing its substance.
g.example: If I didn't pass the exam, it's just because the teacher hates me.

g.description: Proposing an unlikely explanation without considering more plausible ones.
g.example: This glitch ruined my presentation. I'm sure you did it on purpose to sabotage me!

g.description: Including information in an argument that appears to be unobtainable.
g.example: I know this man well. He has never cheated anyone.

g.description: Rejecting an idea by criticizing its origin rather than its content.
g.example: I'm not going to take advice on selecting wine from an American.

g.description: Combining logical propositions incorrectly, leading to flawed reasoning.
g.example: The more Swiss cheese you have, the more holes you have; but the more holes you have, the less Swiss cheese you have. Thus, the more Swiss cheese, the less you have.

g.description: Confusing what is possible, necessary, certain or obligatory, thereby distorting the reasoning.
g.example: Mom says I can't eat candies after I've brushed my teeth; however, I do it anyway without any difficulty.

g.description: Your argument alters the logical meaning by manipulating the scope of modal terms.
g.example: If you know something, you cannot be wrong. If you can't be wrong, then you are certain. Thus, certainty is a necessary condition of knowledge.

g.description: You do not correctly distinguish between what is necessary, obligatory, forbidden, possible, or permitted.
g.example: If you're capable of doing a hundred push-ups, then you're obligated to do them every morning.

g.description: Using mandatory imperative statements like 'must' or 'should' which impose unrealistic expectations on oneself or others.
g.example: I should always be able to control my emotions.

g.description: Using arguments that do not properly take the temporal dimension into account.
g.example: Since the train left late, it is inevitable that we will arrive late.

g.description: Confusing what is necessarily false with what might merely be improbable.
g.example: The President can't not have had an extensive political training.

g.description: Confusing what one knows with what one believes, undermining the validity of one's argument.
g.example: One cannot know the true nature of the universe since it goes beyond human comprehension.

g.description: Mistakenly assuming that different knowledge about objects corresponds to different properties of those objects.
g.example: Lois Lane thinks Superman can fly. Lois Lane thinks Clark Kent cannot fly. Therefore Superman and Clark Kent are not the same person.

g.description: Misusing quantifiers such as "all", "none" or "some".
g.example: All philosophers are wise, although some of them are idiots.

g.description: Erroneously transposing quantifiers.
g.example: In every city, there's a restaurant considered the best in town. Thus, there is a restaurant considered the best in all cities.

g.description: Drawing a conclusion directly from a single premise incorrectly, attributing properties or conclusions that are not logically supported by that premise.
g.example: It's false that all dogs are white, therefore there are no white dogs.

g.description: Incorrectly assuming that the presence of 'some' necessarily implies the existence of 'others' who are not, which is not logically founded.
g.example: Some of our clients are dissatisfied with our service; therefore, there must be clients who are satisfied.

g.description: Arguing that since it is false that all have a property, it is false that some have it.
g.example: As it is false that all birds can fly, it is false that some birds can fly.

g.description: Arguing that, since some do not have a property, none has it.
g.example: Since not all smartphones are waterproof, your smartphone is not waterproof.

g.description: Arguing that, since some have a property, no one can not have the property. (All have it)
g.example: Some cats can swim, so all cats can swim

g.description: Arguing that, it being not true that all have a property, then no noe has it.
g.example: It is not true that all dogs have fangs, so no dog has fangs.

g.description: Incorrectly reversing the relationship between subject and predicate while negating one of them in an argument.
g.example: No Catholic is Jewish; therefore, no non-Jew is non-Catholic.

g.description: Arguing from the non-fulfillment of a rule's specific conditions to affirm the validity of its opposite.
g.example: Businesses need to obtain consent to collect personal data from internet users. Therefore, they can do so without consent for those not using the internet.

g.description: Incorrectly reversing the relationship between subject and predicate in an argument.
g.example: Some mammals are not cats; therefore, some cats are not mammals.

g.description: You confuse the use of a universal quantifier (“all,” “none”) with that of a particular quantifier (“some,” “a few”).
g.example: You can't be from this country because you are short and it has the tallest people.

g.description: Assuming that elements exist in the set on which an argument is based, without providing proof.
g.example: All terrorists will be prosecuted; therefore, some of the people prosecuted will be terrorists.

g.description: Making statements without specifying the quantifier, leading to interpretations as if it applies to all, none, or only some.
g.example: Women can endure more than men.

g.description: Using one or more examples as "proof" for a more general statement.
g.example: Your siblings didn't face these issues. I don't see why it would be any different for you.

g.description: Using basic logical propositions connected by 'and', 'or', 'if... then' incorrectly, leading to false conclusions.
g.example: It can't be both raining and snowing; therefore, if it's not raining, it is snowing.

g.description: Arguing that certain clauses can't be true or false at the same time due to a mistaken belief in their exclusivity.
g.example: One cannot be working and on vacation at the same time. You're not at work, so you must be on vacation.

g.description: To negate 2 assertions linked by "AND," you forget to consider that both can be false.
g.example: It can't be both raining and snowing at the same time. It's not raining, therefore it's snowing.

g.description: Claiming that the terms of an "or" statement can't be simultaneously true.
g.example: To succeed in this industry, you either have to be very rich or very handsome. I am very handsome, so don't assume I am wealthy.

g.description: Reversing an implication by treating its conclusion as if it automatically led back to its starting point.
g.example: If a building is a library, it contains books. This building contains books, therefore it is a library.

g.description: Stating that since the consequent is true, the premisse of an implication is true. That is a confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions.
g.example: After a rain, the ground is always wet. The ground is wet, therefore it must have rained.

g.description: Denying the consequence of a logical deduction by denying a sufficient condition.
g.example: If there is fire, there is smoke. There is no fire, so there is no smoke.

g.description: Invalidating a conclusion on grounds of the Falsity of a sufficient condition.
g.example: If it rains, the ground gets wet. It didn't rain, so the ground isn't wet.

g.description: Assuming a cause-and-effect relationship that is either unproven or incorrect.
g.example: No wonder he gets such good grades at school: he's the teacher's pet!

g.description: Asserting a causal relation between two phenomena on grounds of them being correlated.
g.example: There are more births in regions that have more storks' nests. So it must be the storks that bring the babies.

g.description: Assuming that one event is the cause of another solely because it preceded it in time.
g.example: The blackbird sings just before sunrise; hence, the blackbird's singing makes the sun rise.

g.description: Causally linking two events, forgetting about the possibility of a common cause for them.
g.example: Since my city installed more streetlights, acts of vandalism have increased. Surely, the extra lighting is pushing young people to commit more damage.

g.description: Assuming overly simplistic causes for a phenomenon, neglecting the complexity of factors that might be involved.
g.example: My car, which I was driving while drunk and on the phone, skidded off the road because of a squirrel.

g.description: Wrongly attributing a complex outcome to one singular cause.
g.example: It's the introduction of foxes that led to the disappearance of the rabbits.

g.description: Assigning personal responsibility, including resulting praise or blame, for events over which one has little or no control.
g.example: It's my fault the meeting went poorly.

g.description: Rejecting a conclusion simply because one possible cause did not occur, thereby confusing a cause with a necessary condition.
g.example: If it rains, roads are wet. It hasn't rained, therefore roads are not wet.

g.description: Confusing the cause with the effect, thus reversing the causal dynamic.
g.example: Using a wheelchair is dangerous, since most people who use one have been in accidents.

g.description: A posteriori attributing (often self-serving) causes to a chance event.
g.example: 100% of lottery winners took a chance. You should too.

g.description: Imagining a sequence of events without taking their random independence into account.
g.example: I tossed a coin ten times and it always landed on heads, so next time it will land on tails.

g.description: Mistakenly believing that two combined wrongs can produce a just result.
g.example: The boss does not pay his taxes, so I will not hesitate to help myself from the cash register.

g.description: Encouraging the cause of an issue as a way to solve the issue itself.
g.example: To quit smoking, start by smoking even more so that you grow disgusted by it.

g.description: Proposing to forget a problem by engaging in harmful distractions that might aggravate it.
g.example: John says he drinks to forget his work problems, which have actually worsened because of his excessive drinking.

g.description: Claiming that the source making the argument has spoken or acted in a way inconsistent with the argument.
g.example: How can you promote the benefits of physical exercise when you always take the elevator instead of the stairs?

g.description: Assuming the opposite of what induction suggests.
g.example: It has rained every day this week, so I expect tomorrow will be sunny.

g.description: Mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one.
g.example: If you passed the exam, it means you must have studied hard, right?

g.description: extending the veracity of one element of a tale to thewhole of the tale.
g.example: Archaeologists have found the remains of Sodom and Gomorrah! This means the Bible is true!

g.description: Inferring the antecedent from the consequent of an implication without considering alternate causes.
g.example: After it rains, the ground is always wet; the ground is wet; therefore, it must have rained.

g.description: Making a dubious analogy and assuming without proof that two similar situations will have the same result.
g.example: Many successful individuals dropped out of school to pursue their passions. I'm also not wasting time on my studies; I've got better things to focus on.

g.description: Attempting to prove a proposition by using an argument that takes the proposition for granted.
g.example: It is better to have a cat than a dog, because cats make better pets.

g.description: Feeling the need to constantly prove that one's opinions and actions are correct.
g.example: I must win this argument to show I'm right.

g.description: Rejecting a proposal by predicting an unlikely sequence of negative events.
g.example: If we let him have seconds, he'll get into the habit of overeating and eventually become obese.

g.description: Trying to explain something whose existence isn't proven.
g.example: If billions of children are dying from hunger daily, that's because everyone is too selfish to care.

g.description: Employing an analogy that assumes the conclusion it is meant to demonstrate, dubiously equating two scenarios.
g.example: Internet access is a human right, just like access to clean water. Everyone needs water to survive, so everyone needs internet to live.

g.description: Proving something else than the question being discussed.
g.example: This medication has not received marketing authorization. Yet it has been proven to do no harm.

g.description: Formulating a question that subtly assumes a false or controversial premise.
g.example: Have you stopped mistreating your dog?

g.description: Concluding in a circle, each argument relying on acceptance of the conclusion.
g.example: The existence of the Bible proves the existence of God, since it was God who dictated it to humans.

g.description: Invoking a premise which only makes sense if the conclusion is already accepted, reinforcing the conclusion without genuine argument.
g.example: Clear and distinct perceptions are only possible through God, but proving God's existence needs those same clear and distinct perceptions.

g.description: The reasoning includes inaccuracies in the use of numerical information.
Drawing conclusions based on incorrect mathematical reasoning.
g.example: Car A's average acceleration is greater than Car B's; therefore, Car A is going faster than Car B.

g.description: Using invalid mathematical reasoning.
g.example: In the fable by La Fontaine, each time the hare moves forward, the tortoise moves forward as well, preventing the hare from catching up.

g.description: Presenting unfounded theories as scientific facts.
g.example: I argue that arranging furniture according to Feng Shui principles will improve your health and wealth because it's based on ancient geometrical calculations.

g.description: Using a mathematical symbol in a meaning other than its established one to mislead.
g.example: I use the '%' symbol to mean 'percent' throughout most of my speech, but subtly use it as a sign of proportion in one key case, misleading people.

g.description: You hide or ignore an error in your calculation to support an incorrect argument.
g.example: I divided all the quantities by two, as you advised me, and the cooking time as well. Result: the cake came out completely raw.

g.description: Falsely claiming that two different numbers are equal by hiding a calculation error.
g.example: During a debate, a participant confidently explains that multiplying a number by a million is the same as dividing it by a million, as long as the context is 'proportional'.

g.description: Using reasoning that involves a hidden division by zero.
g.example: By simplifying both sides of this equality by their common factor, we have therefore demonstrated that 1 = 2.

g.description: Making errors in the calculation from which conclusions are drawn.
g.example: Given that a croissant costs one euro and fifty cents, with ten euros you can easily buy eight.

g.description: Using numerical data that are imprecise or misinterpreted to support an argument.
g.example: When you tell me that my investment has increased by 10% in the last two years, you're implying it's increased 20% in total, right?

g.description: Using paradoxical reasoning to muddy the waters.
g.example: Just save water so that we can consume it more in the future.

g.description: Shifting an element from one set to another, confusingly changing the average qualities of both sets.
g.example: When the Okies moved from Oklahoma to California, they managed to raise the average intelligence level in both states.

g.description: You present a paradoxical set that can neither include itself nor exclude itself.
g.example: A barber shaves only those who do not shave themselves. Does he shave himself?

g.description: You exaggerate the scope of a market to evade an accusation of monopoly.
g.example: How can you accuse us of a monopoly when we are just a small player compared to the giants at this trade show?

g.description: You make an erroneous probability calculation when choosing between two options.
g.example: The amount is either double or half. Go ahead—you have more to gain than to lose.

g.description: Creating confusion by adding amounts that should not be added together.
g.example: Three friends each pay $10 for a meal totaling $25. The server returns $3, keeping $2 for himself. By adding the $27 given with $2 the server kept, it seems $1 is missing from the original $30.

g.description: Counting the same element twice in a calculation, thereby distorting the final result.
g.example: If we flip a coin twice, I'm sure I'll win at least once.

g.description: Your arguments are based on imprecise data, which leads to uncertain conclusions.
g.example: Try our new formula with double fresh effect for the same price.

g.description: Erroneously attempting to make a reasonable argument into an absurd one, by taking the argument to the extremes.
g.example: They say exercise is good for health, but running a marathon every day is just going to wear you out.

g.description: Choosing less plausible explanations over more likely ones.
g.example: He must really have a grudge against me for giving me such a poor grade.

g.description: To argue that something must be forbidden because it is sometimes abused.
g.example: Since some parents abusively use television as a babysitter for their children, access to television should be banned for all minors.

g.description: You present dramatic and unlikely consequences as inevitable in order to discourage an action.
g.example: This health policy will lead to endless waiting lists, overwhelmed practitioners, poor quality care, untreated patients, and an unprecedented spike in mortality rates.

g.description: You reject a proposal by predicting an unlikely series of negative events.
g.example: If you let him have another piece, he'll get used to eating too much and end up obese.

g.description: Presenting opposing viewpoints as more balanced than they actually are.
g.example: The reality of global warming is a matter of debate within the scientific community.

g.description: Arguing that destroying things to rebuild them anew enriches society as a whole.
g.example: After the storm, shop windows were shattered. This should boost the local economy with all the necessary repairs.

g.description: Asserting that the truth must be found as a compromise between two opposite positions.
g.example: You prefer Monday and I Wednesday: let's meetup on Tuesday.

g.description: Having a proposal, developed with several other people, lack coherence because no authority unified everyone's ideas.
g.example: Our software includes all the features requested by each department to ensure its relevance.

g.description: Claiming that a conclusion cannot be found on the pretext that experts disagree.
g.example: In this political matter, the experts express so many different opinions that it would be impossible for me to form a sound view. I might as well change nothing and leave things as they are.
g.text: Appeal to conflict as a pretext

g.description: Contradicting the consensus on well-established facts to show the reality as uncertain and defend spurious hypotheses
g.example: Even though cigarette tar is established to be carcinogenic, everyone inhales many carcinogenic fine particles in the street. Cigarettes would therefore be no more harmful.

g.description: Presenting numerical data in a manner that implies better precision than is justified, often to pretend exaggerated accuracy.
g.example: This dinosaur skeleton is 100,000,005 years old, because an expert told me 5 years ago that it was 100 million years old.

g.description: Presenting data in a biased way to support an argument.
g.example: See, after sales collapsed last month, our numbers have almost doubled this month! Our customers have decided to trust us again.

g.description: You establish inaccurate quantitative relationships between elements or data.
g.example: The global warming curve closely follows the decline in the birth rate. The link between the two is therefore established.

g.description: Involving an improper appreciation of infinite notions.
g.example: This statement is true. — But how do you know? I verified it. — But how did you verify that verification? And how did you verify the verification of that verification? … — An infinite regress of epistemic justification: each level of evidence requires another.

g.description: Involving an improper appreciation of an infinite sequence of justifications.
g.example: If the universe is infinite, there must be something beyond every limit. Therefore, what lies beyond? It's an endless question.

g.description: Wrongly denouncing an infinite regress as vicious.
g.example: Asking 'why' to every explanation just leads you into an endless loop of questions with no definitive answer.

g.description: Demanding justification for each justification, in a never ending process.
g.example: But why? Where does that information come from? And why should I believe that source?

g.description: Building an infinite chain of causality that leads to inconsistency.
g.example: But if god made Man, who made God?

g.description: Trying to explain a phenomenon by reducing it to a simpler version of itself, which leads to circular reasoning.
g.example: Consider the retina as a movie screen you are watching from behind your brain to understand the visual system.

g.description: You deny the continuous or gradual nature of a phenomenon and demand strict boundaries where none exist.
g.example: What difference does one more cigarette make?

g.description: Denying the possibility of an opposite state by arguing that there is no decisive boundary between the two states.
g.example: There is risk in everything. If we start wearing helmets to ride a bike, we might as well wear helmets all the time!

g.description: Misusing probabilistic reasoning to bolster an argument, thereby distorting the logical conclusion.
g.example: The DNA left by the perpetrator of this crime has a particular trait found in the accused and in only 10% of the population; one can therefore claim with 90% certainty that this man is guilty.

g.description: You judge a specific situation to be more likely than a more general one, even though it cannot be.
g.example: He has a good chance of winning this match, but his chances would be even better if he lost the first set, as he often does, and then won the next two.

g.description: You present a series of seemingly fair bets without taking into account the risk of losing everything in the long run.
