g.example: I always bet on red at roulette: after several spins, my color is bound to come up eventually. This strategy is therefore infallible, and I will double my bet on the next round to recover my losses.

g.description: Vainly trusting one's self-control to enable them to stop playing while still ahead in winnings and thus avoid bankrupcy.
g.example: I'll stop betting as soon as I've gained more than I've lost.

g.description: Concluding, on the basis of an unlikely outcome of a random process, that the process is likely to have occurred many times before.
g.example: You got three double-sixes in a row? But since when have you been playing?

g.description: Arguing that statistical variations will be compensated by future outcomes of random bets.
g.example: After all the terrible things that have happened to me today, I think my luck is about to change, so I'm going to play the lottery.

g.description: You believe that your recent successes will increase your chances of succeeding again.
g.example: I made my last three baskets: I’m on a hot streak, so I’m definitely going to make the next shot.

g.description: Basing an argument on a conjecture that itself presupposes the occurrence of a given event.
g.example: I think that by taking the 8 a.m. flight tomorrow rather than the 8 p.m. one tonight, I will have a better chance of arriving on time for my meeting, because delays are statistically less frequent in the morning.

g.description: Assuming that, given two events A and B, the probability of A happening given that B has happened is about the same as the probability of B given A.
g.example: 90% of patients who followed this treatment recovered. It is therefore 90% effective.

g.description: Confusing the general probability of an occurrence with the probability that it happened in a specific case.
g.example: The chance of both infants being victims of sudden infant death syndrome is less than one in the entire population of our country. This must mean their mother is guilty.

g.description: Predicting extreme events based on erroneous probabilistic assumptions.
g.example: I know the number of humans who came before us; it is fairly small, so there is a strong chance that the total number of those who will follow us is only a small multiple of it, and therefore our end is near.

g.description: Estimating conditional probabilities without taking into account baseline probabilities.
g.example: I have a sore neck, and it is one of the main symptoms of meningitis. I am really afraid I might have it.

g.description: Treating as certain what is merely a possibility.
g.example: If I forgot to take my umbrella, it's surely going to rain.

g.description: Making an argument based on the worst-case scenario rather than the most probable scenario.
g.example: You should buy an alarm: you never know, these days.

g.description: Attributing a significant relationship to what is merely a simple coincidence.
g.example: The productivity curve clearly follows that of coffee consumption. Coffee must therefore be the cause.

g.description: Perceiving a relationship between two unrelated variables.
g.example: Every time I wear this sweater, my team wins; this sweater therefore brings them luck.

g.description: Perceiving patterns or trends in random or unrelated data, creating a false impression of correlation.
g.example: Look at this sequence of numbers; surely, there's a hidden pattern here!

g.description: Drawing a conclusion from a tendency observed in a sample, but without having declared the searched tendency prior to studying the sample.
g.example: In analyzing the eating habits of one hundred people, we found that those who eat chocolate in the morning are more productive. This proves that chocolate increases productivity.

g.description: Seeing in statistical anomalies the proof of some irrational beliefs.
g.example: Let me show you our latest study based on this insurance company's statistics, finally proving the effect of Mars in our lives.

g.description: You arrange the facts in a biased way to support your claim, with no regard for scientific rigor.
g.example: Labor costs are too high in France. This is proven by our failure to secure the tender.

g.description: Multiplying statistical comparisons untill one proves the hypothesis thanks to luck.
g.example: After conducting 20 studies, one of them showed a statistical risk above 5%. Therefore, this is considered proof of the risk.

g.description: Assigning a common cause to a pattern. This results in forcing the outcome to adjust to one's belief, shaping the facts until they fit the theory.
g.example: Pyramids can be found in Mexico, Egypt, and Cambodia, which proves that the same entity inspired all these peoples.

g.description: Mistakenly attributing a particular effect to what is merely a return to normal after a fluctuation.
g.example: Since I was very ill, I prayed and that healed me.

g.description: Seeing the succession of two phenomena as the proof that the one occuring first is the cause of the one occuring after.
g.example: The blackbird sings just before sunrise, so the blackbird's song must cause the sun to rise.

g.description: Seeing the concomitance of two phenomena as proof that one causes the other.
g.example: Following the stats, global warming trends coincide with increased ice cream sales; hence, ice cream must contribute to global warming.

g.description: Attributing to an entire group the characteristics of its elements, or vice versa.
g.example: A truck consumes more fuel than a car; one can therefore infer that trucks consume, in total, more fuel than cars.

g.description: Attributing properties of a whole set to each of its individual part.
g.example: Royal Bengal tigers are deemed to vanish soon; therefore, this Royal Bengal tiger will likely die young.

g.description: Attempting to explain a thing in terms of what it reduces to but failing to consider the complexity of the issue, thus oversimplifying.
g.example: The team lost the match, so each player must lack talent.

g.description: Deducing, from statistical data, inferences about individuals from inference for the group to which these individuals belong.
g.example: Why complain? You are American; your country is among the richest on the planet.

g.description: Considering that variables applying to individuals are correlated like the variables that apply to the aggregate of individuals.
g.example: The more computers a country has, the more chocolate it sells. So, it's only natural that the more time I spend in front of my screen, the more chocolate I eat.

g.description: Infering the mean value for a subset from the mean value of the general set.
g.example: On average, people in this town live until 75 years old; hence, I should have a good chance of living at least that long.

g.description: Mistaking the mean for the median, two statistical measures that can vastly differ.
g.example: I find it hard to believe all these residential buildings are so rundown given the resources the municipality has.

g.description: You wrongly interpret a statistical trend that reverses when groups are combined, without taking key variables into account.
g.example: I prefer going to the local hospital because the survival rate there is much higher than that at the cancer-specialized hospital.

g.description: Atrributing properties of the parts of a set to the whole set.
g.example: All these plants will die one day, so this garden will disappear.

g.description: Considering that the part used to represent or stand for a whole is an accurate reflection of that whole.
g.example: His suit is of rare elegance, he must have a meeting with the boss.

g.description: Believing that individual development in a living organism retraces the evolutionary stages of its species.
g.example: Human embryos briefly exhibit structures resembling gills, which is taken by some to support aquatic ancestry of humans.

g.description: Applying a general rule to a particular case, ignoring the exceptions that may apply.
g.example: My car goes at 130 km an hour, I only need a few minutes to cross the city.

g.description: Applying a generalization that comes with many qualifications which strip away so many cases, that what is left might seem significantly less impressive than the original claim.
g.example: These companies are very profitable because they employ innovative marketing strategies. Therefore, to be profitable, a company must employ these same strategies.

g.description: Giving too much weight to particular cases and treating them as if they constituted a universal norm.
g.example: We notice an increase in assaults outside bars at 2 a.m. This proves that assaults are mainly caused by alcohol.

g.description: Basing reasoning on an abusive generalisation of common beliefs that categorise objects, people, or groups.
g.example: I can't wait to taste those delicious dishes. I've heard so much good about French cuisine.

g.description: Applying an exception to a generalisation to cases where the generalisation itself should apply.
g.example: If people with multiple sclerosis are allowed to use marijuana, then everyone should be allowed to use it.

g.description: Ignoring that the particular case to which a general rule is applied indeed constitutes an exception to that rule.
g.example: Using a knife on people is a crime. Surgeons use knives on people. Therefore, surgeons are criminals.

g.description: Saving a generalization from a counterexample by changing its definition in order to exclude that counterexample.
g.example: — All Scots are red-haired. — Angus is Scottish, but he is not red-haired. — Then he is not a true Scotsman.

g.description: You draw conclusions from a sample that is not representative of the target population.
g.example: This yoghurt is the best, since it was acclaimed by 80% of the consumers surveyed in our store.

g.description: Selecting or highlighting specific data to support an argument, while neglecting other pertinent data.
g.example: Look at the results of these three exceptional students at our school; it definitely proves the excellence of our educational system.

g.description: Misinterpreting data or results by focusing only on the most noticeable or significant elements, while overlooking less apparent but equally important data.
g.example: We saw an increase in sales in stores where we advertised, so our ad campaign is a success.

g.description: Assuming that the media coverage of a certain class or category is representative of the class or category in whole.
g.example: The media only talks about political scandals; this proves that all politicians are corrupt.

g.description: You establish a general rule based on accurate statistical data, but without taking into account important information that runs counter to your claim.
g.example: There were never any incidents in this amusement park, so it's completely safe to go there; no need to worry about safety measures.

g.description: Concentrating only on past successes of a project while neglecting unseen failures that may also be relevant.
g.example: Look at all these companies worth billions after a few years in business; it demonstrates the huge potential of startups.

g.description: Generalizing based on examples that can only confirm the hypothesis.
g.example: All toupées look fake; I've never seen one that I couldn't tell was fake.

g.description: Focusing only on the evidence that supports an argument, while excluding anything that could challenge it.
g.example: I've read dozens of articles that back up my viewpoint, which surely means I am right.

g.description: Evaluating a group on the basis of the performance of the "best" groupmembers.
g.example: This basketball player is quite tall, all tall people must be excellent at basketball.

g.description: Evaluating a group on the basis of the performance of the "worst" groupmembers.
g.example: The news spoke about all these students who cheated during exams. This proves conclusively that the overall level of education is declining.

g.description: Estimating probabilities on the basis of qualitative subjective information rather than on the basis of quantitative statistical data.
g.example: All my friends love superhero movies; they must be the favorite genre of our time.

g.description: Preferring compelling anecdotes over rigorous statistics to support an argument.
g.example: Do you remember the story about a child attacked by a dog? It goes to show that these animals are dangerous and should be avoided.

g.description: Selectively pointing to evidence that supports a position.
g.example: Mom didn't say no, I got a good mark and it's my favourite color. Please buy me this candy!

g.description: Arguing on the basis of a sample that does not accurately represent reality.
g.example: I asked my friends about their opinions on the latest smartphone on the market, and all of them love it. It must be the best phone available right now.

g.description: Denying an inductive argument its proper conclusion despite strong evidence, claiming the latter is mere coincidence.
g.example: I've ordered several times from this online supplier successfully. Those complaining about bad experiences are just unlucky.

g.description: Inferring a general rule from too small a sample.
g.example: Have you seen the increase in fraud cases among new employees? The new generation is unreliable.

g.description: Not considering the sample size when evaluating data reliability.
g.example: I believe in this poll, even though it only asked 10 people.

g.description: Making a general rule based on a very small number of examples.
g.example: After noticing his last two novels received rave reviews, Mark concludes that all future books by this author will be masterpieces too.

g.description: Using tactics to manipulate the audience rather than using logical reasoning.
Using methods that subtly steer interlocutors' viewpoints, often without them realizing it.
g.example: Remember: there are those who have the privilege to choose and those who endure the choices of others. Act accordingly.

g.description: Seeking to persuade beyond the meaning of words, notably through body language or vocal inflections.
g.example: I sighed and rolled my eyes several times during their speech to destabilize them.

g.description: You use touch to communicate with and influence the person you are speaking to.
g.example: He took me in his arms; I could no longer say no to him.

g.description: Using one's appearance to alter others' perception of one's statements.
g.example: By dressing simply, in a way that inspires trust, I influenced the audience's perception before I even spoke.

g.description: Using a choice of attire as a strategy to affect an audience's opinion.
g.example: My decision to wear a traditional attire to the conference on cultural diversity elicited respect and sparked curiosity.

g.description: Adapting one's appearance to display symbols of group belonging in order to influence an audience.
g.example: By wearing my military jacket during the meeting, I immediately gave the impression of belonging to the veterans' group.

g.description: Utilizing body movements to influence an audience.
g.example: By moving toward the audience and making precise hand gestures, I captivated the audience and made my message more persuasive.

g.description: Positioning the body in a way that sends a message to one's interlocutor.
g.example: Standing tall with shoulders back, I communicated unwavering confidence to the crowd.

g.description: Crossing one's arms can symbolize a closed, defensive stance or signify reluctance to engage.
g.example: By crossing my arms, I intuitively communicated a sense of disagreement and a defensive stance, without uttering a single word.

g.description: Taking up a position in which the hands are on the hips and the elbows are bowed outward, often expressing authority or determination.
g.example: With hands on my hips and elbows out, I broadcasted an aura of authority, indicating that I was ready to handle any challenge.

g.description: Manipulating physical distance with an interlocutor to impact the interaction.
g.example: I stepped back slightly, creating a sense of space and reducing the tension.

g.description: Seeking to influence an audience by deliberately using hand or body gestures.
g.example: I gestured towards the door, subtly suggesting it was time for him to leave.

g.description: Expressing confusion or misunderstanding through disordered hand or facial gestures.
g.example: I shrugged my shoulders while expressing my uncertainty about this upcoming decision to visibly show my indecision.

g.description: Showing uncertainty or nervousness by not knowing what to do with one's hands.
g.example: My hands moved from one place to another on the podium, betraying my apparent nervousness.

g.description: Bringing hands to the face, often indicative of deep thought, surprise, or emotion.
g.example: Covering my face with my hands in shock after hearing the unexpected news.

g.description: Clenching fists, often as a sign of anger, determination, or frustration.
g.example: I clenched my fists to channel my frustration at the unfair comments.

g.description: Rotating thumbs around each other, often indicating boredom or impatience.
g.example: While awaiting a delayed response during the meeting, I absentmindedly twiddle my thumbs.

g.description: Covering one's face with one's hand to express frustration or embarrassment.
g.example: I covered my face with my hand when I realized the glaring mistake I had made during the presentation.

g.description: Accompanying one's words with an aggressive gesture to underline one's resolve and intimidate.
g.example: My pointed finger accented each word as I made my stance clear, ensuring my opposition knew my determination.

g.description: Lowering the thumb to express disapproval or rejection.
g.example: Giving a thumbs-down after a disappointing performance, signaling disapproval without needing words.

g.description: Placing one's hands behind one's head to mimic donkey ears, as a sign of self-deprecation or mockery.
g.example: Placing hands behind my head to mimic donkey ears, jokingly admitting a mistake amid laughter from the team.

g.description: Twirling or tapping one's index finger against one's temple to suggest someone is crazy or foolish.
g.example: Tapping my temple with a finger while chuckling, indicating that someone's idea sounds absurd.

g.description: Snapping one's fingers, often to attract attention or keep rhythm.
g.example: Snapping fingers at a concert, I keep up with the rhythm and connect to the music.

g.description: Raising the hand with the index and little finger apart, a gesture that can have varying meanings depending on the context.
g.example: Raising my hand in the 'sign of the horns' at a concert, I feel connected to the crowd and the rebellious spirit of the music.

g.description: Touching the nose with the thumb to indicate mockery or contempt.
g.example: Thumbing the nose while making a derisive snort, openly displaying contempt for the idea being discussed.

g.description: Raising the middle finger as a sign of insult or defiance.
g.example: Flipping the middle finger defiantly from across the room, challenging someone's authority in a blatant display of disrespect.

g.description: Using the 'bras d'honneur' gesture, considered offensive in many cultures, by bending an arm and lifting the forearm with a clenched fist.
g.example: In the heat of the argument, I flashed the 'bras d'honneur', inciting a not-so-subtle wave of disdain from those around.

g.description: Using a celebratory gesture to suggest the happy occurrence of an agreement in principle.
g.example: We raised our arms in the air shouting 'victory' when the jury announced our project as the winner.

g.description: Raising a clenched fist to the sky, often as a sign of determination or protest.
g.example: Raising a fist in the air during a protest march to show solidarity and defiance.

g.description: Rubbing one's hands together, often as a sign of anticipation or satisfaction.
g.example: Rubbing hands together gleefully before unveiling a surprise.

g.description: Raising a hand with the index and middle fingers apart as a sign of victory or peace.
g.example: Flashing a V sign to the crowd as a symbol of peace during a rally.

g.description: Standing and applauding to express exceptional respect or admiration.
g.example: The audience rising to their feet for a standing ovation after an inspiring speech.

g.description: Raising one's thumb as a sign of approval, satisfaction, or to indicate that all is well.
g.example: Giving a thumbs-up to signal your agreement with the decision made during a meeting.

g.description: Slapping the palm of one's hand against another person's in midair as a sign of celebration or agreement.
g.example: I shared a high five with my teammate after their successful action, acknowledging a job well done.

g.description: Clapping one's hands together to express approval or appreciation.
g.example: A standing ovation at the end of a breathtaking performance to show immense admiration.

g.description: Striking one's hands together rhythmically, often to accompany music or to encourage.
g.example: Clapping along to the beat at a concert to show your enjoyment and support for the artist.

g.description: Using gestures to signify adherence to a particular ideology, reinforcing the message and leaving a lasting impression on the audience.
g.example: Wearing a pin at the rally, I silently show my support for our cause.

g.description: Clasping hands together, often as a gesture of prayer, supplication, request, or gratitude.
g.example: Clasping my hands together, I expressed my heartfelt gratitude to those who supported me during difficult times.

g.description: Raising a finger in the air to draw attention or to indicate having something to say.
g.example: Elevating my finger, I signalled my eagerness to contribute to the debate, hoping to draw the room's attention.

g.description: Raising a clenched fist in the air, often a gesture of solidarity, resistance, or protest.
g.example: I raised my fist high at the protest, uniting with the voices calling for change and justice.

g.description: Extending the right arm forward with the palm down, historically associated with fascism.
g.example: Extending my right arm in the air, I replicated a gesture historically tied to a dark era, to illustrate its power in my presentation on political symbols.

g.description: Raising three fingers in the air, often used as a symbol of resistance or solidarity.
g.example: Raising three fingers in unity during the rally, symbolizing our collective resilience and hope.

g.description: Placing hands upon another person as a gesture of blessing or healing.
g.example: Placing my hands gently on the shoulders of a loved one, imparting a blessing of health and protection.

g.description: Bowing deeply to touch the ground with one's forehead as a gesture of profound devotion or respect.
g.example: As I approach the altar, I bow down in prostration, deeply embodying the gesture of respect and devotion.

g.description: Using the sign of the cross on one's body as a gesture of devotion and prayer within Christianity.
g.example: Making the sign of the cross on my chest as I entered the room, invoking a silent prayer for guidance.

g.description: Performing a greeting gesture to reinforce the notion of agreement.
g.example: I nodded at every proposal put forward to encourage participation and general agreement.

g.description: Separate the middle and ring fingers while raising the hand, referencing the popular salute in the 'Star Trek' series.
g.example: Meeting other Star Trek fans, I give a Vulcan salute to express a shared bond without words.

g.description: Join hands in front of the face and slightly bow the head as a sign of respect, typical of Thai culture.
g.example: While meeting a Thai colleague, I join my hands and bow slightly, showing my respect for their culture.

g.description: Joining palms in front of the heart or forehead as a sign of greeting, respect, or prayer.
g.example: In a calm setting, he performed a Namaste, joining palms in front of his heart, expressing his respect and peaceful intentions.

g.description: Bowing forward with hands on thighs as a sign of respect in Japanese martial arts.
g.example: He bowed to his opponent, showing respect in the martial arts context.

g.description: Raising three fingers of the right hand as a sign of greeting or allegiance to the principles of scouting.
g.example: During a scouting event, participants give a three-finger salute, emphasizing their commitment to scouting values.

g.description: Extending the arm forward, palm down, as a gesture of greeting or respect in a historical or symbolic context.
g.example: During a public gathering, he extended his arm forward, palm down, in a respectful gesture to the audience.

g.description: Raising the hand to the forehead as a sign of respect and hierarchical recognition in a military context.
g.example: During the ceremony, the soldiers gave a salute to the flag as it was raised.

g.description: Briefly touching or lifting one's hat as a sign of respect or greeting.
g.example: As he walked into the room, he gave a quick hat tip in greeting to the assembled group.

g.description: Engaging in the physical act of gripping hands as a form of greeting or to signify agreement.
g.example: After negotiating the terms, both parties shared a firm handshake, symbolizing the conclusion of the agreement.

g.description: Making a formal gesture to show respect and elicit goodwill from an interlocutor.
g.example: We shook hands with each participant at the start of the meeting to demonstrate respect and emphasize the significance of the dialogue.

g.description: Placing a hand over one's heart as a gesture of sincere respect, consideration, or gratitude.
g.example: During the pledge of allegiance, she placed her hand over her heart, signifying her loyalty to the country.

g.description: You bow while holding your dress to express your consideration.
g.example: Performing a curtsy can indicate deep respect or be used ironically to emphasize a supposed superiority.

g.description: A gesture of deep respect and devotion, prostrating oneself before another.
g.example: In a display of utmost respect, the envoy performed a kowtow before the emperor.

g.description: Leaning the body towards an interlocutor to express respect or admiration.
g.example: He bowed deeply to the audience in gratitude after his piano recital.

g.description: Kneeling on one knee as a gesture of devotion.
g.example: In the ancient ceremony, the knight genuflected before the queen, pledging his loyalty.

g.description: Assuming a strict upright posture to salute a superior officer in a military context.
g.example: During the ceremony, the soldiers stood at attention as the national anthem played, showing their respect.

g.description: Kissing someone's hand as a sign of deep respect or devotion.
g.example: At the formal dinner, John respectfully kissed the hand of the elderly lady as a sign of his esteem.

g.description: Building rapport with listeners through a friendly gesture to win their sympathy.
g.example: Placing my hand on his shoulder during the conversation to create a relaxed and friendly atmosphere.

g.description: Crossing the index and middle fingers in hope of luck, or to signal that one is jesting or lying.
g.example: Crossing fingers behind your back while making a promise to signify jest or to keep fingers crossed for luck.

g.description: Extending the hand with the palm out and the thumb and pinkie raised as a friendly and relaxed greeting.
g.example: During a casual meeting, I give a shaka sign, signaling a relaxed and friendly greeting to the group.

g.description: You greet someone by bumping fists, usually to signal camaraderie or agreement.
g.example: A 'fist bump' is sometimes used as a substitute for a handshake to bring casualness or specific camaraderie into play.

g.description: Exchanging a formal embrace to express respect or to signify an official agreement.
g.example: Initiating a hug at a meeting can subtly enforce a climate of familiarity or even superiority.

g.description: Touching noses in an affectionate gesture to create a warm bond.
g.example: Gently approaching and performing an Eskimo kiss, thereby strengthening our emotional bond without words.

g.description: Conveying affection or respect through a kiss, subtly influencing in a positive manner.
g.example: Sending a kiss during a speech to emphasize feelings of appreciation or deep affection.

g.description: Sharing a moment of connection or hinting at a shared secret with an interlocutor by a simple wink.
g.example: You know what to do now, don't you, Mr. Bernard?

g.description: Blinking both eyes, often to express interest or, ironically, disapproval.
g.example: Blinking both eyes to show fascination or, sarcastically, disbelief.

g.description: Indicating discreet agreement or complicity with a tongue click, implying there's nothing left to add or discuss.
g.example: After delivering a complex explanation, the speaker clicks their tongue, suggesting there's nothing more to add or dispute.

g.description: Blinking twice, often to suggest that what was just said should be taken with caution.
g.example: After a sarcastic remark, I blinked twice to indicate that my comment should be taken lightly.

g.description: Seeking to influence an audience by using facial expressions to suggest an emotion or attitude.
g.example: By frowning deeply, I conveyed my disapproval without a single word.

g.description: To better influence the person you are speaking with, you interpret their emotional state from brief, involuntary signs visible on their face.
g.example: Noticing the sudden narrowing of his eyes, I grasped his concern about the situation.

g.description: Using one's gaze, fixed or averted, to convey a message without saying a word.
g.example: I saw you roll your eyes when he said that.

g.description: Looking an interlocutor in the eyes to enhance the impact of the message.
g.example: Look into my eyes when I'm speaking to you.

g.description: Using speaking time and pauses to energize or soothe one's speech.
g.example: You would have preferred something else. I understand. It is natural. And it is your right. Now, trust me: we are going to meet this challenge.

g.description: Seeking to influence an audience by manipulating the tone, volume, or pace of one's speech.
g.example: By lowering my voice and slowing my pace, I gave greater gravity to the potential risks.

g.description: Seeking to convey certain intentions through audible or particular breathing.
g.example: Sigh... You're exhausting me with your problems.

g.description: Gasping to express one's strong feelings about something.
g.example: There, the train, behind, hurry up.

g.description: Expressing weariness or exasperation by sighing in order to influence those nearby.
g.example: Ah! If only...

g.description: Clearing one's throat, for example to signal disapproval.
g.example: Ahem, children, you shouldn't be here.

g.description: Seeking to influence an interlocutor by addressing them as if they were a child.
g.example: Oh? Did someone hurt their little knee and is going to cry about it?

g.description: Seeking to influence an audience by exerting psychological ascendancy over it.
g.example: If your love for me is sincere, then you will understand what I am about to explain to you.

g.description: Manipulating social norms and expectations to influence individual behaviors and beliefs within a group.
g.example: Look, everyone in the team has committed to working weekends to finish this project. If you don't join in, you're really going to stand out.

g.description: You alternate between flattering your superiors, engaging in unfair competition with your peers, and acting authoritarian toward your subordinates.
g.example: To stand out, I constantly flatter my superiors while undermining my colleagues and ruling my team with an iron fist.

g.description: Acting obsequiously or flatteringly to gain the favor of influential people, often to the detriment of one's own or others' principles.
g.example: You're absolutely right, as always, Boss. Your perspective is so enlightened, fortunately you are here to guide us.

g.description: Behaving subserviently toward those who have more power, while being aggressive or contemptuous toward those in an inferior position.
g.example: Your idea in the meeting was absolutely brilliant, boss. All of you, stop twiddling your thumbs and start working harder to achieve the new goals.

g.description: Taking out one's frustration or anger on less powerful or subordinate people, often because one cannot express it where it is caused.
g.example: Look, I don't want to hear your excuses. I know it's not your fault, but someone has to pay for this morning's failure, and it's you.

g.description: Adopting an attitude where if one can't succeed, one makes sure no one else can either.
g.example: If I can't get promoted, I'll make sure no one on my team gets promoted.

g.description: Criticizing or minimizing those who stand out or succeed, often out of jealousy or fear of losing one's own status.
g.example: No matter his accomplishments, we must remember that he is no different from us. He just got luckier, that's all.

g.description: Using one's position or power to manipulate or control others in abusive and damaging ways.
g.example: I decide when and how things should be done here. If you do not follow my instructions, there will be severe consequences.

g.description: Creating conditions in which a person is almost certain to fail, often to justify later criticism or negative actions towards them.
g.example: I'll assign him this impossible project with an unrealistic deadline. When he fails, it will justify sidelining him.

g.description: Exhibiting narcissistic behavior in the workplace, constantly seeking admiration and attention, while denigrating or exploiting colleagues.
g.example: I am clearly the most competent here. Without me, this project would be a disaster. The others are only there to execute my brilliant ideas.

g.description: Isolating an individual to further control and abuse them, often by cutting them off from their support networks and limiting their interactions with others.
g.example: I told you that I no longer wanted you to hang out with these people who don't wish you well.

g.description: Singling an individual or group to blame them for problems that are not their fault, often to distract from one's own failures or responsibilities.
g.example: It's because of the marketing team that we didn't achieve our goals this quarter. They didn't do their job properly.

g.description: Carefully and excessively controlling the work of one's subordinates, leaving little or no autonomy or creative space.
g.example: I want you to report to me every detail of your work. Every email, every call, I have to know everything.

g.description: Creating a work environment so stressful and oppressive that it pushes employees to extreme and rash reactions.
g.example: Since overtime has become commonplace without recognition or compensation, the atmosphere in the office has become electric and unpredictable.

g.description: Destabilizing an interlocutor through ambiguous or confusing messages in order to better influence their reaction.
g.example: I thank you for your excellent work, it's truly admirable. Now, do you think you can do even better for the next quarter?

g.description: Deliberately downplaying elements of truth, the significance of problems, or the feelings of others to lessen their perceived impact or deflect accountability.
g.example: It's not that bad, everyone makes mistakes and it's not going to change anything. No need to make a mountain out of a molehill.

g.description: Involving a third party to indirectly influence someone or a situation.
g.example: The consultant made it clear: there's no point in entering this declining market.

g.description: Portraying oneself as a victim, often in an exaggerated way, to gain sympathy or avoid responsibility.
g.example: Every time something goes wrong, I'm always the one blamed, even when it's not my fault.

g.description: Believing or pretending that everyone is hostile, often without concrete evidence.
g.example: I just know everyone is talking behind my back and plotting to make me fail.

g.description: Exaggerating or fabricating personal problems to garner attention and sympathy.
g.example: Feeling so alone these days... Seems like nobody cares about me.

g.description: Expressing opposition indirectly, through avoidance, insinuations, or signs of irritation, rather than stating it clearly.
g.example: No, it's not because I slammed the door that I'm angry.

g.description: Sharing informal stories or rumors about other people's private lives, often unverified and private.
g.example: I heard our boss is going on vacation with his assistant, how intriguing!

g.description: Systematically refusing to respond or cooperate, often to avoid confrontation or as a strategy to gain time.
g.example: Whenever she asks me something tough, I just act like I didn't hear her. It discourages her from asking more questions.

g.description: Following instructions to the letter in a way that causes an undesirable outcome or highlights the absurdity or flaws of the request.
g.example: As per your instructions, I meticulously adhered to the protocol, even though it set us back by three days. After all, strictly following procedures is key, right?

g.description: Deliberately ignoring and refusing to communicate with someone to exert control or express displeasure.
g.example: I'm not going to talk to him or respond to his messages for days. He'll realize he did something wrong.

g.description: Conveying disagreement or disdain without uttering a word, using subtle gestures or facial expressions to express contempt.
g.example: When the manager announced the new policy, I just rolled my eyes and cracked a mocking smile.

g.description: Expressing displeasure or frustration by remaining silent and distant, often ostentatiously, to influence another person.
g.example: I'll just stay in my corner. Maybe they'll come over and ask what's wrong.

g.description: Exerting constant pressure to compel someone into compliance.
g.example: The manager kept mentioning potential layoffs to pressure the team into working overtime.

g.description: Repeatedly behaving in ways which undermine a person's psychology, in order to make her more compliant.
g.example: I'll need to step up your game. Last week's email responses were clearly not up to scratch, and I will have to discuss your attitude with the manager if you continue to ignore my calls when you leave the office.

g.description: Obsessively and persistently following and monitoring a person, creating a situation of intense fear and anxiety for the victim.
g.example: I keep an eye on all your movements, day and night. You can't do anything without me knowing it.

g.description: Using behaviors, comments, or suggestions of a sexual nature to intimidate or embarrass someone, often in a professional or educational setting.
g.example: You know, if you were more relaxed with me, I could help you get that promotion. You would be so much more comfortable in your job.

g.description: Targeting individuals based on their sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression, often through verbal, physical, or psychological aggression.
g.example: Look at that guy over there. He looks so effeminate. He must be gay. We should show him what a real man is.

g.description: Degrading or humiliating someone, often a woman, for their real or perceived sexual behavior, clothing choices, or appearance, suggesting they are immoral or unworthy.
g.example: Did you see how she's dressed? She's really looking for attention... It's shameful to present oneself like that in public.

g.description: Feigning ignorance and repeatedly asking questions under the guise of earnest inquiry, aiming to destabilize or exasperate the interlocutor.
g.example: Could you explain to me again why this is offensive? And what does that mean exactly? I just want to understand, can you clarify this point?

g.description: Persistently expressing the same request to an interlocutor to irritate them sufficiently until they concede to the request.
g.example: You still haven't told me how you'll manage without this new protection we're offering you in the event of a loss. You're playing with fire, and you know it.

g.description: Using a combination of intense repetition and psychological manipulation to significantly influence or alter someone's beliefs or opinions.
g.example: I understand you're skeptical, but think about it every night before you sleep and you'll see my theory is the only one that makes sense.

g.description: Considering an interlocutor incompetent if they cannot recite specific data or technical details on a subject.
g.example: If you can't quote the latest economic growth statistics, then your views on economic policy are invalid.

g.description: Speaking rapidly to present as many arguments as possible in the least amount of time, making it difficult for the opponent to respond to all points.
g.example: My opponent should now answer my arguments about various economic, social, and environmental policies, covering implications in the short and long term, impacts on vulnerable populations, geopolitical considerations, and legal and ethical aspects.

g.description: Overwhelm the interlocutor with a rapid and continuous flow of arguments, making it difficult for a full and thoughtful rebuttal.
g.example: How can you claim to be competent if you can't even address my arguments on taxation, education, health, and the environment? And I haven't even started on foreign policy yet!

g.description: Insisting on every objection raised to better establish one's point of view.
g.example: But if everything you say is true, why not simply accept the agreement as it is currently proposed?

g.description: Sowing doubt or confusion in one's interlocutor to compromise their perceptual faculties.
g.example: Are you saying I promised you that? You must be confusing things: I never said anything like that.

g.description: Using an opponent's argument to his or her disadvantage.
g.example: It's because he's a child that we need to be especially stern with him.

g.description: Employing fear or threats to compel conformity or silence.
g.example: If you don't follow my instructions, you risk a lot.

g.description: Resorting to verbal attacks to intimidate or dominate.
g.example: If you weren't so incompetent, we wouldn't be in this situation!

g.description: Using degradation and humiliation as a means of manipulation.
g.example: Look everyone, here's someone who can't even add simple numbers!

g.description: Using coercion to force someone into action or to desist.
g.example: If you don't change your behavior, I'm going to get angry.

g.description: Using threat to force someone's agreement with a proposition.
g.example: If you don't let me have the last slice of ham, you will pay dearly for it.

g.description: Seeking to make an opponent lose confidence or courage in order to make them give up the debate.
g.example: Your cause is hopeless. You'll merely spill your blood in vain.

g.description: Using someone's guilt to make them act accordingly.
g.example: You know, I spent the whole week preparing for this event. If you don't attend, it will be a huge disappointment.

g.description: Putting direct pressure on someone by exploiting their feelings of fear, obligation, or guilt, often through clear deals or ultimatums.
g.example: If you really love me, you'll stop hanging out with these deadbeats, and you'll bring me better grades from school.

g.description: Manipulating someone by overwhelming them with guilt to coerce them into acting as desired or to make them feel responsible for something they haven't done.
g.example: I can't believe you're refusing to help me after all I've done for you. I've always sacrificed for you, and now when I need your help, you're just washing your hands of it?

g.description: Overtly presenting oneself as generous or indifferent but actually meaning the opposite, with the intention of making the addressee feel guilty.
g.example: Don't worry about me, I'm fine. Go ahead and hang out with your friends, I'll just stay home alone, it doesn't bother me at all.

g.description: Providing irrelevant information to disrupt the focus of an audience.
g.example: I think about those dates you suggested to me, that tie really doesn't suit you, I need you to move them, you should stop wearing it, would the following week suit you?

g.description: Rapid, repetitive, and continuous broadcasting of a large number of messages across various channels, such as news and social media, without regard for truth or consistency, in order to overwhelm the audience, making it difficult to discern truth amidst the torrent of conflicting information.
g.example: The government's official channels, supported by an army of online bots and anonymous accounts, release a barrage of conflicting reports about the economic situation, each contradicting the other, flooding the information space and making it impossible to understand the real economic conditions.

g.description: Intentionnaly making a targeted individual or members of a group question their own memory, perception, and sanity.
g.example: Don't you remember you promised to come to this meeting? You often forget what you say, which is concerning. Maybe you should take more care.

g.description: Seeking to subject the audience to one's views without appealing to their reason, but by inducing their behavior.
g.example: Your presence here, day after day, shows your commitment. And you know that a good employee is a committed employee.

g.description: Psychologically manipulating people into performing actions or divulging confidential information.
g.example: Hi, this is John from IT. We're doing a security update and need to verify your credentials. Can you confirm your password for me, please?

g.description: Seeking to obtain an interlocutor's agreement by presenting their help as the final effort needed to achieve one's objective.
g.example: We've come so far, all that's left is your expertise on this final part, and you will crown this project with success.

g.description: Achieving compliance by repetitively delivering the same message.
g.example: As I've already repeated many times, we all need to follow the new rules, no matter how hard they might be, and I will not make any exceptions. It's essential for our community.

g.description: First destabilizing an interlocutor with a disorienting message, then reformulating the request in a more acceptable way.
g.example: I know, the price seems high, but we also have an in-house model that should fit your budget and compares very favorably with this beautiful model.

g.description: Seeking to influence the audience's behavior by inviting it to assume a responsibility induced by the proposal.
g.example: Since you support the ecological transition, those of you who are willing to take the train rather than fly on your next trips, raise your hands. — Lewin (1947): public commitment activates private acceptance, regardless of the subject.

g.description: Subtly inducing an interlocutor to commit by strengthening their involvement and agreement with one's propositions.
g.example: You know as well as I do that these regulations are crucial, and I know I can count on you to adopt them immediately.

g.description: Feeling guilty or frustrated because one thinks one should be more grateful in one's current situation, or using this feeling in others to assert control.
g.example: I should be happy to have a job, even though I hate it.

g.description: Using body contact to induce compliance.
g.example: Come on, Jean, I'm counting on you not to let us down (with a pat on the shoulder).

g.description: Winning someone's agreement by reminding them that they are free to agree or not.
g.example: Now, if any of you are still not convinced, you are absolutely free to leave without buying our product, and we would still have been pleased to present it to you.

g.description: Suggesting that any help, however minimal, is appreciated in order to encourage support.
g.example: I appeal to your generosity no matter your situation: Every cent counts; even a small amount can make a difference!

g.description: Getting someone to comply by telling them that they are compliant.
g.example: I know you're a fighter, and fighters never give up until the final whistle.

g.description: Highlighting someone's dissonance between their actions and discourse in order to make them change.
g.example: You all say you want a clean city, but who among you really recycles? Show me what you plan to do to make a change.

g.description: After getting someone to endorse a norm, you remind them of past behavior that went against it to push them to apply that norm.
g.example: Don't you find that ever since we imposed a speed limit, you feel safer? So, wouldn't it be even better for our children if we lowered it further?

g.description: You make your request more acceptable by accompanying it with polite phrases or signs of attentiveness.
g.example: Ah... I forgot to mention the travel expenses. How is your lady doing? I saw her at the market; she seemed quite troubled by that leak. She's very brave, your lady...

g.description: You first frighten the person you are speaking to, then reassure them, making them more receptive to your influence.
g.example: Rest assured, it's for your own good that I've told you all this. If we cooperate intelligently, it's likely we can avoid the worst.

g.description: Convincing someone to comply to a second request because it looks smaller than the first, extortionate one, which they had to decline.
g.example: I understand that you might not be able to personally commit to this essential cause, but maybe a small monthly donation would be more manageable?

g.description: Encouraging someone to progressively commit to increasingly significant requests.
g.example: Our charity starts with small-scale projects before tackling larger initiatives. Support us with this minor community event.

g.description: Attracting the audience with a promising offer, then switching it to achieve one's own ends.
g.example: The concert is cancelled but to thank you for coming, could you fill out this form?

g.description: Persuading of the necessity to invest more so as not to lose what has already been invested.
g.example: You've invested so much time in this project; it would really be a shame to stop now when there's so little left to do to complete it.

g.description: Initially presenting an unattractive offer, then enhancing it before the counterpart has time to decide.
g.example: But for this price, you might get a trip to Lapland, plus a discount on your next purchase.

g.description: Convincing someone to accept a proposal while deliberately omitting details that might deter them.
g.example: Take immediate advantage of our premium subscription benefits. Currently, the first 3 months are free with no commitment. It's the perfect time to try.

g.description: Securing agreement to a minor request as a precursor to gaining acceptance for a larger, related request.
g.example: Having signed our petition for playground areas, would it not make sense for you to also contribute to the fundraising for the park renovation?

g.description: Achieving one's larger goals by gradually winning approval for smaller, associated tasks.
g.example: We set a 10% production cost reduction goal this quarter because you've clearly shown you can achieve it.

g.description: Securing agreement on smaller requests to gradually gain acceptance for larger ones.
g.example: If you could just leave us your email address for our newsletter, you'll find exclusive offers inside.

g.description: Using one's charisma to get one's audience to embrace one's ideas.
g.example: After such a fine opening, I am sure we will manage to get past this unfortunate disagreement.

g.description: Using apparent seduction and surface charisma to persuade or manipulate others, often without real affection or commitment.
g.example: I always know just what to say to charm. A smile here, a compliment there, and everyone's wrapped around my finger.

g.description: Using seduction to gain an interlocutor's support by diverting their judgment.
g.example: You are as critical as you are charming, but I'm sure this product will win over your discerning heart.

g.description: Seeking to be appreciated or to obtain favors by flattering or praising one's interlocutor in an excessive or insincere manner.
g.example: Your insight is always profound. It's my fortune to work alongside someone as enlightened as you.

g.description: Constantly seeking to be the center of attention, adopting behaviors or telling stories to draw attention to oneself.
g.example: You won't believe what happened to me today! I met a celebrity and they invited me to dinner!

g.description: Feigning emotions to move or influence those who are listening.
g.example: Do you really think I'm fully satisfied with this situation? Thinking about the suffering children keeps me awake at night, and that's why I will go all the way regardless of what my detractors say.

g.description: Demonstrating a great deal of affection to persuade others to follow one's lead, even without valid reasons.
g.example: You're such an amazing person. Will we see you on Saturday?

g.description: Putting forward one's own achievements or qualities, often in an exaggerated manner, to impress others or gain their admiration.
g.example: In my last project, I achieved record profits. Some say I turn ideas into gold.

g.description: Bragging loudly or making exaggerated statements about one's abilities or achievements, often without real foundation.
g.example: I'm the best negotiator in town. I've made deals that no one else could even dream of.

g.description: Mentioning names of influential or famous people one knows or has met, to impress or gain the trust of one's audience.
g.example: In my last meeting with the mayor, he mentioned how much he appreciates my ideas. Also, last week I had dinner with a famous author who shared the same view.

g.description: Creating associations between ideas and emotions, influencing behaviors without this being obvious.
g.example: When you see our logo, you immediately think of freedom and adventure. That is what makes our brand so special to our customers.

g.description: Subtly influencing social behaviors and decisions through various strategies and techniques.
g.example: By spreading rumors and partial information, they gradually altered public perception of the reform initiative.

g.description: Using a poll to influence or manipulate public opinion by asking biased or leading questions.
g.example: Would you be supportive of a candidate knowing that they have been involved in financial scandals?

g.description: Spreading frightening and exaggerated rumors about imminent danger to deliberately and unnecessarily instill public fear about an issue.
g.example: Did you know that tap water is very rarely checked and often contaminated, unlike this bottled mineral water?

g.description: Employing deceptive design techniques to manipulate users into actions against their own interests.
g.example: The website used dark patterns by hiding additional costs in fine print, misleading the customers.

g.description: Using catchy or misleading headlines to entice people to click on a link or watch a video.
g.example: You won't believe what this celebrity did! Click here to find out!

g.description: Steering individuals' choices in a non-forcing way to promote beneficial behaviors.
g.example: By placing fruits at eye level in the cafeteria, they nudged employees towards healthier options.

g.description: Exercising a subtle influence on someone without their awareness.
g.example: Notice how this advertisement's melody follows the narration closely.

g.description: Claiming to perceive signals which are not perceivable by others.
g.example: By observing closely, I can infer from his choice of words that he is clearly stressed by the situation you're imposing on us.

g.description: Without realizing it, you give cues that change your interlocutor’s behavior or responses.
g.example: With the right cues, this horse can select the correct answer, leading one to believe it can count and calculate.

g.description: Having one's argumentation unconsciously influenced by one's own expectations or behaviors towards the discussed topic.
g.example: I'm going to ask you to get comfortable for this test.

g.description: Sending barely perceptible signals to an interlocutor to modify their behavior without their realizing it.
g.example: In a commercial, the silhouette of a whiskey glass seems to subtly appear among the ice cubes. Without explicitly mentioning it, the brand thus covertly suggests that consuming their beverage offers naturalness and freshness.

g.description: Using suggestion techniques such as hypnosis to make a person more open to one's ideas.
g.example: Listen carefully to my voice, let yourself be carried away by my words, and imagine a world where our product changes your life...

g.description: Using hypnotic suggestion techniques in everyday conversation, unbeknownst to the listener being influenced.
g.example: You seem really relaxed talking about this. Imagine if you could feel this calm all the time. That would be nice, wouldn't it?

g.description: Deliberately distorting reality through tricks or artifices in order to deceive someone's senses.
g.example: We've arranged the lighting and mirrors in our store so that every tried-on garment appears perfectly fitted.

g.description: Altering images to present a reality different from the original one.
g.example: By adjusting the colors and slightly altering the backgrounds in our vacation photos, we make each destination look like paradise on Earth.

g.description: Using illusion to make false or misleading things be accepted as true.
g.example: A magician swiftly moves the cards on the table, suggesting a free choice to the audience while secretly directing their decision.

g.description: Believing so strongly in a prediction or expectation that one's actions end up making it come true.
g.example: Everyone thought this project was going to fail, and that belief affected our motivation so much that we couldn't make it succeed.

g.description: Making predictions about individuals or groups, based on external expectations or stereotypes, which end up influencing and determining their behavior or success.
g.example: This new team is repeatedly told that it will never do as well as the old one; it eventually loses confidence and achieves poorer results.

g.description: You insinuate that the situation will get worse with a certain solution, banking on the other person's pessimism to magnify a fictitious problem.
g.example: If you keep working with this method, you will definitely fail.

g.description: Rely on the belief in a fake remedy to improve a condition, despite no real evidence.
g.example: Drink a glass of water every night and you'll never have a headache again.

g.description: To influence the attitude of others based on the idea that those who already have advantages are more likely to succeed.
g.example: He comes from a family of doctors; he's bound to be a great surgeon too.

g.description: You attempt to reduce your interlocutor's chances of success by making them understand that you do not believe they will succeed.
g.example: You're nothing but a failure, and you'll end up in the streets.

g.description: Relying on the fact that higher expectations placed upon individuals lead to better performance.
g.example: I know you're going to ace this exam, you've always been the top of your class.

g.description: Believing so strongly in a personal prediction or expectation that it comes true due to one's own actions.
g.example: I've always told myself that I'm bad at public speaking. Now, every time I have to speak in public, I panic and fail.

g.description: Making a prediction that prevents what it predicts from happening.
g.example: I bet you your team will never be able to finish the project on time.

g.description: Having an intense and irrational fear of failure, leading one to avoid situations where there's a risk of failing.
g.example: I'm so terrified of failing that I prefer not to try at all, rather than risk failure.

g.description: Unconsciously organizing oneself in a way that leads to failure, often by overestimating risks or imposing unnecessary additional conditions.
g.example: Even though I know I could succeed, I always find an excuse not to finish my projects. It's like I'm setting myself up for failure.

g.description: Using positive self-suggestion practices, like Coué's method, to boost self-confidence and positively influence one's achievements.
g.example: Every morning, I repeat to myself 'Every day, in every way, I'm getting better and better', and it makes me more optimistic.

g.description: Influencing the behavior of others by means of rewards or punishments, in order to favor the responses one wishes to obtain.
g.example: For every sales goal achieved, there will be a hefty bonus. If the goal is not met, intensive coaching meetings will be scheduled.

g.description: Applying rewards or punishments unpredictably as a form of manipulation.
g.example: Since you have worked well in the past few days without my help, today I'm treating you to a dinner out.

g.description: Introducing weak counterarguments to strengthen the credibility of one's ideas.
g.example: Some argue that our product is too costly, but consider the quality of this cheaper competing product.

g.description: Inducing one's opponent to take a position by contrasting it with the opposite stance.
g.example: You complain that I don't listen to you enough, but do you hear? The neighbors are arguing again.

g.description: Progressively reinforcing behaviors that are increasingly closer to the desired goal, starting with simple actions and gradually increasing complexity.
g.example: I know you're hesitant about cheating, but let's just start by looking at others' answers without copying them.

g.description: Forming a complex sequence of behaviors by linking simple actions in a specific order, each serving as a cue for the next.
g.example: At 10 AM, you pick up the package from the warehouse. Meanwhile, Miguel will take care of the troublesome witness. At 11 AM, you meet at the rendezvous point to switch roles. Then, at 11:30 AM, you deliver the package to the buyer while Miguel erases all evidence.

g.description: Using a motivational strategy that combines rewards (the carrot) and punishments (the stick) to influence someone else's behavior.
g.example: If you meet your targets this month, you will receive a bonus, but if you fail, disciplinary actions will be taken.

g.description: Employing harsh and often damaging educational or disciplinary methods, based on fear, guilt, and humiliation.
g.example: If you don't finish your homework on time, you'll be deprived of all leisure for a week. It's for your own good.

g.description: Imposing a context through wording that steers the conclusions.
g.example: Studies should prepare people for professional life; it would therefore be logical for universities to be administered by chambers of commerce.

g.description: Focusing discourse on unfavorable and pessimistic considerations, neglecting potential positive aspects.
g.example: Sure, there's a chance everything will go well on this trip, but have you heard how often trains have been delayed recently?

g.description: Using sensory or verbal stimuli to influence the behavior or memory of one's audience.
g.example: Succumb to the delicacy of its aromas, its enchanting taste, and the finesse of its texture...

g.description: Disrupting a pattern of thought in order to change the behavior it leads to.
g.example: Every time you think about smoking, replace that image with one of you doing a healthy activity. It's a way to reprogram your desire.

g.description: Projecting one's interlocutor into the future to influence their present decisions.
g.example: Imagine yourself in ten years, fully enjoying your retirement thanks to the investment you make today.

g.description: Inviting one's interlocutor to view themselves as an observer, to consider their own ideas differently.
g.example: Have you seen yourself when you've been drinking?

g.description: Changing how an idea is viewed by presenting it in a different light.
g.example: Don't see this change as a loss, but as an opportunity to explore new professional horizons.

g.description: Imitating an interlocutor's behavior to establish a sense of trust.
g.example: You like flowers? So do I!

g.description: Creating a connection between a cue and a reaction in order to elicit this reaction from one's audience in the future.
g.example: Think of the last time you felt completely relaxed. That's exactly the state of mind our spa seeks to recreate for you.

g.description: Making a proposition acceptable by ensuring that it takes on a particular meaning in the eyes of one's interlocutor.
g.example: You surely worry about the future, don't you? That's why our program is designed for people like you who truly care.

g.description: Carefully observing an interlocutor to infer their needs, then adapting one's discourse to their profile.
g.example: Did you know that the champion ambassador of our brand wears the same watch as you? You like adventure, don't you?

g.description: Projecting many conjectures so that the audience confirms one, which will then be focused on.
g.example: I could see you working in digital marketing, live events, maybe strategic partnerships?

g.description: Paradoxically claiming that the interlocutor has both a quality and its opposite, allowing one to appear consistently coherent.
g.example: You have the firmness necessary to make tough decisions, but you're also flexible enough to adapt to new information.

g.description: Using general descriptions so that the interlocutor recognizes themselves in them and thereby validates one's ability to understand people.
g.example: You have great potential that you haven't used to your advantage yet. On the outside, you're disciplined and know how to control yourself, but inside you tend to be worried and not very confident.

g.description: Addressing a prophetic recommendation to an interlocutor, designed so that future events seem to prove one right in every case.
g.example: If you invest in this technology now, you'll be ahead; if it becomes the standard, you'll be a pioneer, and if it fails, your experience will set you apart from the beginners.

g.description: Formulating psychological observations vague enough to apply to anyone while still seeming personal to the interlocutor.
g.example: You have a strong personality, but sometimes you doubt yourself, right? That's what I sense, and that's why our product is perfect for you.

g.description: Presenting arguments gradually, without revealing the final objective, so that the interlocutor accepts them one by one without understanding where they are leading.
g.example: Start by trying our free version. It has the features you need.

g.description: Being subjected to, or relying on, the fact that sufficiently repeated false information has a greater chance of being accepted.
g.example: I have heard so many times that this diet works, surely it must be effective.

g.description: You appeal to weak arguments, counting on the idea that their substance, rather than their dubious origin, will be remembered.
g.example: Though some experts dispute our data, the key takeaway is that the general trend is in our favor.

g.description: Using formulations which signal non-comitment to what is said.
g.example: The new policy presented here might have a positive impact, though some minor adjustments are still needed.

g.description: Presenting one's arguments in a confused order to mask one's intentions and prevent the aim of one's reasoning from being guessed.
g.example: "Why worry about national debt when there are security problems? But then, doesn't security depend on our robust economy?"

g.description: You rely on a modest, widely accepted position to get a more ambitious and controversial position accepted, as if the former proved the latter.
g.example: Of course the heavenly bodies influence nature: just look at the effect of the Moon on the tides.

g.description: Undermining someone with a compliment that insinuates the opposite of its apparent expression.
g.example: I would not say that his reasoning is worthless; that would probably be an exaggeration.

g.description: Stating a series of uncontroversial statements before introducing the proposed, debatable argument.
g.example: Parents have the duty to educate their children and provide for their needs; it's also up to them to decide which studies their children should undertake.

g.description: Framing a criticism or negative comment between two praises or compliments, to soften the message and make it more palatable.
g.example: Your work on the project was impressive. However, there were a few errors in your calculations. But overall, you showed great commitment. — Management technique: the central criticism is framed by two compliments, which increases the criticism's acceptance rate while reducing how important it is perceived to be.

g.description: Skillfully playing with pros and cons to confuse an audience until it no longer knows what one's real stance is.
g.example: It's important to preserve our traditions, yet enriching our culture is also crucial.

g.description: Stirring strong emotions to divert an audience from rational reflection.
g.example: If you get good grades, your father will be very proud of you.

g.description: Basing an argument on the consequences of an idea rather than on its soundness.
g.example: I never give money to beggars because I fear they might use it to buy alcohol.

g.description: Encouraging the rejection of any information that could contradict the defended position in order to preserve the status quo.
g.example: We don't know everything about this topic, so it's safer to stick with what has always worked rather than risk a change.

g.description: Convincing an opponent to accept a proposal by suggesting personal benefits.
g.example: If you support my proposal, I'll make sure you get the office space with the view you've been longing for.

g.description: Seeking to obtain an audience's agreement by promising an advantage in return, rather than presenting a valid argument.
g.example: Support this stance and I'll make sure your next project gets funded.

g.description: Supporting or rejecting a proposition not because it is valid, but because it satisfies a feeling of vengeance.
g.example: We should stop buying their products, that'll teach them for closing the factory in our town!

g.description: Trading argumentative support for a personal favour.
g.example: I'll cover for you this weekend if you support me on this controversial project — let's square things up.

g.description: Dismissing an argument based on its perceived offensive or disrespectful tone, rather than its substance.
g.example: I'm sorry to inform you that by using that kind of language, you've totally disqualified yourself.

g.description: Disqualification of an argument because the presenter doesn't remain calm, falsely equating emotional expression with lack of reason.
g.example: How can we take his points seriously when he's always so upset? Calmness is key to credibility.

g.description: Presumptuously explaining to women what they already know, implying one's superior understanding.
g.example: Let me handle this problem. This is a job for a man.

g.description: Leveraging the supposed importance or seriousness of a situation to make someone's viewpoint stronger.
g.example: Just because he won the trifecta doesn't mean he can be trusted to send a man to the moon.

g.description: Arguing that threats of retaliation are sufficient proof of the validity of one's argument.
g.example: If you continue to dispute the committee's decision, your promotion prospects might be adversely affected.

g.description: Claiming to know what is best for others, imposing one's view in a domineering or condescending manner.
g.example: You will understand when you are older, but for now, trust me and do what I tell you.

g.description: Seeking to impress or persuade by emphasizing the severity or strictness of one's position.
g.example: In this crisis, we need a leader who isn't afraid of making tough decisions; compassion won't solve our problems.

g.description: Discriminating or marginalizing on the basis of disability, treating it as a valid argument.
g.example: I prefer not to entrust him with important responsibilities; with his disability, he would not be able to keep up with the pace like us.

g.description: Using a threat to win a debate instead of defending one's position through reason.
g.example: If you don't leave that last slice of ham for me, you will pay dearly for it.

g.description: Winning an argument by being the loudest or by intimidation.
g.example: You know, if you don't support this cause, I'm going to be significantly less friendly towards you.

g.description: Showing an idea in a repulsive light instead of rationally arguing against it.
g.example: Collapsologists want to take us back to the Stone Age and abolish all industry. — Foil: a deliberately exaggerated caricature of a real movement, making it easier and more popular to refute.

g.description: You provoke fear in your audience to persuade them, abandoning reasonable arguments.
g.example: Do not stray from the path, or the wolf will eat you.

g.description: You stir up outrage by presenting certain actions as immoral in order to provoke a strong emotional reaction.
g.example: This new dance which is spreading among young people is a sign of moral decadence, which leads straight to depravity.

g.description: Disseminating negative information, often vague, to sow fear and mistrust and rally the public to one's cause.
g.example: I heard that our competitor was in big trouble. With their financial situation, it's a miracle they last until spring.

g.description: Deliberately angering an opponent so that they lose their composure and seem less credible.
g.example: Look at you, with your arguments! It's like you're just discovering the topic. Don't you get tired of hearing yourself ramble on?

g.description: Pushing an opponent into exaggeration in order to discredit their argumentation.
g.example: Do you really think your electric car stories will change the climate? Why not call for a ban on gasoline cars while you're at it!

g.description: You systematically challenge established ideas to unsettle your audience.
g.example: Everyone thinks the Earth is round, but have you checked for yourself? Don't believe everything you're told.

g.description: Repeatedly anoying an opponents until they become angry and lose their mind.
g.example: Another mistake, my dear opponent! At this rate, you'll never finish your presentation without me interrupting you.

g.description: Identifying what irritates your opponent as so many weak points to press.
g.example: Look at my opponent getting carried away after what I just said; he is disqualifying himself in this debate.

g.description: Assuming that presenting an argument in anger proves its validity.
g.example: Are you tired of being ignored by your government? Is it really normal for the 1% to hold so much while the rest hold so little? Vote for me!

g.description: Arousing a feeling of hatred against the opposing thesis.
g.example: Those opposing our policy want to see your country fall into chaos. We must stop them before it's too late.

g.description: Arousing an audience's anger against the opposing thesis in order to discredit it.
g.example: This politician continually switches sides and betrays you. How can you still support them?

g.description: You present something in such a way that it appears reprehensible, unworthy of attention, or unworthy of esteem.
g.example: My son, you won't study in the college of Arts, a notorious gathering of lazy and neurotic folks!

g.description: Attempting to discredit an opponent by declaring that their proposition provokes, through its immoral or revolting character, a feeling of aversion and deep hostility.
g.example: Don't even bother tasting that dish; just from its smell, you can tell it's poison!

g.description: Arguing that an intuitive negative response to some thing, idea, or practice is evidence for the intrinsically wrong character of that thing.
g.example: GMOs are like playing god. Do you really want to eat tomatoes that taste like fish?

g.description: Attempting to discredit an opponent by declaring that their proposition is so unworthy of them that they should feel embarrassed and expect general disapproval.
g.example: Aren't you ashamed for having that opinion?

g.description: Presenting an opponent's argument as absurd, ridiculous, or humorous, and therefore not worth consideration.
g.example: You, the new guy, don't even think about winning the Friday match. You've just arrived, watch and learn, you don't have what it takes.

g.description: Declaring that an opponent's proposition is not worth taking into consideration.
g.example: Charles Darwin's theories are but the harmless dreams of a man napping.

g.description: Creating an emotional bond with an audience to win it's support.
g.example: As parents, we understand the importance of protecting our children, don't we?

g.description: Invoking an audience's sympathy to win support without arguing the merits.
g.example: Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, look at this miserable man, in a wheelchair, unable to use his legs. Can such a man really be guilty of embezzlement?

g.description: Asserting that a belief is true because its advocate has been persecuted or martyrs have died for it.
g.example: This activist, after so many years of fierce struggle and persecution, who has given everything for you, must be sincere in his commitment to the cause.

g.description: Appealing to children's need for protection in order to substitute emotion for reason in a debate.
g.example: If you vote against this law, think of the disastrous message it will send to our children about the importance of education.

g.description: Using praise or ego-boosting implications to seduce the audience.
g.example: A woman as intelligent as you can only accept this exceptional proposal!

g.description: Encouraging an interlocutor to feel proud of adhering to one's propositions.
g.example: You have shown remarkable intelligence by supporting our project, and that honors our entire community.

g.description: Suggesting that supporting one's point of view makes someone a person of worth.
g.example: I will go no further in this campaign, it is so insulting to everyone.

g.description: Claiming that an assertion is true because it goes against the opinion of the majority.
