g.example: Why read those boring chain messages that everyone reads? You know you're better than that.

g.description: Flattering an interlocutor by making them believe they are personally privileged or part of a small group with special benefits.
g.example: As a member of our exclusive program, you will have access to offers that the general public can't even imagine.

g.description: Using a rhetorical technique aimed to capture the goodwill of an audience at the beginning of a speech or appeal.
g.example: My dear assembly, we all share the desire to build a future founded on respect and harmony, where everyone's words will be received with attention.

g.description: Tapping into an audience's desires to influence them.
g.example: Of course your city deserves to host the Olympic Games, just imagine the excitement and energy it would bring to all its citizens!

g.description: Telling an audience what it wants to hear in order to win its support.
g.example: You all say you're tired of the prevailing cynicism and want to live in a better world, right? Well, support our development plan and you'll see!

g.description: Evoking a powerfully emotional element in order to later have one's argument accepted.
g.example: Look at this poor polar bear on the melting ice cap; how can you say then that climate change isn't our most urgent problem?

g.description: You simplify complex religious concepts to make them easy to consume.
g.example: Join our movement: kindness and generosity guide our daily actions, and God's word becomes a grand spectacle of songs and praise not to be missed.

g.description: Distracting from real issues by providing entertainments and simple pleasures.
g.example: Forget the criticism against our pop culture; who needs politics when the new season of our favorite show is out?

g.description: Prioritizing popular passions over reflection in order to gain support.
g.example: My fellow citizens, I will make our nation great again, where every family can truly live the dream of success without any barriers or limitations!

g.description: Relying on consensual and flattering concepts to persuade an audience.
g.example: This politician speaks only of peace, love, and democracy, so he surely must deserve our trust and our votes.

g.description: Using vague statements that seem profound to impress, without any real foundation.
g.example: Our product is not just a mere novelty; it's one of the keys to improving the future of our planet.

g.description: Using the value of work to legitimize an idea while targeting a specific social class.
g.example: As hardworking people who rise early and give their all, you deserve to be listened to more than anyone else.

g.description: Deciding a concept is true simply because it's desirable, regardless of the evidence.
g.example: I'm convinced that my teleportation device will work one day. After all, one must believe in the future!

g.description: Assuming a statement is true based solely on someone's strong belief in it.
g.example: This product will revolutionize your daily life, I assure you that you won't be able to live without it.

g.description: Extending a positive impression about one specific aspect of an entity to the whole entity, in any of its dimension.
g.example: Did you see how great he speaks? Such class, such eloquence. You could hang on his every word.

g.description: Using seductive phrases and a persuasive style to convince, without necessarily founding the point on logical reasoning.
g.example: Your eloquence matches your presence: you truly are exceptional.

g.description: Using imagery and flowery language to make one's argumentation more appealing.
g.example: In the valley, where every flower breathes a sigh of love, our candidate alone, with his extensive experience, knows the secrets of the words that will convince the state to preserve this piece of paradise.

g.description: Replacing a word or idea with another expression to produce a stylistic effect.
g.example: Only battle-hardened captains of industry will be able to navigate the storm that's brewing on the markets.

g.description: Deviating from the main subject to introduce a secondary theme thus diverting attention.
g.example: Before discussing the impact of this reform on small businesses, let me remind you in a few key points how essential it is to support education in our country.

g.description: Inserting a personal comment that diverts the discourse from its main subject.
g.example: Between us, and not to speak too soon, it seems to me that the outcome of this project isn't entirely certain.

g.description: Replacing an idea with another conceptually related one, without clear justification.
g.example: With the number of pens this company distributes, they are clearly writing their success.

g.description: Replacing a term with another closely related one to distort or emphasize an aspect of one's speech.
g.example: Respect his white hair.

g.description: Making an understatement to imply the opposite.
g.example: After years of service, our colleague decided to take a well-deserved break in the great garden of paused work.

g.description: Using concrete imagery to convey an abstract idea.
g.example: In this company, we plant young shoots to cultivate success, watering them with hard work to harvest performance.

g.description: Subtly complimenting a statement while ostensibly criticizing it.
g.example: Starting a meeting at 6 PM on a Friday is such a brilliant idea, it will surely give us plenty of time to discuss everything in detail.

g.description: To use a hidden comparison to express an idea in a more imaginative way.
g.example: His gaze was a deep and mysterious ocean in which sailors drowned.

g.description: Deliberately changing the usual position of words or ideas to produce a stylistic effect.
g.example: Hear the call of those distant lands, where the breeze still murmurs the names of the lost heroes.

g.description: Replacing a direct word with a longer expression to embellish one's speech.
g.example: The moon's clarity tonight reveals, to those who can see, the brilliance and splendor of the firmament in its starry azure robe.

g.description: Replacing a simple word with a long turn of phrase to make the point less direct and less clear.
g.example: There are truths that, to be told, require rhetorical circumvolutions so as not to offend the most sensitive ears.

g.description: Anticipating an objection to dismiss it before it is presented to one.
g.example: We could discuss this all day, yet I choose not to delve deeper.

g.description: Replacing one idea with another related to it, such as a cause with its effect, to make a stronger impression.
g.example: He has lost his tongue.

g.description: Pretending to qualify or strengthen one's point of view to impress one's audience.
g.example: Your caution, or rather your cowardice, has ruined us.

g.description: Turning a fault for which one is criticized into a merit and asserting it with pride.
g.example: This book is criticized for not revealing all the enigmas of such a mysterious painter; on the contrary, that is its merit.

g.description: Creating a mirror effect by reversing the order of terms in two similar expressions to make a memorable impact.
g.example: In times of peace, children bury their parents. In times of war, parents bury their children.

g.description: Omitting key words, thereby producing a shortcut effect.
g.example: You know my desire, and I, what you need.

g.description: Making statements that contradict themselves to create a rhetorical effect.
g.example: I'm not superstitious, it's bad luck.

g.description: Indirectly referencing elements that one's audience is expected to recognize.
g.example: Recent events, which I need not detail, remind us how important it is to stay united.

g.description: Connecting elements that do not naturally go together to create a surprising effect.
g.example: Lending at 15% is preferable to lending to the baffled.

g.description: Using a single word with a double meaning, literal and figurative, in the same context.
g.example: The painting's light, so raw it's almost inviting, gives us a glimpse into the artist's genius.

g.description: Mentioning a topic by explicitly stating that one does not wish to talk about it, thereby drawing attention to it.
g.example: Do I need to tell you how extremely precarious the situation is? I will not speak of his insolence, still less of his rudeness.

g.description: Softening language to avoid offending or startling, often using mitigating expressions.
g.example: Your bill is evolving, so are our rates.

g.description: Using a word in the opposite of its usual meaning, often through irony.
g.example: What a wonderful piece this is, it could surely even please those who still appreciate beauty.

g.description: Abruptly interrupting what one is saying, leaving the rest implied.
g.example: And as I reveal to you, eye to eye, the extent of... No, let me instead take you where the horizon meets our expectations.

g.description: Adding and linking several words or ideas to create a stylistic effect.
g.example: This politician is honest, dedicated, competent, hardworking, empathetic, and thus, the ideal candidate.

g.description: Repeating the same idea using different words, which does not provide an additional argument.
g.example: But the trouble I find is that your father is your father.

g.description: Pairing opposite words together to create a contrast or surprise effect.
g.example: An obscure brightness lit her face.

g.description: Explaining the same idea in multiple ways to cover all its aspects.
g.example: Often, my voice speaks, but sometimes it sings, sometimes it whispers, sometimes it cries, oh, how each tone reflects a facet of the universe!

g.description: List elements in increasing intensity to make a memorable impact.
g.example: I would have followed you, my brother, my captain, my king.

g.description: Repeating the same word or phrase multiple times in one's speech to make a memorable impact.
g.example: Freedom, equality, fraternity: these free, equal, and fraternal words are the foundations of our nation.

g.description: Replacing the logical link between two ideas with a simple 'and' to create a stylistic effect.
g.example: I knew this man and his integrity.

g.description: Exaggerating to the extreme to make an impression rather than to argue.
g.example: This package weighs a ton!

g.description: Gradually intensifying exaggerations to the point of becoming paradoxical.
g.example: He's genius, fantastic, fabulous.

g.description: Pushing exaggeration to its extreme to make an impact.
g.example: Kill one man: you are a murderer. Kill millions: you are a conqueror. Kill them all: you are a God.

g.description: Using words that are similar in appearance or sound to make an impact.
g.example: Comparison is not reasoning.

g.description: Playing with different meanings of a word to captivate attention.
g.example: I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.

g.description: Repeating the same term or phrase at the beginning of several sentences to leave a memorable impression.
g.example: "Paris! Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred! But Paris liberated!"

g.description: Beginning and concluding sentences with repetitions to make an impact on the audience.
g.example: Who is the author of this law? Rullus. Who deprived the majority of the Roman people of their vote? Rullus. Who presided over the assemblies? Rullus.

g.description: Ending sentences with the same words or sounds to reinforce one's message.
g.example: Endlessly, the rain, the long rain, The rain.

g.description: Stacking words or ideas to create an amplifying effect, aiming to leave a memorable impression.
g.example: When they have thrown me away, a sad old flask, decrepit, dusty, dirty, abject, slimy, cracked.

g.description: In order to convince your audience, you enumerate several arguments whose accumulation is supposed to prove the conclusion presented at the end of your argument.
g.example: The defendant asserts both that he had no malicious intent, that he was not present at the crime scene, and that he therefore did not commit this crime.

g.description: Listing various elements that make up a complete idea, aiming to impress.
g.example: It was empty, clear, deep, filled with light!

g.description: Using alliterations or assonances to make one's argumentation more appealing.
g.example: Ah, what a melody those words make, like pearls of dew on morning leaves, dancing together in harmony!

g.description: Playfully altering words to achieve an expressive, often comedic effect.
g.example: Alas, he got sentenced to perpet.

g.description: Simplifying the pronunciation of certain words to make them more familiar.
g.example: Just b’tween us, ’s no need t’make a fuss—we’re all in th’same boat, right?

g.description: Using words that imitate real sounds to create an expressive, often comedic effect.
g.example: The tick-tock of the clock urged him not to waste any more time.

g.description: Creating deliberate dissonance with repetitive sounds to intrigue or amuse.
g.example: “No, there is nothing that Nanine does not honor” — Voltaire, Nanine, III, 8

g.description: Repeating similar vowel sounds to make one's argumentation more appealing.
g.example: Someone weeps their sorrow, and it's my heart!

g.description: Repeating the same group of consonants in successive words to make one's argumentation more appealing.
g.example: For whom do these serpents hiss upon your heads?

g.description: Using humour to make an argumentation more appealing, without relying on facts.
g.example: I'm not old, come on! I've simply been young longer than you have…

g.description: Displaying blatant disdain for norms and public opinion, expressing principles contrary to morality or social standards without restraint.
g.example: Why bother changing the world? After all, corruption has always worked well for those in power.

g.description: Rejecting established beliefs and values to demonstrate their lack of substance in one's argumentation.
g.example: In a world with moral foundations, your arguments would have convinced me.

g.description: Using the comedic device of one's argumentation to reveal one's bitterness toward the world's absurdity.
g.example: When my father beats me, it gets hot, so I drag myself to the window and close it to make sure he doesn't catch a draft.

g.description: Swaying an audience by engaging in mocking criticism of the subject at hand.
g.example: In our society, smartphones have become so essential that soon, we'll be born with touch-sensitive fingers.

g.description: Expressing one's actual thoughts by stating the contrary in order to gain one's audience's favor.
g.example: Shall I add a bit more mess to your room?

g.description: Feigning ignorance in order to lead the other person to reveal their presumptions or errors.
g.example: Ah, so according to you, investing in this obsolete technology will secure our future? Interesting, tell me more.

g.description: Subtly making it understood that one's statements are to be taken non-literally.
g.example: Oh, I always take criticism very seriously, especially when it comes from professionals as persuasive as my own mother.

g.description: Concealing one's mockery under a guise of seriousness to blame or amuse.
g.example: Got any drugs on you? Don't worry, officer, I'm fully stocked.

g.description: Using irony in a biting manner to ridicule or criticize.
g.example: I would agree with you, but then we'd both be wrong.

g.description: Highlighting the contrast between expectation and reality to emphasize the absurdity or malice of some situations.
g.example: After spending years criticizing social media, he became famous... thanks to a viral video on the internet.

g.description: Exaggerating certain aspects to an unreasonable extent to strengthen an argument.
g.example: This handbag is so small that even an ant would find the space limited.

g.description: Satirically imitating a serious discourse or idea to ridicule it.
g.example: Your savings plan is exactly like in Monopoly: invest in hotels on Rue de la Paix, and everything will be fine for the economy.

g.description: Inventing humorous adages to critique or mock something.
g.example: Why make it simple when you can make it complicated?

g.description: Humorously twisting expressions or quotations to enrich a speech.
g.example: In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king, but in our office, they can't even find the coffee machine.

g.description: Amplifying or distorting certain characteristics to mock or criticize something or someone.
g.example: The latest film by this director is so avant-garde that he managed to shoot the first scene after the end credits!

g.description: Winning over an audience by making a subtle and ingenious remark, often with a biting implication.
g.example: You ask me to make a witty remark on your subject, but, Sire, the king is not a subject.

g.description: Using humor to make a discourse more attractive, punctuating it with elements designed to entertain and amuse the audience.
g.example: I'm not an economics expert... but looking at these figures, I think even my grandmother would do a better job!

g.description: Making a speech more appealing by playing on words, especially on the ambiguity of their sounds or meanings.
g.example: I have never lost a game; I just ran out of time to win.

g.description: Making a discourse more appealing by using a formulation that can be understood in two different ways.
g.example: I work in show business, so I can tell you I know what it's like to work with clowns.

g.description: Swapping letters or syllables to create a hidden, often risqué, meaning.
g.example: The general arrived “on foot through China”—in French, “à pied par la Chine,” which becomes the risqué “à chier par la pine” when sounds are swapped.

g.description: Making a speech more appealing by manipulating its terms through their polysemy or homophony with other words.
g.example: In the world of finance, being 'underwater' doesn't mean you need a snorkel, but rather a good accountant!

g.description: Using absurd situations to make people laugh, without regard for logic.
g.example: Of course, if you talk to your plants, they'll grow faster. It's like giving them love as CO2!

g.description: Using an abrupt transition in speech or writing, moving from a serious or lofty subject to a trivial or ludicrous one, creating a comedic or disconcerting effect.
g.example: Our society must fight against the great injustices of the world, like hunger and poverty... and don't forget, the coffee machine is still broken.

g.description: Confusing the audience by stating a proposition that can be neither entirely true nor entirely false.
g.example: This sentence is false.

g.description: Using comic, colloquial, and vulgar terms to evoke noble and serious subjects in order to make a speech more appealing.
g.example: Our dear mayor, during his last speech, seemed more concerned about the color of his socks than the future of our city. A true clown running the show!

g.description: You deliberately complicate your discourse for amusement, avoiding a solid argument.
g.example: Invoking the transcendental exegesis of intuitive states, one might deduce that truth is an illusion... Are you following?

g.description: Using jokes within a speech to charm the audience, without relying on strong arguments.
g.example: They asked me to talk about economic statistics, but I'm afraid that if I start, several people will fall asleep right there!

g.description: Using emotionally charged or connotative language to implicitly shape the debate's framework.
g.example: In your view, can the elites responsible for this situation get us out of it?

g.description: Basing discourse on terms with strong moral connotations that already steer the conclusion.
g.example: Every good believer knows that impure thoughts come from the Devil, and must therefore be resisted at all costs.

g.description: Using different verbs to describe the same behavior depending on whether one approves of the person involved or not.
g.example: I am persistent, but my opponent is stubborn.

g.description: In order to discredit a position, you use contemptuous language against it with the aim of influencing your audience.
g.example: Is refusing to adopt these eco-friendly habits not simply confirming one's contempt for our children's future?

g.description: Resorting to vulgarism to catch the attention and provoke a reaction from the audience.
g.example: What are these so-called representatives of the people doing? Nothing! If this continues, let them go to hell!

g.description: Using nasty comments to polarize the debate and discourage nuanced reflection.
g.example: Do you prefer trusting a horde of trolls?

g.description: Deliberately using wording that will, for a targeted community, take on a meaning different from the one perceived by the general public.
g.example: Talking about 'freedom', I mean the freedom to choose our products, which is the true freedom every consumer is looking for.

g.description: Trying to exploit racism or anti-racism in order to advance a position.
g.example: You are questioning my right to this country's nationality because you are racist.

g.description: Presenting an argument so as to impress the audience or make them feel incompetent, so that they accept it without discussion.
g.example: I remind you that I have a PhD in this field, so I know better than anyone what is true or false here.

g.description: Invoking a large number of sources to lend authority to a weak argument.
g.example: Let me list all the studies that back my development project, dear investors.

g.description: Choosing formulations for their impact on the audience, independently from their explicit meaning.
g.example: The army carried out a “surgical strike” during an incursion that caused no “collateral losses.”

g.description: Employing a writing or speaking style specific to journalism, characterized by sensationalist phrasing, clichés, or trendy terms to capture public attention.
g.example: In a world exclusive, our explosive investigation reveals the scandal rocking the corridors of power, a story full of twists that could shake the highest echelons of government.

g.description: Using a brief style, often with abbreviations, ellipses, and catchy keywords, to quickly grab readers' attention without providing full details.
g.example: Govt Crisis: PM Resigns, Markets Tumble

g.description: Relying on dramatic formulas and eye-catching headlines to grab attention, often at the expense of accuracy and clarity.
g.example: Mountain Tragedy: Bus Plunge Leaves Dozens Dead!

g.description: Adopting the style of celebrity magazines: hyperbole, wordplay, and references to popular culture.
g.example: The rising star of French cinema lights up the red carpet in a breathtaking gown, outshining everyone at this glittering star-studded event.

g.description: Using hollow and pompous formulas that give an impression of depth while remaining devoid of precise content.
g.example: Considering the current situation, it is necessary to take into account each of the issues already in our possession, so that we can take the indispensable measures to respond to them appropriately.

g.description: Basing a confused and barely intelligible discourse on supposedly scholarly language meant to intimidate an audience.
g.example: The emergence of consciousness is dependent on the quantum holographic spirit reflecting within us.

g.description: Impressing with enormous numbers to conceal the lack of solidity in an argument.
g.example: 150,000 women can't be wrong for choosing this perfume.

g.description: Intentionally making information difficult to understand to hide facts.
g.example: At our last meeting, we discussed in depth and comprehensively the multi-factorial implications of our development strategy, taking into account the various possible perspectives and contingencies, as well as the likely ramifications of each possible scenario.

g.description: Presenting theoretical knowledge in a manner that intentionally makes it difficult to understand, either to limit its dissemination or to evade criticism.
g.example: The interpretation of phenomenological data requires an in-depth hermeneutic understanding, which transcends simple empirical analysis and is part of a non-reductive epistemological approach.

g.description: Using deliberately complex terms intended to intimidate an audience.
g.example: All this is yet another consequence of the quantum field.

g.description: You make your argument seem more serious by using complex scientific jargon, even though such terms are unnecessary.
g.example: In accordance with the stipulations set forth in section 1357 of the Civil Code, the debtor irrevocably commits to fulfilling their contractual obligations within the specified timeframe, subject to the suspensive conditions outlined in paragraphs 3 and 4.

g.description: Employing complex and pompous administrative language to create an impression of officialdom and authority.
g.example: Within the framework of applying the statutory provisions outlined in the internal regulations, a procedure for reassessing existing protocols will be implemented in accordance with established institutional standards.

g.description: Employing deliberately vague, complex, and ambiguous language characteristic of Federal Reserve Board chairs to prevent overreactions to one's statements.
g.example: The members of the Board of Governors and the Reserve Bank presidents foresee an implicit strengthening of activity after the current rebalancing is over, although the central tendency of their individual forecasts for real GDP still shows a substantial slowdown, on balance, for the year as a whole.

g.description: Employing a formal, specialized, and often complex language typical of academic settings, which can make one's speech inaccessible to the uninitiated.
g.example: In this research, we posit that the current epistemological paradigms need dialectical reassessment to fully understand the ontological implications of the phenomena observed.

g.description: Giving an argument an air of seriousness by using complex words from scientific jargon which are not necessary.
g.example: Using cutting-edge nanotechnology, we can optimize the quantum energy flow in our systems.

g.description: You use terms specific to the corporate and management world that make your argument harder to understand.
g.example: We will only advance by capitalizing on this leverage.

g.description: Utilizing an overabundance of acronyms and specialized jargon to display expertise and bewildering those unfamiliar with the terms.
g.example: In CGI programming, a WYSIWYG interface doesn't handle PHP or CSS very well. If you enroll in my coaching program, I'll show you how to make a website.

g.description: You use Latin expressions to intimidate your audience.
g.example: As the legal adage states 'Nemo auditur propriam turpitudinem allegans'. Your fault is therefore unforgivable.

g.description: Using too many words to drown out the main point or make the message less clear.
g.example: In order to optimize our ability to achieve the strategic objectives set for the next quarter, it is imperative to reconsider our operational paradigms and reassess potential synergies between the various departments in order to maximize the overall efficiency of our organization.

g.description: Using striking clichés to short-circuit critical thinking or avoid an argued debate.
g.example: We must also apply a zero-tolerance policy to children, because he who steals an egg will steal an ox.

g.description: Presenting an argument in a carefully crafted drama in order to make it more attractive.
g.example: The president, after visiting the scene of the tragedy, met with the bereaved families, then stated that he would meet with union representatives.

g.description: Using as evidence a well-known wise saying, as if that is proven, or as if it has no exceptions.
g.example: Every job deserves a wage, and it's high time for us to reap the fruits of our patiently ripened efforts.

g.description: Slipping a catchy phrase into a public speech to make an impression and convince one's audience.
g.example: Even when I say nothing, it makes noise.

g.description: Using a slogan for its concision and efficacy to support one's argument.
g.example: Our debt is your freedom!

g.description: Defining terms in a biased way to steer the debate in one's favor.
g.example: This man is an atheist, someone who has not been touched by the grace of God.

g.description: Proving a proposition with an argumentation that takes it for granted.
g.example: Owning a cat is better than owning a dog, because cats make better pets.

g.description: Asking a question that subtly assumes a false or controversial premise.
g.example: Have you stopped tormenting your dog?

g.description: Pretending to offer an alternative, whereas its terms lead to essentially similar results.
g.example: Heads I win, tails you lose.

g.description: Asking the interlocutor to answer several complex questions at once.
g.example: Do you agree that cars should be both safer and faster?

g.description: Asking a question that does not expect an answer, as if the answer were obvious.
g.example: Do I need to remind you how much better off we would all be without these extra taxes?

g.description: The arguments used fail to provide adequate support for the conclusion.
Drawing conclusions which exceed what available evidence permits.
g.example: He's lying because he blushes!

g.description: Complicating one's reasoning excessively instead of seeking simplicity.
g.example: Where did my keys go? Surely someone has stolen them. It's a conspiracy to drive me insane.

g.description: Attributing meaning to perceived connections or patterns between seemingly unrelated things.
g.example: There were three power outages the week I moved in. It's a sign I should not stay in this city.

g.description: Perceiving patterns or trends in random or unrelated data, creating a false impression of correlation.
g.example: Look at this sequence of numbers, there must be a secret pattern behind it!

g.description: Perceiving a familiar pattern where none exists.
g.example: That stain on my coffee this morning resembled a smiling face; I'm convinced it portends good luck for the day.

g.description: Granting more rationality than necessary to animal behaviour, tthus risking to slip into anthropomorphic thinking.
g.example: Whenever my cat brings me a dead mouse, it demonstrates that he recognizes the value of labor and wishes to share it with me, feeling part of our household.

g.description: Attributing actions or intentions to natural elements or inanimate objects as though they were living beings.
g.example: Earthquakes are the Earth's way of signaling to us that we abuse it. It's as if the planet is telling us to change our harmful behaviors.

g.description: Attributing human feelings to inanimate things, as if they could experience emotions.
g.example: This abandoned car, sitting for months on the street, looks sad and neglected.

g.description: Interpreting one's interlocutor's words in the least favorable or least reasonable way possible.
g.example: If you start talking about cutting expenses, it clearly means we will have to fight for our salaries and jobs.

g.description: Attributing easily refutable claims to the opposing party, then disproving them easily.
g.example: Ah, so according to you, we should spend all our days digging through trash to sort out the waste? That's no way to live!

g.description: Explaining bad choices by causes worse and more complex than others. For example, by malice instead of error.
g.example: If mistakes were made in this project, it must be because competitors infiltrated the company to make us fail.

g.description: You reject a position by assuming that its author's reasoning or intentions are questionable, rather than examining the argument itself.
g.example: This man has every interest in selling me his car. His description of the vehicle is necessarily lacking in objectivity, so it would be better not to buy it.

g.description: Challenging a thesis by calling into question the motives of its proposer.
g.example: When the mayor suggested moving the sports field closer to downtown, everyone said it was just to make access easier for his own family.

g.description: Challenging an argumentation by showing the psychological reasons for its proponents to develop it.
g.example: You don't like this movie just because you are jealous of the main actress.

g.description: Without judging whether it is valid, you dismiss any proposition made by a woman.
g.example: This theory is typical of speeches given by women, full of emotions but lacking in logic.

g.description: Accusing one's opponent of being angry or holding their beliefs for anger-related reasons, which purportedly disproves their argument or diminishes its weight.
g.example: The candidate opposes the highway construction, but since he rages every time progress is mentioned, his arguments are surely flawed.

g.description: Discrediting a proposal by suggesting a hidden agenda on the part of its author.
g.example: She may propose ideas to reduce pollution, but I believe it's solely to gain ecological credibility among her voters.

g.description: Considering every defense as proof of guilt.
g.example: If you're coming up with so many excuses, it's because you've surely got something to hide.

g.description: Criticizing the editorial intent of the media in which an argumentation is published rather than the argumentation itself.
g.example: This news channel is known for its sensationalism. If they're covering this corruption story, it's probably to boost their ratings rather than because the case is real.

g.description: Discarding a proposal because it benefits its proponents, whithout considering its soundness.
g.example: The congressman proposes an increase in education funding because his wife runs a school. Regardless of his arguments, it's surely for his own benefit and not in the interest of the children.

g.description: You dismiss a proposal without examining its merits, on the grounds that it financially benefits its author.
g.example: No matter what they tell us, it's all to sell more products and enrich their shareholders. Spare me that talk.

g.description: Arguing that a conclusion is false because its proof involves a fallacy.
g.example: He told me to take the road that goes down on the right; but that road goes uphill. Let's take the left instead.

g.description: Concluding that a phenomenon does not exist merely because the theoretical explanation offered is incorrect or inadequate.
g.example: They claim climate change is caused by human activities, but their predictive model has flaws. Therefore, climate change must not be real.

g.description: Approaching complex questions as if they were simple games or easily solvable problems, often using simplistic models or neglecting the real complexity.
g.example: Running a business isn't that different from playing a strategy video game. Just choose the right options and watch the growth happen.

g.description: Asserting a statement which may be clear and even true but which implies that something else is true or false when it isn't.
g.example: Our revolutionary diet promises you'll lose five pounds in a week, coupled with our slimming plan.

g.description: Analyzing or interpreting events or situations using inappropriate temporal or spatial perspectives, applying modern concepts to historical periods, or erroneously transferring ideas from one culture or geographical context to another.
g.example: The citizens of ancient Rome must have surely aspired to the same democratic values we hold today.

g.description: Relying on terms or concepts from the past that are no longer valid or applicable in the present context.
g.example: Look at our valiant ancestors and their solid morals. Yet, today, people are corrupted and decadent.

g.description: Making a claim about the present meaning of a word on the exclusive basis of its etymology.
g.example: I'm an 'athlete' in the etymological sense of the word; I 'suffer' at work, it has nothing to do with sports.

g.description: In analyzing a localized fact, judging the use of ideas and concepts unknown in the area concerned.
g.example: The social problems of this isolated rural community are certainly due to its lack of Internet access.

g.description: Judging people for their application of concepts or perspectives during periods of time when they were not in use.
g.example: The Romans understood the need to use materials and energy sustainably to preserve their environment.

g.description: Analyzing past events with modern-day ideas and perspectives, which were unthinkable at that time.
g.example: It's unthinkable that Joan of Arc didn't advocate for women's rights, considering she was so progressive for her time.

g.description: Projecting anachronistic or inappropriate visions based on one's own experience onto a period or situation.
g.example: Prehistoric humans enjoyed discussing politics at the fireside.

g.description: Thinking, after an event, that its outcome had been foreseen or anticipated.
g.example: I knew from the start that this project was doomed. There was never any doubt about it.

g.description: Claiming that an event was predicted a posteriori, though the prediction at the time was obscure and not understood.
g.example: After the accident, it was clear that the warning signs were there. If only we had known how to interpret them correctly...

g.description: Inferring that because something happened under some circumstances, it was therefore bound to happen due to those circumstance.
g.example: From the moment Julius Caesar declared himself emperor, his assassination was inevitable.

g.description: Criticizing a past decision in the light of subsequent facts, as if its author had the same information at the time as is available today.
g.example: The leaders of the 1920s were enjoying the Roaring Twenties. They should have foreseen the crash of 1929.

g.description: Ignoring the complexity of a situation by offering an overly simplified explanation that leaves out essential elements.
g.example: Paying taxes to help others? That's just theft on a national scale.

g.description: Appealing to the immediate feelings, impressions rather than reason to make a concept easier to grasp for the audience.
g.example: Feel this skin cream, it's pure happiness. It has to work!

g.description: Evaluating real scenarios from an idealized perspective, ignoring flaws and motivations.
g.example: To solve unemployment, there is no mystery: people need to work more.

g.description: Focusing on the most accessible or obvious areas to seek answers or solutions, potentially ignoring more significant but less obvious or more challenging to examine aspects.
g.example: We analyzed the sales data from the last three months because it was readily available, even though it may not reflect the long-term trends that could be more relevant to our market strategy.

g.description: Placing undue importance on numbers and metrics, dismissing critical elements that are not quantifiable.
g.example: This hotel has more stars than the others. It must necessarily be the most pleasant in the city.

g.description: Believing that a single experiment can provide absolute proof of a complex theory.
g.example: Since our company launched this product, we've been profitable, so our business strategy must be flawless.

g.description: Basing one's arguments on received ideas without examining them critically.
g.example: Let your father open that jar of pickles, it's a man's job.

g.description: You judge certain facts to be true or false based on your moral principles rather than on objective evidence.
g.example: These are innocent children. They would not cause so much trouble for their parents.

g.description: Discriminating or marginalizing on the basis of disability, considering it a valid argument.
g.example: I'd rather not give him major responsibilities; with his disability, he couldn't keep up with us.

g.description: Judging an action solely on the basis of its legality.
g.example: So what if I cheated on my wife? It's not like being unfaithful is a crime!

g.description: Confusing what is legal with what is desirable.
g.example: I'm exercising my constitutional right by coming to protest armed in front of your house.

g.description: You judge the validity of an idea based on the wealth of the person proposing it.
g.example: You should definitely listen to Mark—he's a millionaire! Surely, if anyone knows what's best, it would be him.

g.description: You believe an idea is right because the person defending it is poor.
g.example: He comes from a modest background and worked hard for his money, so his views on our country's economy should be respected more than those of inherited wealth.

g.description: Concluding that a statement is correct because the speaker is rich
g.example: If he were wrong, he wouldn't have reached where he is today.

g.description: Judging arguments on their style rather than their substance, considering that good style is sign of soundness.
g.example: Look how brilliantly this idea is presented, with such elegance and flair! It must be the truth.

g.description: Judging that something is so perfect that it must have been designed by a superior, dvine entity, thus proving the xistence of the latter.
g.example: Looking at the complexity of the human eye, it's clear that it must have been designed by some divine being. Nature alone couldn't achieve this level of complexity.

g.description: Judging that something is so beautiful that it must have been designed by a superior, dvine entity, thus proving the existence of the latter.
g.example: See how exquisite this flower is, its delicate form and perfect symmetry. Only a divine hand could craft such beauty.

g.description: Presenting one's arguments as necessarily valid because they seem morally superior.
g.example: This man couldn't have made such a mistake. His morality and public behavior speak for themselves.

g.description: Rejecting or diverting arguments for fear they may cause social or institutional offense.
g.example: Do not look for explanations in terms of beliefs; religion is a matter of conscience and therefore should never be criticized.

g.description: Rejecting arguments on grounds of them being expressed in a manner which does not conform to rules of etiquette.
g.example: I don't pay attention to his words as he didn't even shake my hand when greeting me. It's a clear sign of disrespect.

g.description: Rejecting arguments on grounds of them being blasphemous
g.example: This author should not be published, his blasphemous writings could offend our community.

g.description: Evaluating a discourse according to the social class from which its author comes.
g.example: He doesn't seem like an expert; he comes from a working-class neighborhood.

g.description: Claiming that an assertion is true because it goes against the opinion of the majority.
g.example: Why read those boring email chains that everyone reads? You know you're above that.

g.description: Granting more weight to arguments from individuals considered intellectual elites, over others.
g.example: His argumentation is more credible because he comes from the most prestigious university.

g.description: Arguing that an idea or proposition is good, valid, or true solely because it is newer.
g.example: This technology is the latest, it must be the best option. Why bother with older models?

g.description: Believing an idea is superior merely because it is newer.
g.example: The party introduced unprecedented reforms this year, undeniable proof that its proposal is the wisest for the future.

g.description: Arguing on the basis of assumptions that require an act of faith rather than on rational evidence.
g.example: Just have faith and you'll see that my choice is correct. Don't try to analyze it with your cold logic.

g.description: Arguing that evidence will someday be discovered which will then support the point.
g.example: We can't dismiss this theory right now, as the evidence might be found in the future.

g.description: Believing that something is better simply because it is natural, without considering other important factors.
g.example: Humans have always eaten meat; therefore, being vegetarian is considered against nature.

g.description: Grounding one's argumentation on the assumption that anything natural is good, or that anything non-natural is bad.
g.example: It's natural for men, like most animals, to dominate because they are stronger and more violent.

g.description: Assuming that Man is originally good and that civilisation corrupts him.
g.example: In all primitive societies, people live in harmony with nature. That's why I refuse to live in an apartment and instead decided to move into a cabin in the forest.

g.description: You systematically reject all technological progress, ignoring the benefits it can bring.
g.example: I never use a microwave for cooking. Food becomes toxic due to electromagnetic waves, which is well-known, just like cell phones.

g.description: Dishonestly using ecological arguments to support a position.
g.example: You should buy this multi-surface cleaner; it's made with 95% natural ingredients, therefore it supports the environment.

g.description: Supporting an opinion or practice on the basis of it being traditional.
g.example: Bullfighting has always existed in France; it would therefore be foolish to ban this practice in our country.

g.description: Granting value to an argument because it comes from the alledged wisdom of ancient times.
g.example: As Confucius said in the third century, an apple a day keeps the doctor away.

g.description: Refusing ideas because they come from elsewhere than the group involved in the debate.
g.example: This educational program from abroad cannot address our teaching methods' needs.

g.description: Arguing that because an event has never occurred before, it cannot happen in the future.
g.example: No building of this kind has ever withstood an earthquake of this magnitude. Therefore, it is impossible for it to remain standing after such an event.

g.description: Grounding the validity of a proposition on the fact that many or most people agree with it.
g.example: Most kids want fries every day at the cafeteria; therefore, that's what they should be served.

g.description: Choosing to conform to a norm because one mistakenly believes that the majority approves of it.
g.example: No one in the village has ever spoken ill of the hideous statue in the central square. So it must belong here.

g.description: Basing the degree of truth of a proposition on the number of people who support it.
g.example: Everyone on social media is talking about this movie, so it must be good. I'm going to buy a ticket for the next showing.

g.description: Using peer-pressure to force someone to agree with an idea they know is wrong.
g.example: Every morning, in the open space, all colleagues drink coffee together; you should join this ritual to integrate better.

g.description: Using nationalist symbols or patriotic appeals as a means to substantiate an argument.
g.example: Real patriots are in this room to celebrate our athletes' victories.

g.description: Asserting the truth of a proposition because many people repeat it.
g.example: Haven't you heard that there are crocodiles in the city's sewers?

g.description: Assuming that because something is a practice, it ought to be the practice.
g.example: Since it's a custom in our village to dance around the fire each solstice, it's against our ancestors not to participate.

g.description: Believing that a claim is true solely because an authority supports it, without examining the facts.
g.example: I'm feeling hot but I'll keep my coat on because Mum said it was cold today.

g.description: Claiming authority on a subject outside one's field of expertise.
g.example: Obviously, as a fashion blogger, I can assert that this diet is the most effective. There's no need to be a nutritionist to recognize good food choices.

g.description: Quoting oneself as authoritative source to support one's argument.
g.example: As I've often emphasized in my recent talks, these personal development methods are flawless.

g.description: Creating a deity similar to oneself, and using this persona as an authority to support one's arguments.
g.example: Certainly, our beliefs are pure and just, which is why God definitely sides with us in this struggle.

g.description: You pick from your beliefs only what supports your argument, while ignoring the rest.
g.example: Of course, I attend church services during Christmas even though I'm not religious; it's tradition, after all.

g.description: Using unspecified authoritative sources as evidence for a claim.
g.example: Many experts state that this is the most effective treatment.

g.description: Expressing personal opinions while claiming to be totally impartial.
g.example: I don't want to meddle in something that is none of my business, and I'm not knowledgeable about the issue you disagree on, but I think you should listen to what your friend is trying to tell you.

g.description: To support a claim by citing an expert who lacks the relevant expertise.
g.example: I avoid pencils because John Terry, a world-renowned sailor, claims they're major contributors to global warming.

g.description: Presenting an unqualified person or institution as a source of credible information.
g.example: This astrophysicist, who won a televised cooking contest, now hosts her own gastronomy show; her opinion on best culinary practices would therefore be a guarantee of quality.

g.description: Creating a fake debate by placing a scientific position and a pseudoscientific position on the same level, and claiming that controversy exists where there is consensus.
g.example: Some say the earth is round, others say it's flat; the truth must lie somewhere in between.

g.description: Citing large numbers of seeming experts to argue that there is no scientific consensus on a topic.
g.example: 31,487 Americans with a science degree signed a petition saying humans aren't disrupting climate.

g.description: Citing as a reference an authority whose title is fictitious.
g.example: Professor BAYO is a powerful marabout in Paris whose effectiveness is no longer to be proven.

g.description: You support your argument with sources that are not recognized as authorities in the relevant field, hoping that no one will check.
g.example: It is proven that UFOs visit our planet: many articles and testimonials available online attest to it.

g.description: Grounding the validity of a proposition on the basis that a reputable, respected person or entity supports it.
g.example: This cake must be excellent since it was invented by Albert Einstein.

g.description: Deterring any contradiction of an argument by calling the former immodest in front of an autority supporting the latter.
g.example: Kepler said that rejecting astrology without understanding it is three-dimensional madness. Remember it's Kepler speaking, not just anybody!

g.description: Granting value to someone's claims on the basis of his or her achievements in the field being debated.
g.example: Your opinion on music will interest me when you've released an album!

g.description: Using the celebrity of supporters of an argument to strengthen it.
g.example: I always drink this brand of soda because my favorite celebrity endorses it.

g.description: Using a drastic change in one's opinion as proof that his or her latest belief is truth.
g.example: Since I changed my diet, I've felt much better. If you're feeling bad, you should try it too—it really changes everything.

g.description: Judging a task to be feasible by comparing it to the feat of sending humans to the Moon, without considering essential differences.
g.example: If we can put a man on the Moon, surely we can find a cure for every type of cancer.

g.description: Valuing an argument solely because it is supported by existing authorities.
g.example: The CEO himself requested this new software, so don't tell me you've found bugs in it.

g.description: Accusing one's detractors of betraying one's trust, thereby avoiding having to answer their arguments.
g.example: Do you trust me or not? I don't need to justify myself. If I say it's good, then it must be.

g.description: Citing an authority's opinion on an idea as if that authority's support was the only evidence necessary to uphold said idea
g.example: This concept must be true because it is taught by Professor X, who is a leading authority in his field.

g.description: Treating someone's confidence in an assertion as proof of its validity.
g.example: Trust me on this project. I believe in it wholeheartedly.

g.description: Asserting that a proposition is true solely because a supposedly absolute authority supports it.
g.example: The Pope, being the Pope, can never be wrong.

g.description: Refusing to justify one's claims, claiming that one's position of authority is enough to validate them.
g.example: As your senior, I don't have to explain why my decisions are the best for the family.

g.description: Improvising unfounded justifications in the face of valid objections in order to escape criticism.
g.example: If we don't see extraterrestrials, it's because they give amnesia to everyone who sees them.

g.description: Using any fabricated, even absurd argument, in a desperate attempt to defend an entirely baseless claim.
g.example: But if I tell you that the moon is made of cheese. My astronaut friend back from his last space mission confessed it tasted like Cheddar.

g.description: To invent an unverifiable narrative to explain something and support one's claim.
g.example: Zebras have stripes because, in ancient times, this allowed them to hide from predators by blending in with the tall grasses.

g.description: In the face of contradictory evidence, established beliefs do not change but actually get stronger.
g.example: The more I see all these doctors on TV explaining why we need to wear masks, the more I'm convinced that not wearing one is the right choice.

g.description: Rejecting new evidence or new knowledge because it contradicts established norms, beliefs or paradigms.
g.example: How can we think that doctors' hands might transmit disease? It's absurd to request them to wash their hands.

g.description: Providing insincere justifications to make a claim acceptable, without discussing its validity.
g.example: If I didn't pass the exam, it's just because the teacher hates me.

g.description: Saving a generalization from a counterexample by changing its definition in order to exclude that counterexample.
g.example: - All Scots are redheads. - Angus is Scots but isn't a redhead. - Then he isn't a true Scotsman.

g.description: Offering a n unlikely hypothesis as the correct explanation without first ruling out more mundane explanations.
g.example: This mistake ruined my presentation. I'm sure you did it on purpose to sabotage it!

g.description: To mention information that one, according to one's own statements, should not possess.
g.example: I wasn't there, so I'm sure you used that opportunity to speak ill of me.

g.description: Creating a narrative that ties unrelated elements, falsely implying their connection.
g.example: Imagine buying this product leads you to a life of luxury and success. Doesn't that prove it will change your life?

g.description: Applying the same solution to various problems without taking the specific context into account.
g.example: No matter the complexity of your car's malfunction, just hammer the engine. This fixes all my mechanical problems, so it should work for you too.

g.description: Considering that what is yet unexplained is impossible to ever explain.
g.example: Don't bother trying to find out why it happened. Some things are just inexplicable.

g.description: Invoking the intervention of some powerful invisible entity to explain the unexplainable.
g.example: But why did the candidate I liked discredit himself so badly? Another CIA operation!

g.description: Invoking a divine agent to fill the explanatory gaps of a theory.
g.example: This unexpected recovery can only be the work of a divine intervention.

g.description: Having every level of a line of reasoning rest on an error, leading to equally erroneous conclusions.
g.example: Every natural disaster is a new sign of God's wrath due to your stubbornness in not listening to me.

g.description: Treating a habit, an impression, or an example as if it were evidence.
g.example: I agree that your calculation is correct. But your reasoning is insignificant: this detail changes nothing about the underlying issue. — Rejection of a correct argument based on its perceived importance, not its validity.

g.description: Confusing subjective experience of reality with the essence of that which is being observed.
g.example: I find children terrifying; you deserve a lot of credit for raising yours.

g.description: Considering something to be true because one feels it strongly, even in the absence of evidence.
g.example: I feel like a failure, so I must truly be one.

g.description: Claiming that intuition or emotion are divine truth detectors.
g.example: This candidate doesn't inspire confidence in me, hence they must not be competent to represent us.

g.description: To believe that one's personal way of viewing the world reflects the exact nature of reality.
g.example: In these times of great uncertainty for our company, it seems inconceivable to me that you could refuse this pay cut.

g.description: Justifying choices, methods or actions on grounds that they are common practice.
g.example: Everyone speeds; it shouldn't be penalized.

g.description: Asserting that an idea is common sense in order to impose it without proof, leveraging the opponent's fear of being bizarre.
g.example: It just makes sense not to swim right after eating. Why challenge this popular rule with scientific studies?

g.description: Repeating assertions consistent with an idea within a community in order to convince its members despite lack of evidence.
g.example: Every year at Christmas, we are reminded how unique our family is and that we should be wary of outsiders. Everyone gets the message now.

g.description: Seeking the approval of a scientific community for an unverified idea in order to create a false consensus.
g.example: My theory on the benefits of light therapy was overwhelmingly supported at the last conference. No further evidence needed, the community is persuaded.

g.description: Thinking that by being "like everyone else", one's argument is necessarily valid.
g.example: I'm an ordinary citizen, and I find this measure excessive; hence it's clearly unsuitable.

g.description: Thinking that if something is normal or average, that automatically makes it correct or acceptable.
g.example: 90% of those surveyed use their smartphones right after waking up. It must be the ideal way to start the day.

g.description: Presupposing that everyone shares one's beliefs without them being questioned.
g.example: I'm sure everyone in my neighborhood thinks this road is unnecessary. There's no doubt the local government should abandon it.

g.description: Calling upon a hypothetical mass of citizens that support a proposition, but have not publicly expressed this in any tangible way.
g.example: I am only saying out loud what many people think quietly.

g.description: Basing an argument on an isolated event that is not enough to demonstrate a general rule.
g.example: I had good grades in mathematics after drinking blackcurrant juice; thus, blackcurrant juice makes one strong in mathematics.

g.description: Making claims about reality on the basis of evidence drawn from fictional works.
g.example: In my science-fiction novel, humanity creates a shield against pollution by using the energy of shooting stars. If only our government could do the same to save the planet!

g.description: Instead of relying on objective definitions, asserting one's individual, subjective and arbitrary judgement.
g.example: I may not have concrete evidence, but I just feel this political decision is harmful.
g.text: I know it when I see it

g.description: Invoking a friend within a group in order to fend off accusations of prejudice against that group.
g.example: I'm not antisemitic; I have a Jewish friend.

g.description: Assuming that something which helped one (usually the speaker) will help anyone.
g.example: The uniform helped me get my life back on track. Everyone should therefore go through the military.

g.description: Grounding the validity of an argument on the absence of contrary evidence rather than on supporting evidence.
g.example: I play my music loud and my neighbor never complains, so they must enjoy my taste in music.

g.description: Asserting the accuracy of a theory on the basis of its correct prediction on one or several specific, lucky cases.
g.example: The station clock has been stopped for months, but it sometimes shows the exact time; this proves that it works intermittently.

g.description: Arguing on the basis of an assumption which is not actually true.
g.example: If Caesar had had tanks, Rome would never have fallen.

g.description: Basing an argument on reported and therefore unverifiable statements.
g.example: Many people have told me that the mayor is corrupt. He cannot be trusted.

g.description: Using assertions that contribute nothing to building a convincing argument.
g.example: There is no point in my continuing my studies, because the future is uncertain.

g.description: Basing arguments on ready-made expressions as if they constituted solid evidence.
g.example: All work deserves pay; so it is high time for us to reap the fruits of our efforts.

g.description: Stating platitudes in order to lull one's audience into lowering its guard.
g.example: Don't worry about the economic crisis, old sport. As they say, every cloud has a silver lining!

g.description: Stating a truth so obvious that it supports no argument.
g.example: If I haven't heard from my son, it's because he has nothing to tell me.

g.description: Arguing that the absurdity of something is the main reason to believe it.
g.example: Why do I carry an umbrella in mid-summer with the sun shining bright? Because it's so unlikely to rain today, that it must surely happen.

g.description: Adapting a well-known quote to the context of an argumentation.
g.example: I always say, you don't change a winning team. Why try anything else?

g.description: Rejecting a speculative argument by invoking the cliché that theory never stands up in practice.
g.example: Of course, I didn't consider that theory you taught us. We all know that in the real world, things never happen as they do in books!

g.description: Invalidating a counterexample to one's thesis outright by invoking the cliché of the exception that proves the rule.
g.example: I succeeded without that degree, but I'm the exception that confirms the rule. You definitely need to get yours.

g.description: Asking for a claim to be accepted without providing any reason or logical explanation.
g.example: You can believe me when I say that our product is superior to every other product on the market.

g.description: Making causal connections between two events on the basis of superstition rather than logic or evidence.
g.example: Thanks to the church's decision it rained.

g.description: Basing one's opinions and actions on the magical or mystical interpretation of certain phenomena.
g.example: If we don't perform this ceremony during the eclipse, then the demons will return.

g.description: Asserting that a conclusion or proposition must be accepted because it is the will of God or the will of the gods.
g.example: Because it's God's will, we must do it.

g.description: Defending one's point of view by insisting on the need to act, even without evidence that the proposed action is the right one.
g.example: We can't let the mice keep multiplying in the cellar. So we have to flood it.

g.description: Claiming that an action is desirable simply because something must be done, without showing that it is actually appropriate.
g.example: To improve our situation, change is needed. We are making changes, hence we are improving the situation.

g.description: Judging a proposition to be true solely because it has not been proven false, or false because it has not been proven true.
g.example: God doesn't exist since his existence has not been proven.

g.description: Claiming to know everything about a subject, asserting general truths that should nevertheless be discussed.
g.example: In matters of astronomy, I know what I'm talking about, so do not question my theories about black holes.

g.description: Claiming to provide proof or evidence, when in reality, none is actually presented.
g.example: Everybody claims that this policy is ineffective because they always see discussions about its failures on TV.

g.description: Considering one's explanation to be correct on the pretext that all those considered were false, thus ignoring other hypotheses not yet mentioned.
g.example: It must be a conspiracy; after eliminating all other scenarios, it's the only explanation left.

g.description: Dismissing a statement or proposition summarily, without giving any explanation or evidence.
g.example: What you claim cannot be true because that just sounds completely ridiculous.

g.description: Considering that an idea too complex for oneself is also too complex for everyone, thereby justifying one's own speculations.
g.example: Quantum physics is so complex that no one can truly claim to understand the universe.

g.description: Using the lack of facts contradicting a theory as proof of the theory
g.example: Since we haven't captured any aliens to prove their existence yet, this proves they are advanced enough to evade our detection.

g.description: Rejecting a hypothesis or fact on the grounds that it seems incomprehensible.
g.example: I refuse to accept the Big Bang theory because it is too complex to be credible.

g.description: Refusing to believe a proposition simply because it would be surprising if it were true.
g.example: Of course I don't believe the Earth is round; I've climbed the highest mountain and the horizon was as flat as the palm of my hand.

g.description: Attributing what one cannot understand to divine intervention.
g.example: It is so wonderful that only God could have done it.

g.description: Claiming a subject is too mysterious to be understood or explained.
g.example: Faced with the complexities of the universe, I've always said it's pointless to seek explanations; it must be something beyond our understanding.

g.description: Supporting a dubious claim by asserting that science does not have all the answers.
g.example: Since science can't explain the disappearance of unicorns, they must have existed.

g.description: Voluntarily avoiding knowledge of what could undermine one's argumentative position.
g.example: I'd rather you didn't tell me what they did next: it might contradict what I think.

g.description: Refusing to discuss facts that could invalidate one's argument.
g.example: We don't need to discuss this societal issue; it has always been this way and will stay the same.

g.description: Persisting in an erroneous belief despite solid evidence to the contrary.
g.example: Only aliens could have built these flying saucers.

g.description: Refusing to consider any evidence that contradicts one's beliefs, no matter how strong it is.
g.example: No matter how many studies show the medical treatment's effectiveness, I still believe only this precious stone can heal my illness because I've decided it's so.
